"""Compare a trained AlphaZero model with the known solution of 6x6 Othello.

Perfect play from the standard start ends 16-20 (White wins by 4; Feinstein 1993).
We (1) read the value head's prediction for the start position and (2) let the
model play itself from the start with greedy MCTS at several search budgets.

  python scripts/solved_check.py results/alphazero/seed1
"""
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from othello.env import OthelloEnv  # noqa: E402
from othello.rl.alphazero.mcts import Evaluator  # noqa: E402
from othello.rl.alphazero.selfplay import AZAgent, build_net  # noqa: E402


def main(run_dir, budgets=(64, 200, 800), seeds=(0, 1, 2)):
    d = Path(run_dir)
    cfg = json.loads((d / "config.json").read_text())
    env = OthelloEnv(cfg["board_size"])
    net = build_net(env.n, cfg)
    net.load_state_dict(torch.load(d / "model.pt", map_location="cpu"))
    net.eval()
    s0 = env.initial_state()
    _, v = Evaluator(env, net)([s0])
    out = {"model": str(d.relative_to(ROOT)), "perfect_play": {"black": 16, "white": 20},
           "start_value_black": v[0], "games": []}
    print("value head at start (Black's view):", round(v[0], 3))
    for sims in budgets:
        for seed in seeds:
            black = AZAgent(env, net, sims=sims, seed=seed)
            white = AZAgent(env, net, sims=sims, seed=seed + 100)
            s, moves = s0, []
            while not env.is_terminal(s):
                m = (black if s.player == 0 else white).act(s)
                moves.append(env.action_name(m))
                s = env.step(s, m)
            b, w = env.counts(s)
            out["games"].append({"sims": sims, "seed": seed, "black": b, "white": w, "moves": moves})
            print(sims, seed, f"{b}-{w}", " ".join(moves))
    (d.parent / "solved_check.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1])

    key = f"policy_only/{opp}" if label == "AlphaZero (net only)" else opp

def _games_to(curves, thr, col="score"):
    """Mean over seeds of the first evaluated game count at which `col` >= thr ('--' if any seed never does)."""
    firsts = []
    for cv in curves:
        hit = [float(r["games"]) for r in cv if float(r[col]) >= thr and float(r["games"]) > 0]
        if not hit:
            return None
        firsts.append(hit[0])
    return sum(firsts) / len(firsts)

\section{Next Steps}
\label{sec:next}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Self-play learning.} Self-play PPO, Double DQN with an opponent
        pool of past checkpoints, and an AlphaZero-style agent (residual
        policy--value network, MCTS, symmetry augmentation) on \bx{6}. We
        compare them on final strength, sample efficiency, wall-clock time and
        stability across seeds, and check them against the solved \bx{6} result. The
        strongest of these becomes the project's final model,
        \textit{Oroletto}, and is playable with
        \texttt{othello --play oroletto}.
  \item \textbf{Architecture and search-budget sweep.} Depth, width, input
        planes, head design and MCTS simulations, varied one at a time and
        summarised as a strength-versus-compute Pareto plot.
  \item \textbf{Scaling to \bx{8}.} Re-tune the rule-based bots for \bx{8}
        (Table~\ref{tab:gate} shows the \bx{6} weights are weaker there) and
        train the selected configuration. Optionally, play matches against the
        Edax engine.
  \item \textbf{One network for every board size.} Test zero-shot transfer,
        then train a fully convolutional, globally pooled network on mixed
        board sizes and compare it with a small-to-large curriculum. The result
        is reported as a train-size $\times$ test-size win-rate matrix.
\end{itemize}

%======================================================================
\section{Self-Play Methods}
\label{sec:selfplay}

Every method in \S\ref{sec:classical} learned by playing the heuristic bot, so
it could at best learn to beat \emph{that} bot. In \emph{self-play} the learner
plays against itself, or against frozen copies of its earlier selves. The
opponent therefore improves as the learner does, and no hand-written opponent
is needed during training. This section compares three self-play methods on
\bx{6}. The evaluation is unchanged: the same three rule-based bots, openings
and protocol as before. The heuristic bot is now used \emph{only} for
evaluation and is never trained against. The strongest agent becomes the
project's final model, \textit{Oroletto}.

\subsection{The methods}

\paragraph{DQN+ (Double DQN with an opponent pool).} The DQN of
\S\ref{sec:classical} with two changes. First, the bootstrap target is a
\emph{Double DQN} target \cite{vanhasselt2016},
$r + \gamma\,Q_{\theta^-}\!\big(s',\arg\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s',a')\big)$: the online
network picks the next action and the target network scores it. This removes
the systematic over-estimation that comes from taking a max over noisy
estimates. Second, the opponent is drawn from an \emph{opponent pool}. Every
5{,}000 games a frozen snapshot of the learner joins the pool (at most 20 kept),
and each training game is played against the live learner with probability
$\tfrac12$, otherwise against a random snapshot. Playing past selves protects
against \emph{strategy cycling}, where a learner that only ever plays its latest
self forgets how to beat strategies it has already moved past.

\paragraph{Self-play PPO.} Proximal Policy Optimisation \cite{schulman2017} learns
a policy $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ and a value $V_\theta(s)$ directly. Here an MLP
with a shared trunk, a masked softmax over legal moves and a $\tanh$ value head
is used. Experience is collected from complete games, 4{,}096 learner decisions
per update, with advantages $\hat A_t$ from generalised advantage estimation
($\lambda=0.95$). The policy is improved with the \emph{clipped} objective
\[
  \mathcal{L}^{\text{clip}} = \mathbb{E}_t\Big[\min\big(\rho_t \hat A_t,\;
  \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\,\hat A_t\big)\Big],\qquad
  \rho_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a_t\mid s_t)},
\]
with $\epsilon = 0.2$. Clipping keeps each update close to the policy that
collected the data, which is what makes reusing a batch for several epochs
safe. PPO uses the same opponent pool as DQN+, and only the learner's own moves
are used for updates, so the data stay on-policy.

\paragraph{AlphaZero.} Following \cite{silver2018}, a single residual network
$f_\theta(s) = (\mathbf{p}, v)$ outputs a move distribution $\mathbf{p}$ and a value
$v\in[-1,1]$. It has 4 residual blocks of 64 channels (about 0.3\,M parameters),
and its input planes are own discs, opponent discs and legal moves. Moves are
chosen by \emph{Monte Carlo tree search} (MCTS) guided by the network. Each of
the 64 simulations per move descends the tree by the PUCT rule
\[
  a^\ast = \arg\max_a \Big[\, Q(s,a) + c_{\text{puct}}\, P(s,a)\,
  \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1+N(s,a)} \Big],
\]
where $Q$ is the mean value of the simulations through $(s,a)$, $P$ the network's
prior, $N$ visit counts and $c_{\text{puct}}=1.5$. The leaf is evaluated by the
network rather than by a random rollout. In self-play, Dirichlet noise is mixed
into the root priors, and the first 10 plies are sampled in proportion to visit
counts to diversify the games; after that the most-visited move is played. Each
position stores its visit distribution $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ and the final result
$z$. The network is trained on a sliding window of the latest 150{,}000 positions
to minimise
\[
  \mathcal{L} = (z - v)^2 \;-\; \boldsymbol{\pi

Results on 6x6 (mean of 3 seeds; scores against each bot)

Method vs random vs heuristic vs minimax-d4 Games to 80% vs heuristic Training time
DQN (classical, for reference) 92% 65% 19% never 1.5 h

  • Self-play without search (DQN+, PPO) matches classical DQN without ever training against the heuristic bot. All three level off around 20% against minimax, which is the ceiling for a policy that doesn't look ahead.
  • AlphaZero beats minimax-d4 about 3 times out of 4, the first agent in this project to do so. Its search helps in two ways:
  • At play time: looking ahead adds about 28 points against minimax.
  • During training: the network learns to copy the search's choices, so even without search it ties with minimax, where PPO and DQN+ manage about 20%.
  • Possible confound, noted in the report: AlphaZero's network is a convolutional network while PPO and DQN+ use simple fully connected networks. Part of the gap may come from that difference; the planned architecture sweep can separate the two.
  • Seed spread is small (≤2.3 points), so the gaps between methods are real.

Check against the solved 6x6 game: Oroletto agrees with the known result that White wins. Its value estimate for the start position is −0.63 for Black, and White wins every self-play game at 64, 200 and 800 simulations per move. Its margins are wider than perfect play's 20–16, though: 21–15 at best, 28–8 at worst. A margin that wide proves Black is making mistakes. So it knows who wins but doesn't play perfectly; the report says so.

Oroletto: - Which run: AlphaZero seed 1, chosen for its score against minimax-d4 (78.7%), since random and heuristic no longer separate the seeds. - Pointer: models/oroletto.json. - When you play it: othello --play oroletto searches 200 simulations per move by default, more than the 64 used in evaluation, so it's probably somewhat stronger than the table shows. That isn't measured. - Board size: it refuses other sizes with a clear message, since it was trained only on 6x6.

A limitation the report flags: AlphaZero's score against the heuristic bot plateaus at about 95% by 20k games, so that curve can't show later progress. I only played minimax at the end and didn't save intermediate checkpoints, so we can't tell whether AlphaZero was still improving after that. Next Steps now lists a stronger yardstick (minimax at depth 6 or more, or Edax) with saved checkpoints. The same yardstick would let every agent go on one Elo scale.

# Phase 3: AlphaZero architecture & search-budget sweep (6x6)

## Context
Phase 2 is done: AlphaZero (now released as Oroletto) scores 95% against heuristic and 77.5% against minimax-d4. Phase 3 asks which parts of its design actually matter, and at what compute cost. It varies one choice at a time (depth, width, input planes, head design, search budget) and reports strength against compute as a Pareto plot.

**Decisions from the user:**
- Use a short sweep: each variant gets 30k self-play games and 1 seed. The top configurations are then confirmed with 3 seeds at the full 100k budget.
- Add minimax-d6 plus a round-robin Elo scale as the yardstick. The current bots no longer separate strong agents: heuristic saturates at about 95% and Oroletto beats d4 78% of the time.
- Add an MLP-trunk AlphaZero variant. This resolves the Phase 2 confound: is AlphaZero's edge from search-based training, or from its convolutional architecture?
- Save checkpoints during training, so learning curves can be measured against the stronger yardstick afterwards.
- The user asked for the compute question to be discussed (see **Compute budget** below).

## Compute budget
| Item | Runs | Estimated time per run | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sweep training (30k games, seed 0): baseline-30k, depth 2/6/10, width 32/128, 4 plane sets, separate trunks, MLP trunk | 12 | 2–5 h (Oroletto: 7.8 h per 100k, so about 2.3 h per 30k; depth-10 and width-128 roughly 1.5–2× slower) | **≈ 35–40 h** |
| Search-budget sweep (25/64/100/400 sims, evaluation only on Oroletto, no retraining) | – | – | ≈ 1 h |
| Yardstick: minimax-d6 calibration + checkpoint evaluation + round robin | – | – | ≈ 3–5 h |
| Confirm: top 2–3 configs × 3 seeds × 100k (reuse Phase 2's 3 seeds if the baseline is among them) | 6–9 | ~8 h | **≈ 50–70 h** |

That is about 4–5 days of wall-clock time in total, with everything run sequentially on the 8 cores. The short sweep is justified because AlphaZero's 6x6 curve plateaued against heuristic by about 20k games. **Risk:** 30k games may rank variants differently from 100k games, for example if bigger nets are slower starters. The confirm stage checks this, and the checkpoint curves show whether rankings were still moving at 30k. The report states this caveat.

## Code changes
1. **Configurable AlphaZero inputs** (`othello/rl/alphazero/net.py`, `selfplay.py`, `train.py`)
   - Generalise `FastEncoder` to take a `planes` tuple from config. Allowed planes: mine, theirs, empty, turn, legal. Pass `in_planes=len(planes)` through `build_net`.
   - **Decoupling fix:** `train.py:144` currently reads the legal-move mask from input plane 2. Workers will instead store the legal mask as a separate uint8 array in each example, and `Augmenter` will transform it together with the planes and π. This makes the loss mask correct for every plane set.
2. **Head design** (`AZNet`): add `trunk: "shared" | "separate"`. "separate" means two independent stems and bodies (same depth and width) feeding the policy and value heads.
3. **MLP trunk** (`AZNet`): add `body: "conv" | "mlp"`. The MLP version flattens the planes into 2×256 ReLU layers (the same as PPO's `PolicyValueMLP` in `othello/rl/ppo.py`), with linear policy and value heads. Everything else (MCTS, targets, augmentation) is unchanged.
4. **Checkpoints** (`train.py`): every `checkpoint_every` games (default 5k), save `out_dir/ckpt/g{games:06d}.pt`.
5. **Cost metrics:** add a parameter count (`count_params` already exists) and a forward-pass MAC count (a small forward-hook counter over Conv2d/Linear, so no new dependency). Also record wall-clock training time, already in `meta.json`.
6. **Generic batched arena for MCTS players** (`othello/rl/alphazero/selfplay.py`): generalise `az_evaluate` into `play_games(player_a, player_b, openings)`. Each side is either a plain `Agent` or an MCTS player (net + sims). This allows AZ-vs-AZ round robins. Keep `az_evaluate` as a thin wrapper so existing callers and tests still pass.

# Phase 3: Diverse-opponent training vs self-play (6x6)

## Context
The architecture sweep is dropped entirely. The phases are renumbered:
- **Phase 3 (this plan):** train agents against a *league* of different strategies and test whether that beats pure self-play.
- **Phase 4 (next):** exploiter agents and a blind-spot analysis of all 11 agents. Its design (exploiter type, analysis scope) will be discussed before it starts.
- **Old 8x8 and multi-size phases:** they become Phases 5 and 6.

**User decisions:**
- **Learners:** both PPO and AlphaZero.
- **Opponent mixes:** compare several.
- **League:** weak agents only (3 rule-based + 5 traditional) plus the learner's own past checkpoints.
- **Sampling:** uniform for now. PFSP (AlphaStar's prioritised fictitious self-play) may come later, so the sampler must be pluggable and per-opponent results must be logged.
- **AlphaZero budget:** 30k games × 3 seeds per mix first, then 100k games × 3 seeds for the top configurations.

## Experimental design
- **League L** = {random, heuristic (ε=0.05), minimax-d4, Q-learning, SARSA, MC control, linear, DQN}. The traditional agents are seed 0 of each Phase 1 method. L also contains the learner's own frozen snapshots, added every 5k games (PPO) or 2.5k games (AlphaZero), at most 20 kept.
- **Mix parameter p** = the fraction of training games played against a uniformly sampled league member; the rest are played against the live learner (pure self-play).

| | p = 0 (self-play) | p = 0.5 | p = 1 (league only) |
|---|---|---|---|

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='report.tex'; s=open(p).read()
i=s.index('\\section{Next Steps}')
a=s.index('\\begin{itemize}', i); b=s.index('\\end{itemize}', a)+len('\\end{itemize}')
new=r'''\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Training against a league of strategies.} Train PPO and
        AlphaZero against a league of weak agents (the three rule-based bots,
        the five traditional agents and their own past checkpoints), mixed with
        self-play in several proportions. The question is whether this variety
        beats pure self-play. Two of those bots would then be training
        opponents, so the comparison will rely on held-out yardsticks:
        minimax at depth~6, and head-to-head matches against the self-play
        models.
  \item \textbf{Exploiters and blind spots.} Train exploiter agents whose only
        goal is to beat a fixed model such as Oroletto. Then audit every agent's
        moves with an exact endgame solver to find and categorise its blind
        spots, and measure how far each model's weaknesses transfer to the
        others.
  \item \textbf{Multi-agent co-evolution.} Let several independent agents learn
        by playing one another, and compare the resulting models with the
        self-play models: their strength, how exploitable they are, and whether
        strategies cycle within the population.
  \item \textbf{Scaling to \bx{8}.} Re-tune the rule-based bots for \bx{8}
        (Table~\ref{tab:gate} shows the \bx{6} weights are weaker there) and
        train the selected configuration. Optionally, play matches against the
        Edax engine.
  \item \textbf{One network for every board size.} Test zero-shot transfer,
        then train a fully convolutional, globally pooled network on mixed
        board sizes and compare it with a small-to-large curriculum. The result
        is reported as a train-size $\times$ test-size win-rate matrix.
\end{itemize}'''

**Why:** On 2026-10-04 the user rejected an architecture-sweep plan, redefined Phases 3–5 (league training, exploiters/blind spots, multi-agent co-evolution), then asked that detailed plans for each be added to PLAN.md before approving anything.

Phase 3 (Steps 3.1–3.10), using your decisions: - Learners: PPO and AlphaZero. - League: the 3 rule-based bots, the 5 traditional agents, and the learner's own past checkpoints. - Sampling: uniform. The sampler can be swapped later for AlphaStar-style prioritised sampling, and per-opponent results are logged so that's possible. - Mixes: league share p = 0 / 0.5 / 1. - Budgets: PPO 200k games × 3 seeds. AlphaZero 30k games × 3 seeds, then the best mix at 100k × 3. - Prerequisite: the Q-learning, SARSA and Monte Carlo tables were never saved in Phase 1, so I'll re-train them, with a check that the results match. - Evaluation: heuristic and minimax-d4 will now be training opponents, so beating them proves less (MC control showed that a learner can memorise an opponent it trains against). "Better than self-play" is therefore decided on held-out measures: head-to-head against the self-play model at the same budget, against a new minimax-d6 benchmark, and against Oroletto. Scores against random, heuristic and minimax-d4 are reported but marked as training opponents.

Phase 4 (Steps 4.1–4.8): 1. An exact endgame solver for 6x6. 2. A blunder audit of every agent: each endgame move is labelled optimal, inaccurate or game-losing. 3. A blind-spot taxonomy: blunders grouped by game phase, square type, pass situations and parity. 4. Exploiters trained against Oroletto, PPO and the best Phase 3 model. 5. An exploiter-vs-agent transfer matrix: does one model's weakness work against the others? 6. An analysis of what the exploiters target, with annotated example games. 7. Whether league-trained models are harder to exploit.

Decisions to discuss before Phase 4: - Exploiter type: proposed default is AlphaZero with victim modelling (Wang et al. 2023); alternatives are PPO, or both. - Analysis scope: proposed default is the solver audit for all agents plus exploiters only for the strong ones.

Phase 5 (Steps 5.1–5.6): 1. A population trainer: N independent agents, each with its own network and learner, that only ever play each other. 2. PPO populations first, since they're cheap. 3. An AlphaZero population. 4. Comparison with self-play on strength, held-out benchmarks and exploitability. 5. Population dynamics: Elo over time, rock-paper-scissors cycles, and how different the members' strategies become.

Decisions to discuss before Phase 5: - population size (proposed 4); - same algorithm vs mixed algorithms; - how members are paired (uniform vs by Elo); - how to keep the budget fair: equal games per agent vs equal total compute.

## Phase 3: Training Against a League of Strategies (6x6, ~1.5 weeks)

**Question:** does training against a *variety* of strategies beat pure self-play? Learners are PPO and AlphaZero. The opponent league holds weak agents only: the 3 rule-based bots, the 5 traditional agents and the learner's own past checkpoints. Opponents are sampled uniformly. AlphaStar-style prioritised sampling (PFSP) may be added later, so the sampler is pluggable and per-opponent results are always logged.

**Step 3.1 — Save/load the traditional agents**
Add `save`/`load` to `TabularLearner` (gzipped pickle of the Q table) and support for it in `othello/models.py`. The Q-learning, SARSA and MC tables were never saved, so re-train seed 0 of each. Linear and DQN models already load. Add `results/**/table.pkl.gz` to `.gitignore`.
*Done when:* each re-trained seed-0 `final.json` equals the Phase 1 one (deterministic seeding), and all 8 league agents load through `load_model` / `make_agent`.

**Step 3.2 — League + sampler**
Extend `othello/rl/pool.py` into a `League`. It holds fixed members built from specs, plus snapshots of the learner added every K games (at most 20). `p_league` is the fraction of games against a uniformly sampled league member; the rest are against the live learner. The sampler is a strategy object (`uniform` now, `pfsp` later). It keeps W/D/L per opponent and writes them to the curve CSV.
*Done when:* tests confirm the sampling frequencies for p = 0, 0.5 and 1, and per-opponent stats appear in a smoke run.

**Step 3.3 — Generic batched game runner**
In `othello/rl/alphazero/selfplay.py`, replace the self-play-only loop with `run_games`. Each side of each game is either an MCTS player (net + sims) or a plain `Agent`, and the search is batched per MCTS player across all games. Self-play, league games and evaluation (`az_evaluate` stays as a wrapper) all use it. In league games, only the learner's positions become training examples.
*Done when:* the existing AlphaZero tests pass, and new tests cover MCTS-vs-Agent, MCTS-vs-MCTS, and examples recorded for the learner's side only.

**Step 3.4 — AlphaZero league training**
New config keys: `p_league`, `league`, `snapshot_every` and `checkpoint_every` (save `ckpt/g{games}.pt` every 5k games). Workers build the league opponents once and sample one per game.
*Done when:* a smoke run (p = 0.5, 1k games) produces checkpoints and per-opponent win rates.

**Step 3.5 — Held-out yardstick: minimax-d6**
heuristic and minimax-d4 are now *in* the league, so scores against them are no longer held-out tests. A league learner could beat them by memorising them, like MC control did in Phase 1. Calibrate minimax-d6 against d4 and heuristic.
*Done when:* d6 beats d4 clearly; otherwise pick another held-out anchor.

**Step 3.6 — PPO runs**
Mixes p ∈ {0, 0.5, 1} × 3 seeds × 200k games, with `configs/league_ppo.yaml` → `results/league/ppo/<mix>/seed<k>/`. p = 0 is re-run under the new code, so the baseline is like-for-like.
*Done when:* all 9 runs have `final.json` and checkpoints (~2–3 h).

**Step 3.7 — AlphaZero runs (short)**
The same three mixes × 3 seeds × 30k games, including a p = 0 re-run at 30k (Phase 2 used 100k).
*Done when:* all 9 runs finish (~1 day).

**Step 3.8 — Held-out evaluation**
`scripts/eval_phase3.py` runs, for every model:
- head-to-head against its p = 0 counterpart at the same budget (200 games per seed pair);
- matches against minimax-d6;
- head-to-head against Oroletto (AlphaZero) or Phase 2 PPO (PPO).

Scores against random, heuristic and minimax-d4 are reported but marked "in-league".
*Done when:* `results/league/*.json` exist for all models.

**Step 3.9 — Confirm the best AlphaZero mix at full budget**
Run the best mix by held-out strength for 100k games × 3 seeds, and compare with Oroletto's 3 seeds. If p = 0 already won at 30k, skip this and report that self-play was not beaten.
*Done when:* the comparison is complete. If the league model beats Oroletto head-to-head, update `mode

new=r'''## Phase 3: Training Against a League of Strategies (6x6, ~1.5 weeks)

**Question:** does training against a *variety* of strategies beat pure self-play?
- **Learners:** PPO and AlphaZero.
- **League:** weak agents only: the 3 rule-based bots, the 5 traditional agents, and the learner's own past checkpoints.
- **Sampling:** opponents are drawn uniformly. AlphaStar-style prioritised sampling (PFSP) may be added later, so the sampler is pluggable and per-opponent results are always logged.

**Hypotheses going in** (predictions to test, not results):
- **H1, robustness:** mixing in varied opponents makes the learner more robust. It should lose less to unusual play and score higher against weak bots.
- **H2, signal:** a league of *weak* agents gives a poor training signal once they are beaten, because almost every game is then a win and carries little information. So league-only training (p = 1) should end up weaker than self-play on held-out tests.
- **H3, best mix:** a mix (p = 0.5) keeps self-play's matched-strength curriculum while adding variety. If anything beats self-play, it should be this.

---

**Step 3.1 — Save/load the traditional agents**
- **Why:** the league needs the 5 traditional agents as playable opponents. The linear and DQN models were saved in Phase 1, but the Q-learning, SARSA and MC tables were not. They only ever existed in memory during training.
- **Objective & expectation:**
  - **Objective:** all 8 league agents load from disk and play through the normal agent interface.
  - **Expectation:** Phase 1 seeding was fully deterministic (fixed random seeds, integer-keyed dicts), so re-training seed 0 should reproduce *exactly* the same tables and the same `final.json` numbers. If it doesn't, the re-trained versions are used and the difference is reported.
- **Methodology:**
  - Add `save`/`load` to `TabularLearner` (a gzipped pickle of the flat Q dict, plus visit counts for MC), and a tabular branch in `othello/models.py:load_model`.
  - Re-run `scripts/train_rl.py --run {q-learning,sarsa,mc-control} --seed 0` in parallel (~30 min). Save `table.pkl.gz`, about 100 MB each, which is git-ignored.
  - Compare the new `final.json` against the committed Phase 1 files.
- *Done when:* each re-trained seed-0 `final.json` equals the Phase 1 one, a save → load round-trip test passes, and all 8 agents load through `load_model` / `make_agent`.

**Step 3.2 — League + sampler**
- **Why:** this is the core mechanism of the phase. It controls *who* the learner plays and records *how it fares against each opponent*. The second part is needed both for the analysis and for any later switch to PFSP, which samples by win rate.
- **Objective & expectation:**
  - **Objective:** one component that, for every training game, returns either the live learner (self-play) or a league member.
  - **Expectation:** observed sampling frequencies match p within sampling noise. In training logs, the learner should overtake the weakest members (random, tabular agents) almost immediately and minimax-d4 last.
- **Methodology:**
  - Extend `OpponentPool` (`othello/rl/pool.py`) into a `League`.
    - **Fixed members** are built once from specs with `make_agent` / `load_model`.
    - **Snapshots:** a frozen copy of the learner is added every K games, with K = 5,000 for PPO (200k-game runs) and K = 2,500 for AlphaZero (30k-game runs). That gives ~12–40 snapshots per run; at most 20 are kept, oldest dropped first.
  - Each game: with probability `p_league`, pick a league member uniformly (fixed members and snapshots together); otherwise the live learner.
  - The sampler is a small strategy object (`UniformSampler` now; `PFSPSampler` later can reuse the same per-opponent W/D/L counts).
  - `stats()` writes per-opponent W/D/L for the last evaluation window into the curve CSV.

Phase-level hypotheses, so each step's expectations have something to confirm or refute: - H1, robustness: varied opponents should make the learner more robust. - H2, signal: a league of weak agents gives little to learn from once they're beaten, since almost every game is a win. So league-only training (p = 1) should end up weaker than self-play on held-out tests. - H3, best mix: a 50/50 mix keeps self-play's matched-strength opponent and adds variety. If anything beats self-play, it should be this.

The steps:

Step Why Expectation Methodology highlights
3.1 Save/load traditional agents Tabular tables were never saved; the league needs all 8 agents Seeding was deterministic, so re-training gives identical results Gzipped Q-table save/load; re-train seed 0; compare against the Phase 1 results
3.2 League + sampler The core mechanism; per-opponent stats are also needed for a later switch to PFSP Sampling frequencies match p; the learner overtakes random and the tabular agents first, minimax-d4 last K = 5,000 games (PPO) / 2,500 (AlphaZero) between snapshots, at most 20 kept; uniform sampler as a swappable strategy
3.3 Generic batched runner AlphaZero can only self-play today; league training, AZ-vs-AZ evaluation and Phases 4–5 all need mixed players Pure refactor: p = 0 should reproduce the Phase 2 curve Group games by player to move; batch search per MCTS player; record examples per side
3.4 AlphaZero league training Connects the league to AlphaZero's workers League games give about half as many training positions, and minimax games are slower; both logged League built once per worker; the learner's search is unchanged; checkpoints every 5k games
3.5 Minimax-d6 benchmark heuristic and d4 become training opponents, so memorising them is possible (as MC control did) d6 beats d4 about 60–75% Calibrate against d4, heuristic and Oroletto; fallback: d7 or Edax
3.6 PPO runs Cheap early test of H1–H3 Scores against training opponents rise with p; held-out scores worst at p = 1 p0 / p50 / p100 × 3 seeds × 200k games; p = 0 re-run under the new code
3.7 AlphaZero runs (30k) Strongest learner; Phase 2 had levelled off by ~20k games Smaller gaps than PPO; is p50 > p0? Same mixes, 30k games; p0 re-run at 30k
3.8 Held-out evaluation Decides the phase's question Per H1–H3 Head-to-head vs p0 at equal budget, vs d6, vs Oroletto or Phase 2 PPO; a difference counts only if it holds across seeds and its 95% interval excludes 50%
3.9 Full-budget confirm 30k games might rank the mixes differently from full training A smaller but real edge, if one existed at 30k The best mix runs 100k games × 3 seeds; Oroletto is replaced only if the new model beats it head-to-head with a 95% interval that excludes 50%
3.10 Report section Document the result, including if self-play wins Held-out and training-opponent scores shown side by side Bar graphs, per-opponent curves, head-to-head matrix; H1–H3 each explicitly confirmed or refuted

Two things are spelled out that weren't before: - The p = 0 baseline is re-run under the new code for both learners, rather than reusing Phase 2. Phase 2 PPO trained partly against its own past snapshots, so it's a slightly different baseline and is kept only as a reference. - A fixed rule for replacing Oroletto, so the decision can't drift after seeing the data.

I'll narrow Phase 3 to DQN only. Removing PPO and AlphaZero has a few knock-on effects worth flagging:

  • Steps that drop out: the generic batched runner, AlphaZero league training, the AlphaZero runs and the full-budget Oroletto confirmation. Phases 4 and 5 still need the runner, so it moves to the start of Phase 4.
  • H4 drops out: it compared DQN with PPO, and there's no PPO now.
  • The held-out benchmark has to change:
  • Why minimax-d6 no longer fits: it was chosen to separate strong agents like Oroletto. DQN only scores about 19% against minimax-d4, so against d6 every mix would score near zero and look the same.
  • The new panel: benchmarks near DQN's strength that it never trains against: minimax-d2 and minimax-d3, plus Phase 2's PPO and DQN+.
  • Mixes: DQN runs are cheap (about 1.3 h each), so I'll test five league shares, p = 0 / 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 / 1. That gives a dose-response curve instead of 3 points, for about 3–4 hours of compute.

Spelling the details out surfaced one design point to fix now. With uniform sampling over "8 fixed agents + up to 20 snapshots", the learner's own snapshots would gradually take over the league: by the end only 8 of 28 members (29%) would be the weak agents. That would quietly turn "league" games back into self-play. I'll specify two-level sampling instead: half the league games go to the 8 fixed agents and half to snapshots, each uniform within its group, so the league's make-up stays constant. 3.5 Held-out evaluation A table of matches per model (which opponents, how many games, held-out or training opponent); a 5×5 head-to-head matrix between mixes; checkpoint curves for H4; statistics including a seed-level bootstrap; the decision rule for "beats self-play"; output files; ~1–2 h
3.6 Report Each figure and table by filename, how they're generated, and where the section goes

Three choices I made while writing the details (tell me if you'd prefer otherwise): 1. Two-level league sampling. Half of league games go to the 8 fixed agents and half to the learner's own snapshots, each uniform within its group. With plain uniform sampling, snapshots would grow to 71% of the league by the end and quietly turn league games back into self-play. 2. Learning curves are now measured against minimax-d3, not heuristic. Heuristic is a training opponent in this phase, so a curve against it could be inflated by memorisation. 3. The "beats self-play" rule is fixed in advance. A mix counts as better only if its bootstrap 95% interval against p = 0 lies entirely above 50%, and it is no worse than p = 0 against any held-out benchmark.

    save_name = "table.pkl.gz"

    def save(self, path):

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, env, path, seed=0):

        learner.q, learner.visits, learner.states = d["q"], d["visits"], d["states"]
        return learner

def test_tabular_save_load_roundtrip(tmp_path):
    from othello.models import load_model
    env = OthelloEnv(6)
    rng = random.Random(0)
    L = TabularLearner(env, 0, method="mc")
    for _ in range(20):                       # a few short random "episodes"
        s = env.initial_state()
        traj = []
        for _ in range(6):
            a = rng.choice(env.legal_moves(s))
            traj.append((s, a))
            s = env.step(env.step(s, a), rng.choice(env.legal_moves(env.step(s, a))))
        L.end_episode(traj, [0.0] * 5 + [rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0])])
    (tmp_path / "config.json").write_text('{"board_size": 6, "run": "mc-control"}')
    L.save(tmp_path / L.save_name)
    agent = load_model(tmp_path, env)
    L2 = agent.learner
    assert L2.q == L.q and L2.visits == L.visits and L2.states == L.states and L2.method == "mc"
    s = env.initial_state()
    for _ in range(10):                       # greedy choices agree wherever values differ
        _, v1 = L._values(s)
        _, v2 = L2._values(s)
        assert v1 == v2
        s = env.step(s, env.legal_moves(s)[0])
        if env.is_terminal(s):
            break

Step Role in comparing the mixes
3.3 Held-out evaluation panel Chooses the opponents the mixes are judged against: minimax-d2 and d3, Phase 2 PPO and DQN+. None of them is a league member, so a mix can't look better just by having memorised them.
3.4 DQN runs Produces the 5 mixes (p = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) × 3 seeds, plus learning curves against minimax-d3 during training.
3.5 Held-out evaluation ← the comparison Every mix plays the held-out panel, plus a head-to-head against every other mix: a 5×5 matrix over all seed pairs. Each mix is compared with self-play (p = 0) using a seed-level bootstrap.
3.6 Report Main figure: score vs p, with held-out and in-league curves side by side. Also a 5×5 head-to-head heat-map and a bar graph of the best mix vs p = 0.

How "better" is decided (fixed in advance in Step 3.5's experiment details): - A mix beats self-play only if: 1. its bootstrap 95% interval for its score against the p = 0 models lies entirely above 50%, and 2. it is not worse than p = 0 against any held-out panel opponent. - The best mix overall is the one with the highest held-out score against p = 0. The 5×5 head-to-head matrix also shows how the mixes rank against each other. - Scores against random, heuristic and minimax-d4 are reported but don't count, because those three are training opponents. Comparing them with the held-out scores shows whether a mix only learned to beat its training opponents.

In PLAN.md, look under Step 3.5, in its "Experiment details" block (the match table and the "Decision rule" bullet).

Two things that differ from the plan: - The "same score as the live learner" check had to be loosened. The agents break ties at random, and that random state isn't saved with the table, so an exact game-by-game replay isn't possible. I accepted any score within 2× the 95% interval of the recorded one. - SARSA's gap is the largest, at about 1.6× the interval. It's within tolerance and expected: SARSA has seen so few positions that most of its moves are random tie-breaks. - The tables are 33–41 MB each, smaller than the ~100 MB I estimated. """Opponent pool for self-play.

Every `snapshot_every` games the learner's current policy is frozen and added
to the pool (oldest dropped beyond `max_size`). Each training game is played
against the learner itself with probability `p_latest`, otherwise against a
uniformly chosen past snapshot. Playing past selves keeps the learner from
forgetting how to beat earlier strategies (strategy cycling), which pure
latest-vs-latest self-play is prone to.
"""

Bash: Add League, member builder, result hook
cat >> othello/rl/pool.py <<'EOF'


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- league
class UniformSampler:
    """Every member of a group is equally likely. A PFSP sampler (AlphaStar) can
    replace this later: it gets the same per-opponent W/D/L counts via `counts`."""

    name = "uniform"

    def choose(self, rng, names, counts):
        return rng.choice(names)


class League:
    """Opponents for one training game: the live learner, or a league member.

    With probability `p_league` the opponent is a league member, otherwise the
    live learner (pure self-play). League sampling is two-level, so the league's
    make-up stays constant over training: with probability `fixed_frac` one of
    the fixed agents, otherwise one of the learner's frozen snapshots (all
    league games go to fixed agents until the first snapshot exists). Within a
    group the `sampler` picks the member.

    Per-opponent results are recorded through `record()` and reported (then
    reset) by `stats()` for each evaluation window. Snapshots are reported as
    one aggregate opponent, "snapshots".
    """

    def __init__(self, learner, fixed: dict, p_league: float, snapshot_every=5_000, max_snapshots=20,
                 fixed_frac=0.5, sampler=None, seed=0):
        self.learner, self.fixed, self.p = learner, dict(fixed), p_league
        self.snapshot_every, self.max_snapshots, self.fixed_frac = snapshot_every, max_snapshots, fixed_frac
        self.sampler = sampler or UniformSampler()
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
        self.snapshots: list[tuple[str, Agent]] = []
        self.self_agent = SelfAgent(learner)
        self.total = {}                      # name -> [W, D, L] over the whole run (for PFSP)
        self._window = {}
        self._last = None

    def maybe_snapshot(self, games: int):
        if games > 0 and games % self.snapshot_every == 0:
            name = f"snap@{games // 1000}k"
            self.snapshots.append((name, self.learner.snapshot(seed=self.rng.randrange(10**9))))
            if len(self.snapshots) > self.max_snapshots:
                self.snapshots.pop(0)

    def sample(self) -> Agent:
        if self.rng.random() >= self.p:
            self._last = ("self", "self")
            return self.self_agent
        if self.snapshots and self.rng.random() >= self.fixed_frac:
            names = [n for n, _ in self.snapshots]
            name = self.sampler.choose(self.rng, names, self.total)
            self._last = ("snapshot", name)
            return dict(self.snapshots)[name]
        name = self.sampler.choose(self.rng, list(self.fixed), self.total)
        self._last = ("fixed", name)
        return self.fixed[name]

    @property
    def last_kind(self):
        return self._last[0] if self._last else None

    def record(self, learner_margin: int):
        """Result of the game just played, as the learner's final disc margin."""
        kind, name = self._last
        idx = 0 if learner_margin > 0 else 1 if learner_margin == 0 else 2
        key = "snapshots" if kind == "snapshot" else name
        for table, k in ((self._window, key), (self.total, name)):
            table.setdefault(k, [0, 0, 0])[idx] += 1

    def stats(self):
        out = {}
        n_all = sum(sum(v) for v in self._window.values())
        for key in ["self", *self.fixed, "snapshots"]:
            w, d, l = self._window.get(key, [0, 0, 0])
            n = w + d + l
            out[f"vs_{key}_n"] = n
            out[f"vs_{key}_score"] = (w + 0.5 * d) / n if n else float("nan")
        n_fixed = sum(sum(self._window.get(k, [0, 0, 0])) for k in self.fixed)
        out["mix_self"] = sum(self._window.get("self", [0, 0, 0])) / n_all if n_all else float("nan")
        out["mix_fixed"] = n_fixed / n_all if n_all else float("nan")
        out["mix_snapshots"] = sum(self._window.get("snapshots", [0, 0, 0])) / n_all if n_all else float("nan")
        out["pool_size"] = len(self.snapshots)
        self._window = {}

import pytest

from othello.agents import RandomAgent
from othello.env import OthelloEnv
from othello.rl.pool import League


class FakeLearner:
    def __init__(self, env):
        self.env = env

    def act(self, state, explore):
        return random.choice(self.env.legal_moves(state))

    def snapshot(self, seed=0):
        return RandomAgent(self.env, seed=seed)


def make_league(p, snapshots=0, fixed_n=8, seed=0):
    env = OthelloEnv(6)
    fixed = {f"f{i}": RandomAgent(env, seed=i) for i in range(fixed_n)}
    lg = League(FakeLearner(env), fixed, p_league=p, snapshot_every=5_000, seed=seed)
    for g in range(1, snapshots + 1):
        lg.maybe_snapshot(5_000 * g)
    return lg

        c[lg.last_kind] += 1
    return {k: v / n for k, v in c.items()}

a5c4f6b Step 3.2: league + sampler

Step 3.2 is done: the league and its sampler work, they're tested, and a smoke run behaves as designed. It's marked ✅ in PLAN.md and committed.

What was built: - League (in othello/rl/pool.py): - Each game, it picks the live learner with probability 1 − p; otherwise a league member, chosen two-level: 50% from the 8 fixed agents, 50% from the learner's own snapshots, uniform within each group. - Snapshots: taken every 5k games, at most 20 kept. Until the first one exists, all league games go to the fixed agents. - Swappable sampler: the uniform sampler can later be replaced by prioritised sampling (PFSP). Win/draw/loss totals per opponent are already kept for the whole run, which PFSP needs. - Logging: each evaluation window writes per-opponent score and game count, plus the realised mix, to the learning-curve file. The columns are the same in every row. - build_fixed_members: builds the 8 league agents from the config, with rule-based bots by type and Phase 1 agents from their saved files. - A small hook in the training loop that reports each game's result to the league. - configs/league_dqn.yaml: the full Step 3.4 setup. - The 5 mixes (p0–p100) and the 8 league members. - Learning curves are measured against minimax-d3 (held-out). - Final evaluation covers held-out minimax-d2 and d3, plus the in-league bots, flagged as such.

Tests: 7 new tests, 65 in total, all passing. - Sampling frequencies for p = 0, 0.5 and 1 are within ±2 points. - Only fixed agents are drawn before the first snapshot. - The 8 fixed agents are drawn uniformly. - The snapshot cap and schedule work. - Logged columns stay the same in every window, and counts reset per window.

  • The realised mix is exactly as designed: half self-play, and the league half splits evenly between fixed agents and snapshots once the first snapshot appears at 5k games.
  • The learner overtakes the weakest members first, random and Q-learning, and minimax-d4 last, as Step 3.2 predicted.
  • Speed: 10k games of training took about 3 minutes, so a full 200k-game run should take roughly 1–1.3 hours. Step 3.4's estimate (15 runs in about 3–5 hours on 8 cores) holds.

def _lg_score(r, key):
    """Model result dict -> score vs a panel opponent (averaging the seed-level entries)."""
    if key in ("p0", "ppo", "dqn+"):
        pref = {"p0": "p0-s", "ppo": "ppo-s", "dqn+": "dqn+-s"}[key]
        v = [x["score"] for k, x in r.items() if k.startswith(pref)]
        return sum(v) / len(v)
    return r[key]["score"]


def _boot_vs_p0(ev, mix, n=10_000, seed=0):
    """Mean score of `mix` vs the p0 models over seed pairs, with a seed-level bootstrap 95% CI."""
    import numpy as np
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    S = [0, 1, 2]
    M = {(a, b): ev[f"{mix}/seed{a}"][f"p0-s{b}"]["score"] for a in S for b in S
         if f"p0-s{b}" in ev[f"{mix}/seed{a}"]}
    mean = sum(M.values()) / len(M)
    boots = []
    for _ in range(n):
        A, B = rng.choice(S, 3), rng.choice(S, 3)
        v = [M[(a, b)] for a in A for b in B if (a, b) in M]
        if v:
            boots.append(sum(v) / len(v))
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    return mean, lo, hi

Claude's response

So far it's used only in the early part: Section 3.5 rates the three rule-based bots, separately for each board size. Nothing after that uses it.

Where Is Elo used?
Section 3, rule-based bots ✅ Elo for random / heuristic / minimax-d4 on 6x6, 8x8 and 10x10, with a check that the ratings are consistent
Section 4, traditional methods ❌ Results are scores against each bot separately
Section 5, self-play (DQN+, PPO, AlphaZero/Oroletto) ❌ Same. PLAN.md Step 2.8 planned a "round-robin Elo across every agent", but I didn't do it.
Phase 3 (running now) ❌ Not in the plan; the mixes are compared by head-to-head scores and the held-out benchmarks
Phase 5 (co-evolution) Planned: Step 5.5 fits Elo for every population checkpoint over time

So the report defines Elo and explains why one scale is useful ("any agent that plays the reference bots can be placed on the same scale"), but then never does it. The single ranking of all agents we discussed earlier is still missing.

It could be added cheaply, mostly from existing games. Every agent has already played the same reference bots under the same protocol: - Phase 1 and 2 agents: against random, heuristic and minimax-d4. - Phase 3 models: additionally against minimax-d2 and d3, Phase 2 PPO and DQN+, and each other.

The rating fit only needs every agent to be connected to the others through some games; it doesn't need everyone to play everyone. So I could fit one Elo scale on 6x6 covering all agents (rule-based, the 5 traditional ones, DQN+, PPO, Oroletto and the 15 Phase 3 models), plus a consistency check like Section 3.5's.

Two caveats: - Oroletto is near the top of what the benchmarks can measure. It beats minimax-d4 about 78% of the time, which is fine for rating it, but if it beat everything nearly always its rating would only be a lower bound. A minimax-d6 benchmark would firm that up and costs a few hundred extra games. - MC control won't fit one scale well. It beats heuristic but only draws with random, so its residuals would be large. That's the point the report already predicts.

Should I add this combined Elo ranking? Its natural place is the Phase 3 report section (Step 3.6), or a short new subsection after Self-Play. It would run after the Phase 3 evaluation finishes tonight.

%======================================================================
\section{Rule-Based Bots}
\label{sec:bots}
Rule based bots are those that don't need any learning and have clear hand written rules. We use these as a benchmark for our RL models described later in the report. 3 rule based bots work on different general ideas and have been adapted to Othello for the purpose of this project.
Every learning method is judged against fixed, rule-based opponents.We compare the performance of these three bots and rate them according to the ELO rating. We also consider the three bots for three different board sizes and compare and rate them for the three different board sizes independently.
In this section we use the shared evaluation protocol summarised below and
detailed in \S\ref{sec:protocol}.
j
\paragraph{Evaluation protocol (summary).} Every match is played from $K$
openings of six random plies, and each opening is played once with each colour.
----
size. Each bar is the score of the first-named (stronger) bot. Whiskers: 95\% CI;
dashed segments: gate thresholds; dotted line: 50\% (parity). The \bx{6}-tuned weights of
the heuristic were used on every size.}
\label{fig:bots_h2h}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Elo ratings}
\label{sec:elo}
----

\paragraph{Limitations.} Where a bot almost never loses, as minimax-d4 does on
\bx{8} and \bx{10}, the data only say that the gap is \emph{large}. The rating
is then set mostly by the prior, and is best read as a lower bound. Ratings are
also relative to this pool and protocol: they are not comparable with human or
engine Elo ratings measured elsewhere. Finally, the scale assumes strength is
one-dimensional. An agent that exploits one particular opponent, like the Monte
Carlo learner of \S\ref{sec:classical}, would fit poorly, and the fit's
residuals would show it.

Fig.~\ref{fig:bots_h2h} and Tables~\ref{tab:gate} and~\ref{tab:elo} confirm the intended ordering
random $<$ heuristic $<$ minimax on every board size. The gap between minimax
and heuristic widens as the board grows. We attribute this to two effects.
Larger boards mean longer games with more decisions, so lookahead has more
chances to pay off. And the weights were tuned on \bx{6}, which likely suits the
greedy bot less on bigger boards, while search partly makes up for a mis-tuned
evaluation.

%======================================================================

Fig.~\ref{fig:bots_h2h} and Table~\ref{tab:gate} confirm the intended ordering
random $<$ heuristic $<$ minimax on every board size. The gap between minimax
and heuristic widens as the board grows. We attribute this to two effects.
Larger boards mean longer games with more decisions, so lookahead has more
chances to pay off. And the weights were tuned on \bx{6}, which likely suits the
greedy bot less on bigger boards, while search partly makes up for a mis-tuned
evaluation.

%======================================================================
\section{Traditional Training Methods}
\label{sec:classical}

In this section we look at five classical RL methods and train them on \bx{6}. All of them use the
same fixed opponent and the same budget, and each is then compared against all
three rule-based bots. The question is not only how well each method plays, but
\emph{why} it stops improving where it does.

\subsection{Common Experimantal Setup for Training and Evaluation}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Opponent and episodes.} Each learner plays the heuristic bot
        (\S\ref{sec:bots}), alternating colours and starting from random
        6-ply openings, for \TrainGames{} training games per run, with 3 seeds
        per method.
  \item \textbf{The learner's view.} The learner sees only its own decision
        points. Its state $s_t$ is the position when it is to move, and the
        opponent's reply is part of the environment's transition to $s_{t+1}$.
        The reward is $+1$, $0$ or $-1$ at the end of the game and zero
        otherwise, with no discounting ($\gamma=1$).
  \item \textbf{Exploration.} $\varepsilon$-greedy, with $\varepsilon$ decaying
        linearly from 0.3 to 0.05 over the first half of training.
  \item \textbf{Evaluation.} Every 5{,}000 games the greedy policy plays 200
        evaluation games against the heuristic bot (for the learning curves).
        At the end it plays 1{,}000 games against random and against heuristic,
        and 500 against minimax-d4 (for the comparison). The evaluation
        openings are fixed and shared across methods.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{The Tradional RL Methods}

\paragraph{Tabular Q-learning \cite{watkins1992}.} Keeps a table entry $Q(s,a)$
for every state--action pair it has visited and updates it toward a bootstrapped
one-step target:
\[
  Q(s_t,a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t) + \alpha\big[r_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a') - Q(s_t,a_t)\big].
\]
The $\max$ makes it \emph{off-policy}: it learns the value of the greedy policy
while it behaves $\varepsilon$-greedily. To give the table its best chance, each
position is stored in a canonical form under the 8 symmetries of the board, so
symmetric positions share one entry. Unvisited entries read as 0.

\paragraph{SARSA \cite{rummery1994}.} Identical to Q-learning except that the
target uses the action $a_{t+1}$ the agent \emph{actually} took next, i.e.
$r_{t+1} + \gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})$. It is therefore \emph{on-policy}: it values
the exploring policy itself, including its exploratory mistakes.

\paragraph{First-visit Monte Carlo control \cite{sutton2018}.} Does not
bootstrap. After the game ends, every visited pair is moved toward the observed
return $G_t$ (here the final result) by a sample average,
$Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a) + \tfrac{1}{N(s,a)}\,[G_t - Q(s,a)]$. Its targets are
unbiased but have high \emph{variance}: each one is a single noisy game outcome
that depends on every later move by both players. (Positions never repeat within
an Othello game, so first-visit and every-visit MC coincide.)

\paragraph{Linear function-approximation Q-learning.} Replaces the table with a
weighted sum of features, $Q(s,a)=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(s\!\oplus\!a)$,
where $s\!\oplus\!a$ is the \emph{afterstate}: the position right after the
learner's move. The features are disc difference, mobility difference, corner
difference, X-square difference, stable-e
… [1,539 more characters not shown]

All five methods (and the ablation variants) are trained and evaluated under

\paragraph{Training.}
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[Common opponent:] the heuristic bot of \S\ref{sec:heuristic}, with the
        tuned weights of Table~\ref{tab:heuristic_weights} and
        $\varepsilon=0.05$ random moves. It is the same fixed opponent for every
        method, run and game; nothing else is ever played during training.
  \item[Training algorithm:] the method being studied
        (\S\ref{sec:classical_methods}): tabular Q-learning, SARSA, Monte
        Carlo control, linear function-approximation Q-learning or DQN. Every
        method runs inside one shared training loop
        (\texttt{othello/rl/common.py}), so they differ only in how they choose
        moves and update their values.
  \item[Learner's view (state):] the position at each of the learner's own
        decision points, from the side to move. The opponent's reply is part of
        the environment's transition from $s_t$ to $s_{t+1}$.
  \item[Reward:] $+1$ for a win, $0$ for a draw, $-1$ for a loss, given only at
        the end of the game; every other step gets $0$. There is no discounting
        ($\gamma=1$). (The disc-margin ablation replaces the final reward by the
        final disc margin.)
  \item[Exploration:] $\varepsilon$-greedy, with $\varepsilon$ decaying linearly
        from 0.3 to 0.05 over the first half of training and held at 0.05
        afterwards.
  \item[Step sizes:] tabular Q-learning and SARSA $\alpha=0.1$; Monte Carlo the
        sample average $1/N(s,a)$; linear $\alpha=0.01$; DQN as described in
        \S\ref{sec:classical_methods}.
  \item[Games and openings:] \TrainGames{} training games per run. Each game
        starts from a random 6-ply opening drawn from a fixed pool of 20{,}000,
        and the learner alternates between Black and White every game.
  \item[Seeds:] 3 independent runs (seeds 0, 1, 2) per method.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[What is evaluated:] the learner's \emph{greedy} policy: no exploration
        ($\varepsilon=0$), ties broken at random, and no learning during
        evaluation games.
  \item[Learning curves (during training):] every 5{,}000 training games the
        current policy plays 200 games (100 fixed openings, each with both
        colours) against the heuristic bot. The same openings are used at every
        checkpoint and for every method, so all the curves are directly
        comparable. Note that this opponent is the \emph{training} opponent, so
        the curves measure progress against the bot each method is learning
        to beat.
  \item[Final comparison (after training):] the final policy plays all three
        rule-based bots: 1{,}000 games against random, 1{,}000 against
        heuristic and 500 against minimax-d4 (fewer, because each minimax move
        costs a 4-ply search). These games use a \emph{different} fixed set of
        random 6-ply openings from the learning curves, shared by every method
        and seed.
  \item[Why three opponents:] each answers a different question. Random asks
        whether the method plays sensible Othello at all. Heuristic asks how
        well it beats the opponent it trained against. Minimax-d4 asks how it
        fares against a much stronger player it never saw. Real playing skill

If Step 3.5 confirms this, pure self-play is best everywhere, and more league games make DQN slightly worse. That includes the in-league bots it trains against directly, which goes against my expectation that in-league scores would rise with p. That would support H2 (weak opponents give a poor training signal) and possibly H4 (the replay buffer filling with easy wins).

The differences are only 2–5 points, though, so the head-to-head matches, the bootstrap test and the checkpoint curves will decide whether they're real. I'll write Step 3.6 when the evaluation finishes.

%======================================================================
\section{Does Opponent Variety Help DQN?}
\label{sec:league}

Self-play always faces an opponent of exactly the learner's own strength and
style. A common alternative, used at scale by AlphaStar \cite{vinyals2019}, is
to train against a \emph{league}: a population of different opponents, so that
the learner meets many styles of play and cannot overfit to one. This section
asks whether such variety helps DQN on \bx{6}. The test is a controlled,
dose-response experiment: everything is held fixed except the share of training
games played against the league.

\subsection{Design}

\paragraph{The league.} The league consists of weak, fixed agents plus the
learner's own past snapshots (Table~\ref{tab:league_members}). Each game is
played against a league member with probability $p$, the \emph{league share},
and against the live learner (pure self-play) otherwise. League games go half to
a uniformly chosen fixed agent and half to a uniformly chosen snapshot, so the
league's make-up stays the same throughout training (until the first snapshot
exists, all league games go to fixed agents). We ran $p \in \{0, 0.25, 0.5,
0.75, 1\}$, with $p=0$ being pure self-play. The learner is the Double DQN of
\S\ref{sec:selfplay}, with identical network and hyperparameters: \TrainGames{}
games and 3 seeds per mix, so 15 runs in total.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{League members. ``Strength'' is each fixed agent's score against the
heuristic bot from the earlier sections (\S\ref{sec:bots}, \S\ref{sec:classical}).}
\label{tab:league_members}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Member & Kind & Strength vs heuristic (\%) \\
\midrule
\tabinput{report/tables/league_members.tex}
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Hypotheses.} Stated before the runs:
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[H1 (robustness):] variety makes DQN more robust, so it loses less to
        unfamiliar opponents.
  \item[H2 (weak signal):] once the weak members are beaten, games against them
        teach little, so league-only training ($p=1$) ends up weaker than
        self-play.
  \item[H3 (best mix):] an intermediate mix keeps self-play's matched-strength
        opponent while adding variety, so held-out strength peaks at an
        intermediate $p$.
  \item[H4 (replay dilution):] at high $p$ the replay buffer fills with games
        against weak opponents, which slows learning from the start.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Held-out evaluation.} Heuristic and minimax-d4 are now
\emph{training} opponents. As Monte Carlo control showed in
\S\ref{sec:classical}, a learner can score well against an opponent it trains
on without having learned the game. ``Better than self-play'' is therefore
judged on opponents the league learners never trained against, chosen to be
close to DQN's own strength so that differences are visible:
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[Head-to-head vs self-play:] every model plays the three $p=0$ models,
        200 games per pair of seeds.
  \item[Minimax at depths 2 and 3:] not in the league. They share the heuristic's
        evaluation function, so they are \emph{partly} related to two league
        members. A calibration run put Phase~2 DQN+ at 33\% and 25\% against
        them, so neither is too easy nor too hard.
  \item[Phase 2 PPO and DQN+:] completely unseen learned agents (3 seeds each,
        200 games per pair).
  \item[In-league bots:] random, heuristic and minimax-d4 are reported too, but
        marked as training opponents.
\end{description}
All matches use paired colours and fixed random 6-ply openings, separate from
those used in training. A mix \emph{beats self-play} only if the seed-level
bootstrap 95\% CI of its score agains

Phase 3 is complete. The answer is no: mixing in a league of weak opponents does not help DQN. The more league games, the weaker it gets. It's written up as a new report section, "Does Opponent Variety Help DQN?" (pages 23–28), the report compiles cleanly at 35 pages, and everything is committed.

Main result (score %; mean of 3 seeds; the first column is against the self-play DQNs, with a 95% interval):

p (league share) vs self-play vs minimax-d2 vs minimax-d3 vs Phase 2 PPO vs Phase 2 DQN+ vs heuristic (in-league)
0 (self-play) 50 [47.5, 52.5] 35.9 23.9 39.5 51.8 61.5
0.25 47.6 [45.7, 50.9] 33.7 23.7 40.3 48.8 61.0
0.5 48.4 [44.8, 51.2] 32.2 23.0 38.1 47.0 58.8
0.75 45.5 [41.9, 48.2] 30.8 21.1 35.0 45.5 55.6
1 (league only) 42.6 [38.7, 45.8] 30.4 21.2 33.8 41.6 55.0
  • No mix beats self-play under the rule fixed in advance. At p = 0.25 and 0.5 the result is a statistical tie; at p = 0.75 and 1 DQN is significantly worse.
  • The head-to-head matrix between mixes agrees without any outside opponent: lower-p mixes score level with or above every higher-p mix.
  • Surprise: scores against the training opponents (heuristic, minimax-d4) also fall as p grows. Each fixed member appears in only p/16 of games (about 6% even at p = 1), too few to memorise it, so in-league scores follow the learner's general strength downward.

Why it happens: the training logs show the league is a poor teacher. - Half of the fixed members (random and the three tabular agents) are beaten about 90% of the time almost from the start, and minimax-d4 wins most of its games. Lopsided games say little about which moves mattered. - Self-play gives an evenly matched game every time. - So replacing self-play games with league games means fewer informative games, and slower learning.

Hypotheses: - H1 (robustness): refuted. No gain against unfamiliar opponents. - H2 (weak signal): supported. - H3 (best mix): refuted. There's no peak at an intermediate mix; strength falls steadily. - H4 (replay dilution): partly supported. League-only runs lag from the first checkpoint, and the gap narrows but doesn't close. That can't be separated from the simpler explanation that they get fewer self-play games.

Side finding: pure self-play DQN is level with Phase 2's DQN+ (52%), so playing old snapshots of itself made no difference for DQN.

Report: the section contains: - the design, a league-members table and the four hypotheses stated before the runs; - the held-out evaluation and the decision rule; - six figures and two tables (score vs p, head-to-head matrix, best mix vs self-play, training scores per opponent, checkpoint curves, replay-buffer composition); - a verdict for each hypothesis, and limitations.

Next Steps now proposes rerunning the experiment with prioritised (PFSP) sampling, which picks opponents near the learner's strength.

Other notes: - Timing: the evaluation took about 3 hours instead of my 1–1.5 h estimate, so the phase finished around 11 pm. - Background "failure": the evaluation task was reported as failed, but only because my final summary command was malformed. All three stages completed and their outputs are correct. - Committed: the run results and final models. - Not committed: the 105 checkpoints are git-ignored (about 40 MB) but kept on disk, since Phase 4's exploiters can use them.

Next is Phase 4 (exploiters and blind spots). As agreed, its design needs your decisions first. The two still open: - Exploiter type: AlphaZero with victim modelling, PPO, or both. - Analysis scope: the exact-solver audit of all agents plus exploiters for the strong ones, or one exploiter per agent.

add an experiment to motivate self play. Claude's response

I'll add this as a motivation experiment for self-play: three DQNs, each trained against a different fixed opponent, then compared. I'll write it into PLAN.md as Step 2.9 first, since it motivates Phase 2's self-play, and then run it. Design choices I'm making (tell me if you want any changed):

  • Learner: Double DQN, the same as Phase 3's pure self-play DQN, so the self-play DQN can be the reference: "does self-play break the ceiling?"
  • Budget: 200k games × 3 seeds per opponent, the same as every other DQN in the project. That's 9 runs, about 2.5 h.
  • Comparisons:
  • Head-to-head: a round robin among DQN-random, DQN-heuristic, DQN-minimax-d3 and the self-play DQN, over all seed pairs.
  • Each against all the bots: against random, heuristic, minimax-d2, d3 and d4, which shows where each learner's strength tops out relative to its own trainer.
  • Learning curves: measured against minimax-d2, which none of the three trains against.
Bash: Add Step 2.9 to PLAN.md
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='PLAN.md'; s=open(p).read()
anchor="---\n\n## Phase 3: Does Opponent Variety Help DQN?"
assert anchor in s
step=r'''**Step 2.9 — Motivation: the fixed-opponent ceiling**
- **Why:** to motivate self-play. A learner trained against a fixed opponent only needs to become good enough to beat *that* opponent, so its strength may be capped near the opponent's level. Self-play has no such cap, because the opponent improves with the learner.
- **Objective & expectation:**
  - **Objective:** show that a DQN trained against a weaker opponent ends up weaker.
  - **Expectations** (hypotheses):
    - **(a)** strength orders by trainer: DQN-random < DQN-heuristic < DQN-minimax-d3, both head-to-head and against held-out bots;
    - **(b)** each learner does well against its own trainer and much worse against stronger ones, so its strength tops out near its trainer;
    - **(c)** the self-play DQN (Phase 3, p = 0) is at least as strong as DQN-minimax-d3, despite never playing a fixed opponent.
  - **Risk:** if the trainer is *too* strong, wins are rare and the learning signal is sparse. DQN+ scores about 25% against d3, so d3 should still be learnable.
- **Methodology:**
  - Three learners (DQN1, DQN2, DQN3), identical to Phase 3's self-play DQN (Double DQN, same network, buffer and schedule). The only difference is the training opponent: random, heuristic (ε = 0.05) or minimax-d3.
  - Compare them with each other, with the self-play DQN, and against a common panel of bots.
- **Experiment details:**
  - **Config:** `configs/fixed_opponent_dqn.yaml`, with runs `vs-random`, `vs-heuristic`, `vs-minimax-d3` × seeds {0, 1, 2} × 200k games; random 6-ply openings; alternating colours.
  - **Learning curve:** every 5k games, 200 games against **minimax-d2**, which none of the three trains against.
  - **Final evaluation** (openings seed 4243): random, heuristic and d2/d3/d4 (1,000 games each).
  - **Head-to-head round robin:** the 4 learner groups (DQN-random, DQN-heuristic, DQN-d3, self-play DQN), all 9 seed pairs per group pair, 200 games each. That's 6 group pairs × 1,800 games.
  - **Statistics:** mean ± std over seeds; 95% CIs per pairing; a seed-level bootstrap CI for each group-vs-group score.
  - **Output:** `results/fixed_opponent/`. The report gets a subsection at the start of the self-play section, "Why self-play? The ceiling of a fixed opponent".
  - **Resources:** 9 runs on 8 cores, ~2–2.5 h, plus ~30 min of evaluation.
- *Done when:* the head-to-head matrix, the bot-panel table and the learning curves are in the report, with hypotheses (a)–(c) explicitly confirmed or refuted.

'''
s=s.replace(anchor, step+anchor,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)

Bash: Write round-robin eval script and assets
cat > scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py <<'EOF'
"""Step 2.9 evaluation: round robin between fixed-opponent DQNs and the self-play DQN.

  python scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py
Writes results/fixed_opponent/h2h.json (every seed pair of every group pair).
"""
import json
import sys
from itertools import combinations
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from othello.eval.arena import play_match  # noqa: E402

GROUPS = {
    "dqn-random": "results/fixed_opponent/vs-random",
    "dqn-heuristic": "results/fixed_opponent/vs-heuristic",
    "dqn-minimax-d3": "results/fixed_opponent/vs-minimax-d3",
    "dqn-selfplay": "results/league/dqn/p0",
}
SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
OUT = ROOT / "results/fixed_opponent/h2h.json"


def main():
    res = json.loads(OUT.read_text()) if OUT.exists() else {}
    for ga, gb in combinations(GROUPS, 2):
        for sa in SEEDS:
            for sb in SEEDS:
                key = f"{ga}/seed{sa}|{gb}/seed{sb}"
                if key in res:
                    continue
                a = {"path": str(ROOT / GROUPS[ga] / f"seed{sa}")}
                b = {"path": str(ROOT / GROUPS[gb] / f"seed{sb}")}
                res[key] = play_match(6, a, b, 100, opening_plies=6, seed=4246, workers=8).summary()
                OUT.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
        print(ga, "vs", gb, flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF

The experiment is set up and the 9 training runs are going in the background: 8 now, and the 9th (minimax-d3, seed 2) starts when the first one finishes. All of them should be done in about 2½–3 hours.

What I did: - PLAN.md: added it as Step 2.9, "Motivation: the fixed-opponent ceiling", inside the self-play phase it motivates. It follows the usual format (why, objective and expectation, methodology, experiment details, done when) and states three hypotheses up front: - (a) strength orders by trainer: trained vs random < vs heuristic < vs minimax-d3; - (b) each learner tops out near its own trainer: good against it, much worse against anything stronger; - (c) the self-play DQN is at least as strong as the one trained against minimax-d3. - Learners: three Double DQNs, identical to Phase 3's self-play DQN except for the training opponent (random, heuristic or minimax-d3). 200k games × 3 seeds each. - Code: a run can now set its own training opponent, separate from the learning-curve opponent. I checked that each run trains against the right bot, and a smoke run works. - Learning curves are measured against minimax-d2, which none of the three trains against. - Already written: - scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py: a round robin between the three fixed-opponent DQNs and Phase 3's self-play DQN, over all seed pairs (6 group pairs × 1,800 games). - Report assets: a table of each learner against all five bots, with its own trainer's cell marked; grouped bars; a 4×4 head-to-head heat-map with bootstrap intervals; and learning curves with a reference line at the self-play DQN's final score.

One risk is written into the plan: if a trainer is too strong, the learner rarely wins and gets little signal. DQN scores about 25% against minimax-d3, so it should still be learnable. If DQN-d3 underperforms, that would be a result in itself: an opponent can be too strong as well as too weak, which is another argument for self-play's always-matched opponent.

When training finishes, I'll run the round robin (about 30 min), generate the figures, and write the new subsection at the start of the self-play section: "Why self-play? The ceiling of a fixed opponent".
