Turn 44

in the traditional method phase - how are the Q learning method doing bootstrap if there is a singular +-1 reward at the end of the game "?
Claude's response

Q-learning bootstraps from its own estimates of later positions, not from rewards. The reward stays zero until the end, but every intermediate step still has a target: the value the table currently assigns to the next position.

The update in our implementation (othello/rl/tabular.py, end_episode): - For the learner's last move: target = the final reward, +1 / 0 / −1. - For every earlier move: target = r + γ · maxₐ′ Q(s′, a′) = 0 + 1 · maxₐ′ Q(s′, a′). Here s′ is the learner's next decision position (after the opponent replies), and unvisited entries read as 0.

So intermediate targets are not "zero reward". They're "whatever I currently believe about the next position". The ±1 enters only at the final step, and bootstrapping is how it travels backwards.

How the reward travels back, one step per visit. Take a line of play that ends in a win: 1. First game: only the last position's entry moves toward +1. Every earlier entry bootstraps from next positions that are still 0, so they get target 0. 2. The next time the same second-to-last position comes up: its target is now that last position's value, which is no longer 0, so it moves too. 3. And so on: each revisit carries the information back one more move.

After a 6-ply opening a 6x6 game has roughly 20 more plies, so the learner makes about 10 moves. The result therefore needs about 10 separate revisits of the same line to reach its early positions.

That is exactly why tabular Q-learning fails here. The tables end with 1–2 million positions, and fewer than 1 in 10 positions met against random were ever seen in training. Lines are almost never revisited, so the result never gets past the last few moves: early-game entries keep target 0 and the agent plays essentially at random. The report attributes the tabular TD methods' failure to this, under "Why Q-learning and SARSA are indistinguishable". When the next position is unvisited, the greedy entry (Q-learning) and the actually-taken entry (SARSA) both read 0, so their targets coincide.

Why the other methods do better with the same single reward: - Monte Carlo control doesn't bootstrap. It moves every visited entry straight toward the final result after each game, so one game informs the whole line at once. That's why it learned something, though mostly lines specific to its training opponent. - Linear function approximation and DQN bootstrap the same way, but max Q(s′, ·) is a prediction from features or network weights, not a table lookup. It's informative even for positions never seen before, so the reward spreads through similarity between positions instead of needing exact revisits.

One implementation detail: we apply the updates at the end of each game, in forward order. Since Othello positions never repeat within a game, that's identical to standard online Q-learning, which also passes the reward back only one step per visit. Processing the game backwards, or using eligibility traces as in TD(λ), would carry it further per game. We deliberately kept textbook one-step Q-learning.

Turn 45

No my question is , if there is a line hit, what is the value of r for an update to the table entry?
Claude's response

r = 0 on every move of the line except the learner's last one, even when the line has been seen before. Our rewards are only ever +1 / 0 / −1 at the end of the game. A revisit doesn't change r; what changes is the bootstrap term, because the table now holds non-zero values from earlier games.

Q-learning / SARSA (α = 0.1, γ = 1). Say the same winning line is played twice, with learner positions … s₈, s₉, s₁₀ (s₁₀ = its last move):

Update r Target New Q
Game 1, last move s₁₀ +1 1 0 + 0.1·(1 − 0) = 0.1
Game 1, s₉ 0 0 + max Q(s₁₀,·) = 0 (forward order: s₁₀ not yet updated) 0
Game 2, s₉ 0 0 + max Q(s₁₀,·) = 0.1 0 + 0.1·(0.1 − 0) = 0.01
Game 2, s₁₀ +1 1 0.1 + 0.1·(1 − 0.1) = 0.19
Game 3, s₈ 0 0 + max Q(s₉,·) = 0.01 0.001

So the "line hit" itself always gets r = 0. The value creeps backwards by one position per revisit and shrinks along the way. After a few revisits the early positions still hold values close to 0.

Monte Carlo control (which the lines you selected, 717–718, are about) is different. It doesn't use per-step r at all. After the game, every position on the line is updated toward the final result G = +1 / 0 / −1 directly: Q ← Q + (1/N)·(G − Q). So when the same line comes back, all of its entries move toward that line's outcome immediately: after the first win each is at 1.0, and after win, win, loss each is at 1/3. That's why MC could "memorise" winning lines against the near-deterministic heuristic bot while Q-learning and SARSA, stuck with r = 0 and tiny bootstrapped values, never could.

Turn 46

where is the algorithm for the linear bot? how do we know it gneralizes between symmetric positions ?
Claude's response

The algorithm is in othello/rl/linear.py, class LinearQLearner, and the report describes it in Section 4.1 under "Linear function-approximation Q-learning".

How it works: - phi(after, me) computes 6 features of the afterstate (the position right after the learner's move), each "own minus opponent" and scaled to roughly unit range: bias, disc difference, mobility difference, corner difference, X-square difference, and stable-edge-disc difference. - The value of a move is a weighted sum: Q(s, a) = w · φ(after(s, a)). - act() plays ε-greedily over the legal moves by this value, breaking ties at random. - end_episode() applies semi-gradient Q-learning to each of the learner's moves. The target is r + max over next moves of w · φ, or the final ±1 for the last move, and the update is w ← w + α(target − w · φ(after)) · φ(after), with α = 0.01.

Why it handles symmetric positions: every feature is a quantity that doesn't change when the board is rotated or reflected:

Feature Why it's unchanged under the 8 board symmetries
disc difference just counts discs
mobility difference the number of legal moves is unchanged (move generation commutes with the symmetries; tests/test_symmetry.py checks all 8)
corners each symmetry maps corners onto corners
X-squares X-squares map onto X-squares, and their adjacent corners onto corners
stable edge discs edges map onto edges and corners onto corners, so edge runs anchored at corners map onto each other
bias constant

So a position and all its rotations and reflections have identical feature vectors, and the linear model gives them exactly the same value. This isn't learned; it's built into the features. The tabular methods only got this by explicitly storing positions in a canonical form, and DQN, which sees raw board planes, does not have it.

I hadn't actually tested this before, so here's a quick check:

Bash: Verify linear features are symmetry-invariant
python3 - <<'EOF'
import random, numpy as np
from othello.env import OthelloEnv, State
from othello.symmetry import get_symmetry
from othello.rl.linear import LinearQLearner
env=OthelloEnv(6); sym=get_symmetry(6); L=LinearQLearner(env,0); rng=random.Random(0)
worst=0.0; n=0
for g in range(300):
    s=env.initial_state()
    while not env.is_terminal(s):
        for t in range(8):
            st=State(sym.transform_bits(s.black,t), sym.transform_bits(s.white,t), s.player, s.passes)
            for me in (0,1):
                worst=max(worst, float(np.abs(L.phi(s,me)-L.phi(st,me)).max())); n+=1
        s=env.step(s, rng.choice(env.legal_moves(s)))
print(f"compared {n} (position, transform, side) feature vectors; max abs difference = {worst}")
EOF
Output
compared 155920 (position, transform, side) feature vectors; max abs difference = 0.0

The algorithm is in othello/rl/linear.py (class LinearQLearner), and the report describes it in Section 4.1 under "Linear function-approximation Q-learning".

How it works: - Features: phi() turns the position right after the learner's move into 6 features, each "own minus opponent": bias, disc difference, mobility difference, corner difference, X-square difference and stable edge discs. - Value of a move: a weighted sum of those features. - Learning: end_episode() updates the weights with standard Q-learning targets (learning rate 0.01).

Why it generalises between symmetric positions: every feature is unchanged when the board is rotated or reflected: - discs, mobility and the bias don't depend on orientation; - corners always map to corners, X-squares to X-squares, and edges to edges.

So a position and its 7 rotated or reflected versions get identical features, and therefore identical values. The tabular methods only got this because their tables explicitly store one canonical version of each position. DQN, which sees the raw board, doesn't get it.

I checked this directly: across 300 random games, every position and all 8 symmetries, from both players' sides (155,920 feature vectors in total), the features were identical.

The same property is also what limits the linear model. Many genuinely different positions share the same feature values too, so it can't tell them apart. That's the capacity ceiling behind its early plateau at roughly the heuristic bot's strength in Section 4.

This check isn't in the test suite yet. Should I add it as a unit test and mention it in the linear paragraph of Section 4.1?

# Othello Player — Specification

A desktop application for playing Othello on your own machine. You can play against the computer at several difficulty levels, with the hardest levels played by **Oroletto**, the AlphaZero-style agent trained in the companion research repo [OthelloRL](../OthelloRL). Two people can also play each other on the same computer.

The user interface will be designed in iterations, so the architecture keeps the **UI layer cleanly separate** from the game engine and the AI.

Status: **draft v0.1** — sections marked ❓ need a decision before implementation starts.

---

## 1. Goals and non-goals

**Goals (v1)**
- A real, self-contained **application binary** that anyone can **build from source** on Linux, macOS and Windows. It runs offline, with no Python or ML framework installed.
- A polished, responsive UI that is easy to restyle and iterate on.
- **Play vs Computer** at graded difficulty levels, with Oroletto behind the hardest ones.
- **Two-player (local, same screen)** mode.
- Correct rules in every situation, including forced passes, double-pass endings and full boards.

**Non-goals (v1)**
- Online or networked multiplayer, accounts, matchmaking, ratings.
- Training or modifying models inside the app; models are produced in OthelloRL and shipped as files.
- Mobile apps (the architecture shouldn't rule them out later).

---

## 2. Users and core flows

1. **Launch** → home screen with: *Play vs Computer*, *Two Players*, *How to Play*, *Settings*.
2. **Play vs Computer** → choose difficulty, your colour (Black / White / Random) and board size → game screen.
3. **Two Players** → optional player names, board size → game screen. Players take turns on the same device.
4. **Game screen** → play to the end → result dialog (score, winner) → *Rematch*, *Swap colours* or *Home*.
5. **How to Play** → short illustrated rules: placing, flipping, passing and the end of the game, with the same examples as the report's rules figure.

---

## 3. Functional requirements

### 3.1 Board and rules
- Board sizes: **6×6** and **8×8** ❓ (see §8.2). Standard start position; **Black moves first**.
- Legal-move generation, flipping in all 8 directions, **forced pass** when a player has no legal move (shown clearly, never silent), game ending after two consecutive passes or a full board, and disc counts.
- The engine must reproduce OthelloRL's results exactly: perft counts on 8×8 (depth 1–6: 4, 12, 56, 244, 1396, 8200) and the 6×6 rules cases from OthelloRL's test suite.

### 3.2 Game screen
- Board with discs, coordinates (a–h / 1–8), **legal-move hints** (toggleable), **last-move highlight**, and **flip animation**.
- Live disc counts and a whose-turn indicator. In vs-Computer mode, a "thinking…" indicator while the AI moves.
- **Pass banner** ("White has no legal move — Black plays again").
- Controls: **Undo** (vs Computer: undoes your move and the AI's reply; Two Players: one move), **New game**, **Hint** (vs Computer only; optional, uses Oroletto), **Resign**.
- Move list / history panel (optional in v1, desirable).
- Input: mouse/touch click on a square; keyboard navigation (arrows + Enter) for accessibility.

### 3.3 Play vs Computer — difficulty levels
The rule-based levels port the bots from OthelloRL (same evaluation weights). Oroletto plays the harder levels. Its strength is controlled by the number of MCTS simulations, so the same network gives a smooth range of difficulty.

| Level | Name | Engine | Approx. strength (from the OthelloRL report, 6×6) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Beginner | random legal moves | — |
| 2 | Easy | greedy disc-count bot | barely above random |
| 3 | Medium | tuned heuristic bot (corners 50, mobility 5, discs 1, X-squares −25) | beats random ~90% |
| 4 | Hard | **Oroletto, network only** (no search) | ~level with minimax depth 4 |
| 5 | Expert | **Oroletto + MCTS, 64 simulations** | beats minimax-d4 ~78% |
| 6 | Master | **Oroletto + MCTS, 400 simulations** | stronger still (not yet measur

how will I take alpha zero from here and put it there also how should the bots for the four different levels be chosen/trainedn?
Claude's response

Part 1: Moving AlphaZero (Oroletto) from OthelloRL into the app

Oroletto is more than a weights file. It's three things, and the app needs all three: 1. The network: results/alphazero/seed1/model.pt, about 1.2 MB of PyTorch weights. 2. The search: MCTS with the same rules: c_puct = 1.5, no root noise when playing, the most-visited move chosen, and values flipped each ply. 3. The input format: 3 planes (own discs, opponent discs, legal moves) from the side to move, and 37 outputs (36 squares + pass).

The hand-off, step by step:

Step Where What
1. Export OthelloRL, new scripts/export_onnx.py Load the network and export it to ONNX, a framework-neutral model format that runs without PyTorch. Input [batch, 3, 6, 6] → outputs policy_logits [batch, 37] and value [batch].
2. Verify the export OthelloRL On a few hundred real positions, the ONNX outputs must match PyTorch's to within 1e-5.
3. Manifest OthelloRL → app oroletto-6x6.json: board size, plane order, c_puct, simulations per level, run id, OthelloRL commit hash, and a checksum of the .onnx file. You can always trace which experiment the app's Oroletto came from.
4. Reference cases OthelloRL → app tests/fixtures/ A JSON file of positions with the expected network outputs and the move OthelloRL's search picks at fixed settings (deterministic tie-break).
5. Copy in app models/ oroletto-6x6.onnx and its manifest. At 1.2 MB it's fine to keep in git.
6. Re-implement the search app The move generator, the encoder and MCTS, written in the app's language (Rust if Tauri). The model runs through tract-onnx (Rust) or onnxruntime (Python).
7. Parity tests app CI The app must reproduce the reference outputs and moves from step 4. If they don't match, the app isn't playing the real Oroletto.

Later Orolettos: a new model (e.g. from Phase 5, or an 8x8 one from Phase 6) gets re-exported as a new versioned file, and the app picks the model by board size.

Part 2: Choosing the levels

I'd not train a separate bot per level. Better: - Take a few strong agents we already have. - Make them weaker or stronger with one adjustable setting. - Measure the ladder with real games so the steps are even.

Adjustable settings, roughly best to worst: - Search budget (simulations per move): fewer simulations means a weaker but still sensible player. This is the main control for the hard levels. - Move temperature: sample from Oroletto's move preferences instead of always taking the top move. Its mistakes look plausible, like a human's near-misses. - Random blunders (ε): occasionally play a random move. It's simple, but feels "dumb" (giving away corners for no reason), so use it only on the easiest levels.

Proposed 4-level ladder. Your message says four levels; the spec currently has six, so this is a condensed version:

Level Engine Why
1 Easy Greedy disc-count bot, with some randomness Plays the classic beginner mistake (grabbing discs), so it's beatable and teaches the disc-count trap
2 Medium Tuned heuristic bot Values corners and mobility; beats random about 90% of the time
3 Hard Oroletto, network only (maybe with a small temperature) About level with minimax depth 4, plays instantly
4 Expert Oroletto + MCTS, about 200–400 simulations Beats minimax-d4 about 78% of the time at 64 simulations; stronger with more

Two alternatives worth knowing about: - Checkpoints as levels: early training snapshots of AlphaZero are naturally weaker, and their mistakes come from a less-trained model rather than random noise. Phase 2 didn't save AlphaZero checkpoints, though, so this would need a retraining run of about 8 hours with checkpointing on. - "Meet the agents" mode: let players face the project's own learners (Q-learning, linear, DQN, PPO) as a showcase of the report. It's fun, but their strength is uneven (MC control is the obvious example), so they make a poor difficulty ladder.

Calibrating the ladder. This would be a small experiment, run with OthelloRL's evaluation tools: 1. Choose candidate settings for each level (e.g. simulations 0 / 16 / 64 / 200 / 400, a few temperatures). 2. Play each candidate against its neighbours, 400 games each with the usual openings and colour swaps. 3. Pick settings so that each level beats the one below it about 70–75% of the time. That's a clear but not crushing step. 4. Measure the time per move on an ordinary laptop and keep every level under 2 seconds. 5. Write the chosen settings into the manifest, so the app just reads them.

The project's final combined Elo step (F.0) would put these levels on the same scale as every other agent, which makes a neat "app levels vs research agents" table for the report.

Board-size note: Oroletto plays only 6x6. On 8x8, the app would need minimax (depth 3–5) for the hard levels until the Phase 6 model exists.

Next steps, once you confirm: 1. Write the ONNX export script, manifest and reference cases in OthelloRL. It's small, and verified against PyTorch. 2. Run the level-calibration experiment. About an hour of compute after the current training finishes.

Do you want 4 levels or 6? And are you happy with Oroletto taking the top two?

1. Distilling Oroletto into 4 levels

Yes. Distillation means training a smaller "student" network to imitate a stronger "teacher", here Oroletto. It suits the app well. A small student can't represent everything the teacher knows, so it comes out naturally weaker. Its mistakes are "almost Oroletto's move" rather than random blunders, so every level feels like the same player at a different skill level.

One caveat: Oroletto is already small (0.3M parameters, 1.2 MB), so we don't need distillation for speed. Its value here is the ladder, plus an interesting research result: how much of Oroletto's strength survives compression.

Proposed design: - Teacher data: Oroletto with 200 MCTS simulations plays itself from random 6-ply openings, recording each position, its search visit distribution and the final result. About 300–500k positions, a few hours of compute. - Students: the same input and outputs as Oroletto, at decreasing sizes:

Student Size Expected role
S-tiny fully connected network, ~5k parameters Level 1
S-small 1 residual block × 16 channels, ~10k parameters Level 2
S-medium 2 blocks × 32 channels, ~40k parameters Level 3 (or Oroletto network-only, whichever calibrates better)
Oroletto + MCTS 4 × 64 channels + search Level 4
  • Training: cross-entropy to the teacher's search distribution, mean-squared error on the value, and random rotations and reflections, as in AlphaZero. These are cheap, a few minutes to an hour each.
  • Bonus result: a teacher-sized student trained on search distributions may even be stronger than Oroletto's own network without search. That would be "distilling search into the network", worth one row in the report.
  • Calibration:
  • Play each candidate against its neighbours (400 games, standard protocol).
  • Choose the 4 levels so that each beats the one below about 70–75% of the time.
  • Check that every level stays under 2 s per move.
  • Record the chosen settings in the app manifest.

If the smallest student is still too strong for a beginner, Level 1 can add a little move temperature. - Export: each chosen student is exported to ONNX with its own manifest, through the same pipeline as Oroletto.

I'd add this to PLAN.md as an "App models" side track, with the usual why / objective / methodology / experiment details / done-when.

To confirm before I start: - Level 1: should it be a tiny distilled student, or stay a simple rule-based bot (greedy disc-count)? - Teacher data: is the ~3–4 h data-generation run OK? It would start after the current experiment finishes.

Claude's response

Step 2.9 is already running, with design choices I made when you asked for the experiment. Here they are, so you can confirm or change them. The random and heuristic runs are done; the minimax-d3 runs are about half-way. Changing anything means rerunning the affected arm: about 2 h for the random or heuristic arm, about 4.5 h for the d3 arm.

Decisions taken so far

# Decision What I chose Why Alternatives / risks
1 Learner Double DQN, identical to Phase 3's self-play DQN The only difference from the self-play learner is who it trains against Vanilla DQN as in Phase 1. A side benefit of the current choice: the arm trained vs heuristic can be compared with Phase 1's classical DQN, which had the same opponent and a different DQN variant.
2 Fixed opponents random, heuristic (5% random moves), minimax-d3 Clearly increasing strength. DQN still wins ~25% against d3, so it isn't hopeless. minimax-d4 is stronger, but DQN only scores ~19% against it, and every training move would cost a depth-4 search. Caveat: heuristic and d3 share the same evaluation function, so the ladder from heuristic up differs mainly in lookahead, not style.
3 Budget 200k games × 3 seeds each Equal games for every learner, matching every other DQN in the project Equal compute would give the d3 arm fewer games, since it is about 2.5× slower per game
4 Learning-curve opponent minimax-d2, which none of them trains against A common yardstick during training d2 shares the heuristic's evaluation, which may slightly favour the arms trained vs heuristic and d3. The fully unseen PPO agent would be cleaner, but costs more.
5 Main comparison A round robin between the 3 fixed-opponent DQNs and the self-play DQN, plus each against all 5 bots Head-to-head needs no outside reference, so it can't be biased by one Adding Phase 1's classical DQN as a fifth group costs little

Two points worth discussing

A. The hypothesis needs sharper wording. "Limited by the strength of its opponent" isn't literally true. Phase 1's DQN, trained only against the heuristic bot, beats it 65% of the time, so a learner can outgrow its trainer a little. The real limit is that the learning target is frozen: - once the learner beats its opponent reliably, almost every game is a win, which carries little information, so progress stalls; - self-play keeps raising the bar, because the opponent improves with the learner.

So the clearest evidence won't only be the final ranking. It will be the training curves against each learner's own opponent: e.g. the DQN trained vs random should hit about 95% early and then stop improving against everything else. I'd make that the central figure.

B. The result might be an inverted U rather than a clean ordering. Phase 3 showed lopsided games teach little. That cuts both ways: against random almost every game is a win, and against d3 most are losses. So the d3 arm might not end up strongest. If that happens, the conclusion becomes richer, and still favours self-play: a fixed opponent is the wrong difficulty either way, too easy to learn from or too hard to win against, while self-play is always evenly matched. I'd write the decision rules in advance so neither outcome can be explained away after the fact.

Possible additions

  • A curriculum arm: random → heuristic → d3, switching when the learner wins about 70% of the time. A hand-made "rising opponent" sits between fixed opponents and self-play and is a natural bridge to the self-play section. It's one more arm, 3 seeds, about 3–4 h.
  • Pre-specified decision rules, like Phase 3's:
  • (a) ordering: each adjacent pair's head-to-head bootstrap interval excludes 50% in favour of the stronger-trained one;
  • (b) ceiling: each learner's score against its own trainer plateaus while it stays well below 50% against stronger bots;
  • (c) self-play: the self-play DQN's interval against every fixed-opponent DQN lies at or above 50%.

"""Step 2.9 evaluation: fixed-opponent DQNs vs each other, the self-play DQN and the bots.

  python scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py panel     # Phase 1 classical DQN vs minimax-d2/d3
  python scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py trainer   # checkpoints vs own trainer + other fixed bots
  python scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py h2h       # round robin between the 5 learner groups
  python scripts/eval_fixed_opponent.py all

Outputs (all resumable) in results/fixed_opponent/: classical_panel.json,
trainer_curves.json, h2h.json.
"""
import argparse
import json
import shutil
import sys
import tempfile
from itertools import combinations
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from othello.eval.arena import play_match  # noqa: E402
from othello.utils.config import load_json  # noqa: E402

OUT = ROOT / "results/fixed_opponent"
SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
W = load_json(ROOT / "results/baselines/heuristic_tuning.json")["best"]
BOTS = {"random": {"type": "random"},
        "heuristic": {"type": "heuristic", "kwargs": {"epsilon": 0.05, "weights": W}},
        "minimax-d2": {"type": "minimax", "kwargs": {"depth": 2, "weights": W}},
        "minimax-d3": {"type": "minimax", "kwargs": {"depth": 3, "weights": W}}}
RUNS = {"vs-random": "random", "vs-heuristic": "heuristic", "vs-minimax-d3": "minimax-d3"}
GROUPS = {
    "dqn-random": "results/fixed_opponent/vs-random",
    "dqn-heuristic": "results/fixed_opponent/vs-heuristic",
    "dqn-minimax-d3": "results/fixed_opponent/vs-minimax-d3",
    "dqn-selfplay": "results/league/dqn/p0",
    "dqn-classical": "results/classical/dqn",
}


def match(a, b, n_open, seed):
    return play_match(6, a, b, n_open, opening_plies=6, seed=seed, workers=8).summary()


def _load(path):
    return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else {}


def panel():
    """Phase 1 classical DQN vs the bots its final.json lacks (minimax-d2/d3)."""
    path = OUT / "classical_panel.json"
    res = _load(path)
    for s in SEEDS:
        for bot in ("minimax-d2", "minimax-d3"):
            key = f"seed{s}/{bot}"
            if key not in res:
                res[key] = match({"path": str(ROOT / f"results/classical/dqn/seed{s}")}, BOTS[bot], 500, 4243)
                path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
                print(key, round(res[key]["score"], 3), flush=True)


def trainer():
    """Each fixed-opponent run's checkpoints vs its own trainer and the other fixed bots."""
    path = OUT / "trainer_curves.json"
    res = _load(path)
    tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    for run in RUNS:
        for s in SEEDS:
            d = ROOT / "results/fixed_opponent" / run / f"seed{s}"
            cks = [(int(c.stem[1:]), c) for c in sorted((d / "ckpt").glob("g*.pt"))] + [(200_000, d / "model.pt")]
            for games, ck in cks:
                key = f"{run}/seed{s}/g{games:06d}"
                if key in res:
                    continue
                rd = tmp / key.replace("/", "_")      # a run-like dir so load_model works
                rd.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                shutil.copy(d / "config.json", rd / "config.json")
                shutil.copy(ck, rd / "model.pt")
                me = {"path": str(rd)}
                res[key] = {"games": games, "trainer": RUNS[run],
                            **{b: match(me, BOTS[b], 100, 4247) for b in ("random", "heuristic", "minimax-d3")}}
                path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
                print(key, {b: round(res[key][b]["score"], 3) for b in ("random", "heuristic", "minimax-d3")},
                      flush=True)


def h2h():
    path = OUT / "h2h.json"
    res = _load(path)
    for ga, gb in combinations(GROUPS, 2):
        for sa in SEEDS:
            for sb in SEEDS:

Phase 4 brainstorm: multi-agent co-evolution vs self-play

Motivation

  • Phase 3 left a question open. Variety from a weak, fixed league hurt DQN. But that experiment changed two things at once: it added variety, and it mismatched the opponent's strength, since most games were lopsided. Co-evolution keeps the variety but makes every opponent adaptive and roughly matched, because the other agents are learning too. It separates the two effects: does variety help when the opponents are well matched?
  • Self-play may overfit to its own style. One agent playing copies of itself only ever sees one way of playing. Independent agents may each find different strategies, and test each other's weaknesses. That's the idea behind competitive co-evolution (Rosin & Belew 1997), population-based training (Jaderberg et al. 2017/2019) and AlphaStar's league.
  • It might cycle instead of improving. Populations can chase each other in rock-paper-scissors loops: A beats B, B beats C, C beats A. Whether Othello allows this or is largely transitive is interesting in itself.
  • It may be a better use of each game. In a co-evolution game both players are learners, so one game trains two agents. Our self-play DQN learns only from its own side's moves.

Methodology

  • Population: N independent DQN learners: separate networks, replay buffers, optimisers and seeds, all identical to the self-play DQN from Phases 3 and 2.9.
  • Games: each game pairs two different members, so nobody plays its own copy. Both learn from their own moves.
  • Self-play is N = 1 (Phase 3's p = 0 models), which makes it the natural baseline.
  • Pairing (matchmaking):
  • uniform: any two members;
  • strength-matched: partners with similar recent win rates; this is closest to Phase 3's lesson that matched games teach most;
  • optionally prioritised (AlphaStar-style), preferring opponents the agent struggles against.
  • Budget fairness: report two comparisons:
  • F1, equal games per agent: each member plays 200k games, like each self-play DQN.
  • F2, equal total compute: the population shares the same number of games as one self-play run.
  • Why DQN first, not AlphaZero: it continues Phase 3 and Step 2.9 directly, it's cheap, and its baselines already exist. An AlphaZero population would need the batched runner (Step 4.0) and 5+ hours per run, so it would come later, if DQN shows something.

Experiments

# Experiment Purpose Cost (approx.)
E1 DQN populations, N ∈ {2, 4, 8}, uniform pairing, F1, 3 seeds Core: population size vs self-play N = 8 is 800k games per run; ~8–10 h wall in parallel
E2 N = 4, strength-matched pairing Does matched pairing beat uniform? ~4 h
E3 N = 4 with 50% self-play mixed in Co-evolution as a supplement to self-play, not a replacement ~4 h
E4 (optional) AlphaZero population, N = 4, 30k games per agent Does the answer hold for the strongest learner? ~1 day

Evaluation (same panel as Phase 3 and Step 2.9, so everything is comparable): - head-to-head against the self-play DQN; - held-out opponents: minimax-d2 and d3, Phase 2 PPO and DQN+; - the population's best member, chosen by within-population results only, so we don't pick the member that happens to do best on the test; - diversity: how often members disagree on their move over a fixed set of 1,000 positions. Key baseline: how often independent self-play seeds disagree, since some diversity appears without co-evolution; - non-transitivity: a win-rate matrix between members' checkpoints, counting rock-paper-scissors cycles that are statistically significant; - strength over time: checkpoints every 25k games against fixed opponents; - exploitability: later, in Phase 5, whose exploiters also target the population models.

Expected results (hypotheses)

  1. Per-agent strength (F1): members end up about level with self-play. Their opponents are matched only roughly, so we don't expect a big gain. The population's best member may edge ahead.
  2. Variety helps once opponents are matched: if Phase 3's loss came from lopsided games rather than variety itself, co-evolution should not show Phase 3's decline. Seeing it again would mean variety itself hurts DQN.
  3. Diversity: members' policies differ more than independent self-play seeds do. If they don't, the population has effectively collapsed into one strategy.
  4. Robustness: gains, if any, show up most against unseen learned opponents (PPO, DQN+) rather than against the minimax bots.
  5. Transitivity: Othello is largely transitive (it's a small game with a clear best strategy), so we expect few or no significant cycles. Any cycle we did find would be a notable result.
  6. Population size: larger N gives more diversity but slower early progress per agent, since partners match less closely. Strength-matched pairing should reduce that cost.
  7. Equal compute (F2): each game trains two learners, so co-evolution might match self-play even with the budget split N ways. That's the most practically useful question.

Decisions needed

Claude's response

Pairing: who plays whom

Every training game needs two different population members. The pairing rule decides which two. Two facts apply to every option: - At N = 2 every rule is the same: the two members always play each other. Pairing only matters at N = 4 and 8. - Each game trains both players. If a rule picks some members more often, they get more training. So any rule other than uniform needs a scheduler that keeps each member's game count equal: the member with the fewest games so far chooses its partner by the rule. Without that, strength differences could just reflect more training.

1. Uniform - How: each game picks two different members at random. Everyone plays everyone about equally often. - For: the simplest, with no tuning and no feedback loops. It's the clean baseline: "does co-evolution itself help?" - Against: if members drift apart in strength, many games become lopsided, which Phase 3 showed teach little. Members share the same algorithm and budget, so they'll probably stay fairly close, but at N = 8 some spread is likely.

2. Strength-matched (prefer evenly matched opponents) - How: keep a running win rate p for each pair of members over recent games. The chooser picks partner j with weight p(1 − p), which is highest for a 50/50 matchup. The first 10k games use uniform pairing to get these estimates. This is AlphaStar's "PFSP-even" weighting. - For: it targets Phase 3's lesson directly, since evenly matched games are the informative ones. It's the most direct test of "variety plus matched strength". - Against: the population can split into cliques that mostly play among themselves, which reduces the very variety we want to test. We'd watch the pairing matrix for this.

3. Prioritised, "hard" (PFSP) (prefer opponents you lose to) - How: weight (1 − p)², so the opponents the chooser struggles against come up most. This is AlphaStar's main league rule. - For: it attacks each member's weaknesses, and could make members more robust (relevant for Phase 5's exploiters). - Against: if one member pulls ahead, everyone keeps playing it, and the dynamics can be unstable. It's also the rule we set aside for later in Phase 3.

4. Uniform + 50% self-play - How: each member plays half its games against its own live copy (pure self-play) and half against other members, chosen uniformly. - For: it tests co-evolution as a supplement to self-play, the natural follow-up to Phase 3, where mixing in a weak league hurt. If anything helps without risk, it's this. - Against: any effect is diluted, so differences from pure self-play will be small and need the full 3 seeds to detect.

My recommendation: - Uniform as the main rule, across N = 2, 4 and 8. - Strength-matched and +50% self-play as two extra variants at N = 4 only. - PFSP stays deferred, as in Phase 3.

That's 3 + 2 = 5 configurations × 3 seeds.

Your questions have been answered: "Which pairing rules should Phase 4 run?"="Uniform at N=2,4,8 (Recommended)". You can now continue with these answers in mind.

Pairing is decided: uniform pairing at N = 2, 4 and 8. With uniform pairing every member plays about the same number of games automatically, so no scheduler is needed.

Budget fairness: what counts as a fair comparison with self-play

The self-play baseline is one DQN playing 200k games against its live copy, learning only from its own moves. In a population each game involves two members, and both learn. So "same budget" can mean two different things:

F1: equal games per agent - Each member plays 200k games, the same experience as the self-play DQN. - Total games: N × 200k / 2, i.e. 200k (N = 2), 400k (N = 4), 800k (N = 8). - The question it answers: with the same experience, does an agent learn more from varied, adaptive opponents than from itself? That's the scientific question. - Compute: the population uses about N times the total compute. N = 8 is the expensive one (~10 h per seed; seeds run in parallel). - Comparison: the average member against self-play is the primary measure. - The best member of 8 has an unfair advantage, since picking the luckiest of 8 inflates it. We have only 3 self-play seeds to match it against. - The best member is still reported, chosen using games within the population only, and flagged as best-of-N.

F2: equal total compute - The whole population shares 200k games, the same total as one self-play run. - Per member: 2 × 200k / N games, i.e. 200k (N = 2), 100k (N = 4), 50k (N = 8). - The question it answers: with a fixed compute budget, are you better off training one agent by self-play or a population? That's the practical question. - Expected outcome: members get less experience as N grows, so they'll probably be weaker at N = 8. The interesting question is whether training two learners per game makes up for it at N = 4. - N = 2 is identical in F1 and F2, so it isn't run twice. - Cost: each F2 run costs the same as one self-play run (~2–3 h). The extra runs are N = 4 and 8 × 3 seeds, all in parallel. - A shortcut that doesn't quite work: F2 at N = 4 resembles the 100k-game checkpoint of the F1 N = 4 run. But the exploration schedule depends on the planned budget (ε decays over the first half), so the two aren't identical. Running F2 properly is cheap enough.

My recommendation: report both. F1 is primary (N = 2, 4, 8), and F2 adds runs at N = 4 and 8. That's 5 configurations × 3 seeds = 15 runs, roughly 10–12 h of wall-clock time, dominated by the F1 N = 8 run.

"""Co-evolution: N independent learners that train only by playing each other.

Every game pairs two *different* members drawn uniformly at random; both
members act with their own exploration schedule and both learn from their own
moves (one game trains two learners). Members never play a copy of themselves.
Each member keeps its own game counter, which drives its epsilon schedule,
its evaluation/checkpoint timing and its logs, so a member is directly
comparable with a single self-play DQN that played the same number of games.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import json
import random
import time
from pathlib import Path

from othello.agents.registry import make_agent
from othello.eval.arena import make_openings
from othello.rl.common import epsilon_at, evaluate, final_eval


def play_pair(env, a, b, opening, a_is_black):
    """One training game between learners a and b. Returns (traj_a, traj_b, margin_a)."""
    s = env.initial_state()
    for m in opening:
        s = env.step(s, m)
    colour = {0: a if a_is_black else b, 1: b if a_is_black else a}
    trajs = {id(a): [], id(b): []}
    while not env.is_terminal(s):
        mover = colour[s.player]
        act = mover.act(s, explore=True)
        trajs[id(mover)].append((s, act))
        s = env.step(s, act)
    margin_black = env.score(s)
    margin_a = margin_black if a_is_black else -margin_black
    return trajs[id(a)], trajs[id(b)], margin_a


def _rewards(traj, margin):
    outcome = (margin > 0) - (margin < 0)
    return [0.0] * (len(traj) - 1) + [float(outcome)]


def train_population(learners: list, cfg: dict, out_dir: Path):
    """Train `learners` by uniform pairwise co-evolution for cfg['games_per_member'] games each (in expectation)."""
    n = len(learners)
    assert n >= 2, "a population needs at least two members"
    env = learners[0].env
    seed = cfg["seed"]
    rng = random.Random(seed + 7)
    per_member = cfg["games_per_member"]
    total = n * per_member // 2
    openings = make_openings(env, 20_000, cfg["opening_plies"], 1_000 + seed)
    eval_openings = make_openings(env, cfg["eval_openings"], cfg["opening_plies"], cfg["eval_seed"])
    eval_opp = make_agent(cfg["opponent"], env, seed=10_000 + seed)
    dirs = [out_dir / f"m{i}" for i in range(n)]
    for d in dirs:
        d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    count = [0] * n
    # pairwise results for the current logging window: wdl[i][j] = [W, D, L] of i against j
    window = [[[0, 0, 0] for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]
    files = [open(d / "curve.csv", "w", newline="") for d in dirs]
    writers = [None] * n
    t0 = time.time()

    def log(i):
        learners[i].epsilon = 0.0
        row = {"games": count[i], "total_games": sum(count) // 2, "seconds": time.time() - t0,
               **evaluate(learners[i], eval_opp, eval_openings), **learners[i].stats()}
        for j in range(n):
            if j != i:
                w, d, l = window[i][j]
                tot = w + d + l
                row[f"vs_m{j}_n"] = tot
                row[f"vs_m{j}_score"] = (w + 0.5 * d) / tot if tot else float("nan")
                window[i][j] = [0, 0, 0]
        if writers[i] is None:
            writers[i] = csv.DictWriter(files[i], fieldnames=list(row))
            writers[i].writeheader()
        writers[i].writerow(row)
        files[i].flush()
        print(f"m{i}", {k: (round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in row.items()
                        if k in ("games", "score", "seconds")}, flush=True)

    for i in range(n):
        log(i)
    try:
        for g in range(total):
            i, j = rng.sample(range(n), 2)
            for k in (i, j):
                learners[k].epsilon = epsilon_at(cfg, count[k], per_member)
            ti, tj, mi = play_pair(env, learners[i], learners[j], rng.choice(openings), a_is_black=g % 2 == 0)
            if ti:

"""Population diversity and non-transitivity measures (Phase 4).

* Policy disagreement: on a fixed set of positions, the fraction where two
  agents' greedy moves differ. Population diversity = mean over member pairs.
* Non-transitivity: directed 3-cycles A > B > C > A in a head-to-head score
  matrix, counting only edges whose 95% CI excludes 50%.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random

from othello.env import OthelloEnv


def position_set(env: OthelloEnv, agents: list, n: int = 1000, seed: int = 6161, sample_every: int = 3):
    """Positions from games between randomly paired `agents` (with 10% random moves for variety).

    Only positions with at least two legal moves are kept (forced moves carry no information).
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    out = []
    while len(out) < n:
        a, b = rng.choice(agents), rng.choice(agents)
        s = env.initial_state()
        ply = 0
        while not env.is_terminal(s) and len(out) < n:
            moves = env.legal_moves(s)
            if len(moves) > 1 and ply % sample_every == 0:
                out.append(s)
            agent = a if s.player == 0 else b
            m = rng.choice(moves) if rng.random() < 0.1 else agent.act(s)
            s = env.step(s, m)
            ply += 1
    return out


def greedy_moves(agent, positions):
    return [agent.act(s) for s in positions]


def disagreement(moves_a, moves_b):
    return sum(x != y for x, y in zip(moves_a, moves_b)) / len(moves_a)


def mean_pairwise_disagreement(move_lists):
    pairs = list(itertools.combinations(range(len(move_lists)), 2))
    vals = [disagreement(move_lists[i], move_lists[j]) for i, j in pairs]
    return sum(vals) / len(vals), vals


def significant_beats(score, games):
    """True if `score` (of A vs B over `games`) is above 50% with a 95% CI excluding 50%."""
    half = 1.96 * math.sqrt(max(score * (1 - score), 1e-12) / games)
    return score - half > 0.5


def count_cycles(names, score, games):
    """score[(a, b)] = a's score vs b (both orders present or derivable); returns significant 3-cycles."""
    def s(a, b):
        return score[(a, b)] if (a, b) in score else 1 - score[(b, a)]

    def n(a, b):
        return games[(a, b)] if (a, b) in games else games[(b, a)]

    beats = {(a, b) for a in names for b in names if a != b and significant_beats(s(a, b), n(a, b))}
    cycles = set()
    for a, b, c in itertools.permutations(names, 3):
        if (a, b) in beats and (b, c) in beats and (c, a) in beats:
            cycles.add(tuple(sorted((a, b, c))))
    return sorted(cycles), len(beats)

def test_cycle_counting_on_toy_matrices():
    from othello.eval.population_metrics import count_cycles
    names = ["A", "B", "C"]
    games = {(a, b): 1000 for a in names for b in names if a < b}
    rps = {("A", "B"): 0.7, ("B", "C"): 0.7, ("A", "C"): 0.3}       # A>B, B>C, C>A
    cycles, n_beats = count_cycles(names, rps, games)
    assert cycles == [("A", "B", "C")] and n_beats == 3
    transitive = {("A", "B"): 0.7, ("B", "C"): 0.7, ("A", "C"): 0.8}
    assert count_cycles(names, transitive, games)[0] == []
    weak = {("A", "B"): 0.51, ("B", "C"): 0.51, ("A", "C"): 0.49}  # not significant at 1000 games
    assert count_cycles(names, weak, games) == ([], 0)


def test_disagreement_metric():
    from othello.eval.population_metrics import disagreement, mean_pairwise_disagreement
    assert disagreement([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 2, 0, 0]) == 0.5
    mean, vals = mean_pairwise_disagreement([[1, 1], [1, 2], [2, 2]])
    assert vals == [0.5, 1.0, 0.5] and abs(mean - 2 / 3) < 1e-12

Overnight 2026-10-05→06 the machine's `python3` switched from 3.10 to 3.12 (system dist-packages replaced), which removed torch from the default interpreter and broke python3.10's numpy. Fix: project venv `OthelloRL/.venv` (`python3 -m venv --without-pip --system-site-packages`; torch CPU + pytest>=8 installed via `python3 -m pip --python .venv/bin/python install ...`). `pytest.ini` disables ROS 2 pytest plugins (`-p no:launch_testing -p no:launch_ros`) because PYTHONPATH includes /opt/ros/humble.

**Why:** Runs launched with plain `python3` fail with `ModuleNotFoundError: torch`.
**How to apply:** Always run scripts/tests as `.venv/bin/python ...` (subprocess launchers use sys.executable, so they inherit it). The `othello` CLI launcher already prefers `.venv/bin/python`. numpy is now 1.26 (was 1.21) — earlier results were produced on 3.10/numpy 1.21.

cat > /tmp/claude-1001/-home-palak-raisinghani-my-courses-OthelloRL/bdad683d-7fba-464a-be96-7414ac7e0812/scratchpad/frozen.tex <<'EOF'
\subsection{Why self-play? The frozen target of a fixed opponent}
\label{sec:frozen}

The \emph{Point to Ponder} in \S\ref{sec:classical} asked whether DQN is held
back by its fixed training opponent. Before turning to self-play methods, we
test this directly.

\paragraph{Design.} We train three Double DQNs that are identical to the
self-play DQN used later in this report (same network, replay buffer,
exploration schedule and budget). The only difference is their training
opponent: the random bot, the heuristic bot, or minimax at depth~3, one fixed
opponent each for the whole run. We compare them with two references trained
under the same conditions: the \emph{self-play} DQN, whose opponent is its own
live copy (\S\ref{sec:league}, $p=0$), and Phase~1's classical (vanilla) DQN,
which was also trained only against the heuristic bot. Every learner gets
\TrainGames{} games and 3 seeds.

The learners are compared in three ways:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Trainer curves:} each fixed-opponent learner's saved checkpoints
        (50k, 100k, 150k and 200k games) play its own trainer and the other
        fixed bots;
  \item \textbf{Bot panel:} every final model plays all the rule-based bots;
  \item \textbf{Round robin:} the five learner groups play each other, over all
        9 seed pairs per group pair.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Hypotheses.} We frame the question as a \emph{frozen target}. A
fixed opponent never improves, so once the learner beats it reliably, almost
every game is a win that carries little information, and learning stalls.
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[(a) Frozen target:] each learner's score against its own trainer rises
        and then plateaus, and its general strength stops improving.
  \item[(b) Ordering:] strength follows the trainer, random $<$ heuristic $<$
        minimax-d3.
  \item[(c) Self-play:] the self-play DQN matches or beats every fixed-opponent
        DQN.
\end{description}
The strict reading of the question, that a learner is \emph{capped} at its
opponent's strength, is already contradicted by Phase~1: the classical DQN
trained only against the heuristic bot beats it 65\% of the time.

The new Section 5.1, "Why self-play? The frozen target of a fixed opponent", answers the "Point to Ponder", which now links to it. It includes trainer curves, general-strength curves, a bot-panel table and a 5×5 head-to-head heat-map, and it's committed.

vs random vs heuristic vs minimax-d2 vs minimax-d3 vs self-play DQN (head-to-head)
Trained vs random 86 41 18 12 27
Trained vs heuristic 92 63 36 27 43
Trained vs minimax-d3 91 59 40 34 43
Self-play 92 61 35 26 —
Classical DQN (Phase 1) 92 65 36 26 44
  • The frozen target shows clearly at the weak end. The DQN trained vs random reaches its final level against random by the first checkpoint (50k games) and stays there. Its general strength flatlines after about 20k games, far below everyone else.
  • The heuristic-trained learner improves slowly and then flattens.
  • The minimax-d3-trained learner is still improving at 200k games. It still loses most of its training games, so each game still teaches it something. We never reached the "opponent too strong" end.
  • On the bots, strength follows the trainer, and the d3-trained learner leads against minimax-d2 and d3. But those bots share its trainer's evaluation function, so they flatter it.
  • Head-to-head, self-play beats every fixed-opponent DQN (57–73%), including Phase 1's classical DQN (56%). The d3-trained learner only ties the heuristic-trained one.
  • The DQN variant doesn't matter: Double and vanilla DQN with the same opponent are statistically tied.
  • So the answer is "yes, but not as a hard cap." A fixed opponent freezes the learning target and narrows what's learned to that opponent's style. Self-play removes both limits.

  • Damage: Phase 4 runs already in progress finished fine (F1 at N = 8 and N = 4, and N = 2 seeds 0–1). The 7 that launched after the switch failed immediately: F1-N2 seed 2 and all 6 F2 runs. Nothing was corrupted.

- Board size: **8×8 only** (decided). Standard start position; **Black moves first**.

- **Conventions** (same as OthelloRL, since the model layout depends on them): square `(row, col)` = index `row*8 + col`, `a1` = 0 top-left, `h8` = 63, pass = 64; start position white d4/e5, black e4/d5; Black moves first.

### 3.2 Game screen
- Board with discs, coordinates (a–h / 1–8), **legal-move hints** (toggleable), **last-move highlight**, and **flip animation**.
- Live disc counts and a whose-turn indicator. In vs-Computer mode, a "thinking…" indicator while the AI moves.
- **Pass banner** ("White has no legal move — Black plays again").
- Controls: **Undo** (vs Computer: undoes your move and the AI's reply; Two Players: one move), **New game**, **Hint** (vs Computer only; optional, uses Oroletto), **Resign**.
- Move list / history panel (optional in v1, desirable).
- Input: mouse/touch click on a square; keyboard navigation (arrows + Enter) for accessibility.

### 3.3 Play vs Computer — difficulty levels
**Four levels, one model.** Every level is played by the same AlphaZero-style network, Oroletto. Difficulty comes from three search settings:
- **MCTS simulations:** fewer simulations means shallower, weaker play.
- **Move temperature:** the move is sampled from visit counts ∝ N^(1/T). High T gives varied, error-prone play; T → 0 is greedy (most-visited move).
- **Root noise:** Dirichlet noise mixed into the root priors (weight ε) makes weaker levels explore moves the network does not favour.

| Level | Name | Simulations | Temperature | Root noise ε |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Easy | ~10 | 1.0 | 0.3 |
| 2 | Medium | ~50 | 0.5 | 0 |
| 3 | Hard | ~200 | 0.1 | 0 |
| 4 | Master | ~800 (as many as fit the 2 s budget) | 0 (greedy) | 0 |

The numbers are **placeholders**. They are tuned empirically once the 8×8 model exists: play the levels against each other and against reference bots (random, greedy, minimax from OthelloRL), then adjust until the gaps between levels are clear (e.g. each level beats the one below it ≥ 70%). The final values live in the model manifest or a settings file, not in code.

- The AI must respond within **≤ 2 s per move** on a typical laptop at every level; simulation counts are capped to that budget.
- The rule-based bots from OthelloRL (random, greedy, heuristic, minimax) are **not** player levels. They are kept as test baselines and as stand-ins during development before the model is ready.
- Temperature and noise apply only to the in-game move choice. Hints and the parity test use temperature 0 and no noise.

### 3.4 Two Players (local)
- Hot-seat play on one screen: same board UI, no AI, optional names, Undo of one move, and a result dialog naming the winner.

Shell cwd was reset to /home/palak_raisinghani/my/courses/OthelloRL

I've recorded your three decisions. Nothing runs yet, because the levels can only be tuned once an 8×8 model exists (Phase 6).

  • Temperature on visit counts: the move is sampled with probability ∝ N^(1/T), as in the SPEC §3.3 table. OthelloRL's search code already does this (MCTS.choose); the playable agent just needs temperature and root-noise settings.
  • 8×8 only: the levels will be tuned on the 8×8 model, not on 6×6 Oroletto.
  • No distillation: dropped. All four levels come from the one model.

Added to PLAN.md (committed): - Step 6.6, export the 8×8 model for the app: - ONNX file (65 outputs for 8×8); - a check against PyTorch; - a manifest with its source run and a checksum; - reference test cases for the app's parity tests. - Step 6.7, calibrate the app's four levels: - start from the SPEC values (Easy: ~10 simulations, T 1.0, noise 0.3; Medium: ~50, 0.5, 0; Hard: ~200, 0.1, 0; Master: ~800, greedy); - play adjacent levels against each other, and against the 8×8 bots; - adjust until each level beats the one below at least 70% of the time, and every level stays under 2 s per move; - write the final values into the app's model manifest.

I updated the memory note about the app with these decisions. I didn't edit the Othello-Player repo: its SPEC already matches, and it has new commits (Tauri shell, Svelte UI) that someone else appears to be working on.

"""Phase 4 evaluation (Steps 4.5-4.6). All stages are resumable.

  .venv/bin/python scripts/eval_coevo.py members   # each member vs self-play DQN, Phase 2 PPO, DQN+
  .venv/bin/python scripts/eval_coevo.py within    # all member pairs inside each population
  .venv/bin/python scripts/eval_coevo.py ckpt      # member checkpoints vs minimax-d3 and PPO seed 0
  .venv/bin/python scripts/eval_coevo.py all

Scores against the rule-based bots come from each member's final.json (written at
the end of training: 1,000 games vs random/heuristic, 500 vs each minimax depth).
"""
import argparse
import json
import shutil
import sys
import tempfile
from itertools import combinations
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from othello.eval.arena import play_match  # noqa: E402
from othello.utils.config import load_json  # noqa: E402

OUT = ROOT / "results/coevo"
SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
W = load_json(ROOT / "results/baselines/heuristic_tuning.json")["best"]
REFS = {**{f"selfplay-s{k}": f"results/league/dqn/p0/seed{k}" for k in SEEDS},
        **{f"ppo-s{k}": f"results/selfplay/ppo/seed{k}" for k in SEEDS},
        **{f"dqn+-s{k}": f"results/selfplay/dqn-plus/seed{k}" for k in SEEDS}}


def members():
    for run_dir in sorted(OUT.glob("F*/seed*")):
        for m in sorted(run_dir.glob("m*")):
            if (m / "final.json").exists():
                yield f"{run_dir.parent.name}/{run_dir.name}/{m.name}", m


def match(a, b, n_open, seed):
    return play_match(6, {"path": str(a)}, {"path": str(b)} if not isinstance(b, dict) else b, n_open,
                      opening_plies=6, seed=seed, workers=8).summary()


def _load(p):
    return json.loads(p.read_text()) if p.exists() else {}


def stage_members():
    path = OUT / "eval_members.json"
    res = _load(path)
    for key, m in members():
        if key in res:
            continue
        res[key] = {name: match(m, ROOT / rel, 100, 4243) for name, rel in REFS.items()}
        path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
        print(key, {k: round(v["score"], 3) for k, v in res[key].items()}, flush=True)


def stage_within():
    path = OUT / "within_h2h.json"
    res = _load(path)
    for run_dir in sorted(OUT.glob("F*/seed*")):
        ms = sorted(run_dir.glob("m*"))
        for a, b in combinations(ms, 2):
            key = f"{run_dir.parent.name}/{run_dir.name}/{a.name}|{b.name}"
            if key not in res:
                res[key] = match(a, b, 100, 4248)
                path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
        print(run_dir.parent.name, run_dir.name, flush=True)


def stage_ckpt():
    path = OUT / "ckpt_curves.json"
    res = _load(path)
    d3 = {"type": "minimax", "kwargs": {"depth": 3, "weights": W}}
    tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    for key, m in members():
        cks = [(int(c.stem[1:]), c) for c in sorted((m / "ckpt").glob("g*.pt"))]
        cks.append((json.loads((m / "final.json").read_text())["games"], m / "model.pt"))
        for games, ck in cks:
            k = f"{key}/g{games:06d}"
            if k in res:
                continue
            rd = tmp / k.replace("/", "_")
            rd.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            shutil.copy(m / "config.json", rd / "config.json")
            shutil.copy(ck, rd / "model.pt")
            res[k] = {"games": games, "minimax-d3": match(rd, d3, 100, 4245),
                      "ppo-s0": match(rd, ROOT / REFS["ppo-s0"], 100, 4245)}
            path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
        print(key, flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("stage", choices=["members", "within", "ckpt", "all"])
    a = p.parse_args()
    for name, fn in (("members", stage_members), ("within", stage_within), ("ckpt", stage_ckpt)):
        if a.stage in (name, "all"):
            fn()

def _co_best(W, cfg, sd, n):
    """Best member of one population by its mean score inside the population (never by test results)."""
    tot = {i: [] for i in range(n)}

        run, pair = k.rsplit("/", 1)[0], k.rsplit("/", 1)[1]
        if run != f"{cfg}/seed{sd}":

        a, b = pair.split("|")
        tot[int(a[1:])].append(v["score"])
        tot[int(b[1:])].append(1 - v["score"])

''','''def _spec(x):
    return x if isinstance(x, dict) else {"path": str(x)}


def _job(args):
    """Worker: play one whole match single-process (the pool parallelises across matches)."""
    key, sub, a, b, n_open, seed = args
    import torch
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    return key, sub, play_match(6, _spec(a), _spec(b), n_open, opening_plies=6, seed=seed, workers=1).summary()


def run_jobs(jobs, path, res, merge):
    """Run (key, sub, a, b, n_open, seed) jobs on 8 processes, saving after every result."""
    from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
    import multiprocessing as mp
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(8, mp_context=mp.get_context("spawn")) as ex:
        for i, (key, sub, r) in enumerate(ex.map(_job, jobs, chunksize=1)):
            merge(res, key, sub, r)
            if i % 8 == 0 or i == len(jobs) - 1:
                path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
    path.write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=2))

%======================================================================
\section{Co-Evolution vs Self-Play}
\label{sec:coevo}

\S\ref{sec:league} showed that a league of \emph{weak, fixed} opponents makes DQN
worse. That experiment changed two things at once, though: it added variety,
and it made most games lopsided. This section separates the two. Several
\emph{independent} DQN agents learn only by playing each other, so the
opponents are varied but always adaptive and of similar strength. Is a
population of co-evolving learners better than a single learner playing
itself?

\subsection{Design}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Population:} $N\in\{2,4,8\}$ Double DQNs, identical to the
        self-play DQN of \S\ref{sec:league} ($p=0$). Each has its own network,
        replay buffer, optimiser and seed.
  \item \textbf{Pairing:} each game pairs two \emph{different} members chosen
        uniformly at random. No member ever plays a copy of itself. Both
        members learn from their own moves, so one game trains two learners.
        Each member's exploration schedule runs on its own game count.
  \item \textbf{Budget}, compared two ways:
        \textbf{F1}, equal games per agent: every member plays \TrainGames{}
        games, like the self-play DQN.
        \textbf{F2}, equal total games: the whole population shares one
        self-play run's 200{,}000 games, so 100k games per member at $N=4$
        and 50k at $N=8$ ($N=2$ is the same under F1 and F2).
  \item \textbf{Evaluation:} the same held-out panel as \S\ref{sec:league}.
        Every member plays the three self-play DQN seeds head-to-head and the
        Phase~2 PPO and DQN+ agents (200 games per pairing), and the minimax
        bots (from its end-of-training evaluation). The \emph{average member} is
        the main measure, with a seed-level bootstrap 95\% CI. The \emph{best
        member} of each population is chosen using games inside the population
        only, never test results, so picking the luckiest of $N$ cannot
        inflate it.
  \item \textbf{Diversity:} the fraction of 1{,}000 fixed positions on which two
        agents would choose different moves, averaged over member pairs. Its
        baseline is the same measure between the three \emph{independent}
        self-play seeds: separate training runs already differ.
  \item \textbf{Non-transitivity:} inside each population of $N\ge3$, the
        number of rock--paper--scissors cycles (A beats B, B beats C, C beats
        A) in which every win is statistically significant.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Hypotheses} (stated before the runs):
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[H1:] at equal games per agent, members are about level with self-play.
  \item[H2:] matched-strength variety does \emph{not} show \S\ref{sec:league}'s
        decline.
  \item[H3:] members differ from each other more than independent self-play
        seeds do.
  \item[H4:] any gain is largest against unseen \emph{learned} agents.
  \item[H5:] Othello is largely transitive, so there are few or no
        significant cycles.
  \item[H6:] larger populations are more diverse but learn more slowly early
        on.
  \item[H7:] at equal total games, training two learners per game partly
        offsets the split budget at $N=4$.
\end{description}

\subsection{Results}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Co-evolution vs self-play (\%, 3 population seeds each). ``vs self-play''
is the average member's score against the three self-play DQN seeds, with a
bootstrap 95\% CI. ``Best'': the best member of each population, chosen using
games inside the population only. Diversity: share of positions on which two
members choose different moves. The reference row is the self-play DQN itself.}
\label{tab:coevo}
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}

There's nothing extra to edit: Step 4.0 no longer exists, because the runner had already been folded into Step 4.7, whose note now says it moves to Phase 5.

Phase 4 is complete. The answer: co-evolution neither helps nor hurts DQN. At equal experience, a population member is indistinguishable from a self-play agent. The report has a new section, "Co-Evolution vs Self-Play", it compiles cleanly at 43 pages, and everything is committed.

Config Games/agent vs self-play DQN (95% CI) Best member Diversity
Self-play (reference) 200k 50 – 57%
F1, N=2 200k 49.2 [47.7, 50.8] 49.2 59%
F1, N=4 200k 49.8 [48.8, 51.0] 49.6 54%
F1, N=8 200k 49.3 [48.1, 50.3] 49.8 56%
F2, N=4 100k 46.2 [45.4, 47.0] 46.2 56%
F2, N=8 50k 43.4 [42.7, 44.1] 44.0 58%
  • Equal games per agent (F1): a tie with self-play at every population size, against the self-play DQN and every held-out opponent. Even the best member of each population is no stronger.
  • Strength depends only on games per agent. Learning curves for all 5 configurations and self-play lie on top of each other.
  • Equal total games (F2): members are significantly weaker. They aren't weaker than self-play at the same number of games; they just stop earlier. Training two learners per game doesn't help either learner.
  • No extra diversity: members disagree about as often as independently trained self-play agents (about 57%).
  • No cycles: members end up nearly equal in strength, with only 0–2 significant wins among 18–84 pairs. Rock-paper-scissors cycles can't form; it's consistent with Othello being transitive, but a weak test of it.
  • Hypotheses:
  • Supported: H1 (level with self-play); H2 (no Phase 3-style decline, which pins Phase 3's loss on weak, mismatched opponents rather than variety itself).
  • Refuted: H3 (diversity), H6 (population size), H7 (equal-compute compensation).
  • Not supported: H4 (robustness).
  • Consistent, weakly tested: H5 (transitivity).
  • Interpretation: the population is homogeneous (same algorithm, settings and budget), so a peer is effectively another sample of the self-play agent. For a population to help, its members must be genuinely different, for example exploiters. That leads straight into Phase 5.

Process notes: - Overnight Python switch: 7 of the 15 runs had to be rerun after the 3.10 → 3.12 change. - Slow evaluation: my first evaluation script would have taken about 8 hours, because every match started a fresh pool of 8 processes. I stopped it and ran the matches in parallel instead; it finished in about 15 minutes. - Smaller fixes: a figure where final checkpoints didn't line up on the 25k grid, and an import-path problem in the asset script. - Deviations from the plan: - The minimax scores come from each member's end-of-training evaluation: 500 games per depth instead of the planned 1,000. - The optional AlphaZero population (Step 4.7) was skipped, as the plan specified when DQN shows no effect.

Next is Phase 5, exploiters and blind spots. Its two design decisions are still open: - Exploiter type: proposed default is an AlphaZero exploiter that models its victim (Wang et al. 2023); alternatives are a PPO exploiter, or both. - Analysis scope: proposed default is the exact-solver audit of all agents plus exploiters for the strong models only, versus one exploiter per agent.

42:- The engine is **8×8 only** (no other sizes) and must reproduce OthelloRL exactly, as checked against `tests/golden/engine_8x8.json`: perft counts (depth 1–7: 4, 12, 56, 244, 1396, 8200, 55092), forced-pass / double-pass / full-board cases, and 100 seeded random games with legal moves and resulting positions at every ply.
66:The numbers are **placeholders**. They are tuned empirically once the 8×8 model exists: play the levels against each other and against reference bots (random, greedy, minimax from OthelloRL), then adjust until the gaps between levels are clear (e.g. each level beats the one below it ≥ 70%). The final values live in the model manifest or a settings file, not in code.
90:- The UI talks to a backend through `ui/src/lib/api.ts`: inside Tauri that is the Rust engine; in a browser it is a **TypeScript port** of the engine and session (`ui/src/lib/engine/`), with settings in localStorage. **Step 5.8 — Package the model and link it into the Othello-Player app**
- **Why:** the app (`../Othello-Player`, GitHub `O-Rolleto-PlayOthello`) is 8×8 only and plays every level with this model. It should start working as soon as the model exists.
- **Methodology:**
  - Copy the outputs of Steps 5.6–5.7 into the app repo, using the paths its SPEC expects:
    - `models/oroletto-8x8.onnx`;
    - `models/oroletto-8x8.json` (manifest: planes, c_puct, the calibrated per-level simulations / temperature / root noise, provenance, SHA-256);
    - the parity fixtures under `tests/golden/`.
  - The files are copied, not symlinked, so the app builds on other machines.

# Phase 5 — AlphaZero on 8x8 (design decided 2026-10-07): 6 blocks x 64 channels,
# 150 MCTS simulations per self-play move, 3 seeds x 100k games. Otherwise as 6x6,
# adapted only where the larger board requires it.
out: results/alphazero_8x8
board_size: 8
seeds: [0, 1, 2]
train_games: 100000
eval_every: 5000
checkpoint_every: 10000
eval_openings: 100
final_eval_openings: 250
opening_plies: 6
eval_seed: 4242
start_pos_frac: 0.25

# network
channels: 64
blocks: 6
# search
sims: 150                   # per self-play move (6x6: 64)
eval_sims: 150
c_puct: 1.5
dirichlet_alpha: 0.5
noise_frac: 0.25
temp_plies: 20              # 8x8 games are ~2x longer than 6x6 (6x6: 10)
# self-play / training (8x8 games give ~2x the positions per game)
games_per_iter: 256
workers: 7
concurrent_games: 40
buffer_positions: 300000    # 6x6: 150k
min_buffer: 10000
batch: 256
train_steps: 200            # keeps ~4 samples per new position, as on 6x6
lr: 0.001
weight_decay: 0.0001
train_threads: 4

# learning-curve opponent: minimax-d4 (heuristic saturates on 8x8 for strong agents)
opponent: {type: minimax, kwargs: {depth: 4, weights: TUNED}}
final_opponents:
  random: {type: random}
  heuristic: {type: heuristic, kwargs: {epsilon: 0.05, weights: TUNED}}
  minimax-d4: {type: minimax, kwargs: {depth: 4, weights: TUNED}}
EOF

import time, numpy as np, torch, yaml
from othello.env import OthelloEnv
from othello.rl.alphazero.selfplay import build_net, play_selfplay_games
from othello.eval.arena import make_openings
cfg=yaml.safe_load(open('configs/alphazero_8x8.yaml'))
torch.set_num_threads(1)
env=OthelloEnv(8); net=build_net(8,cfg).eval()
ops=make_openings(env,40,6,1)
t=time.time(); ex,n=play_selfplay_games(net,env,cfg,ops,np.random.default_rng(0)); dt=time.time()-t
print(f"self-play: 40 games in {dt:.0f}s -> {dt/40:.2f} s/game/worker, {n/40:.0f} positions/game")
# training cost
torch.set_num_threads(4); net.train()
opt=torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(),1e-3); x=torch.randn(256,3,8,8)
t=time.time()
for _ in range(20):
    p,v=net(x); loss=p.mean()+v.mean(); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(f"train: {(time.time()-t)/20*1000:.0f} ms/step")
EOF

"""Edax (https://github.com/abulmo/edax-reversi), a world-class 8x8 Othello engine, as an Agent.

Built from source into third_party/edax (see PLAN Step 5.4). Each agent drives one
Edax process through its native text interface: `setboard` with the current
position, then `go`, then parse "Edax plays XY". Strength is set by the search
`level` (depth). The opening book is off, so play comes from search alone.
Only 8x8 is supported.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import os
import select
import subprocess
import time
from pathlib import Path

from othello.agents.base import Agent

EDAX_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "third_party" / "edax"
EDAX_BIN = EDAX_DIR / "bin" / "lEdax-x86-64-v2"


class EdaxAgent(Agent):
    name = "edax"

    def __init__(self, env, level: int = 5, seed=None, timeout: float = 60.0):
        super().__init__(env, seed)
        if env.n != 8:
            raise ValueError("Edax plays 8x8 only")
        if not EDAX_BIN.exists():
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"Edax binary not found at {EDAX_BIN} (see PLAN Step 5.4)")
        self.level, self.timeout = level, timeout
        self.name = f"edax-l{level}"
        self.proc = subprocess.Popen([str(EDAX_BIN), "-n", "1", "-book-usage", "off", "-l", str(level),
                                      "-verbose", "0"], cwd=EDAX_DIR, stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
                                     stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True, bufsize=1)
        self._read()
        self._cmd("mode 3")          # Edax never moves on its own

    def _read(self):
        buf, end = "", time.time() + self.timeout
        fd = self.proc.stdout.fileno()
        while time.time() < end:
            r, _, _ = select.select([fd], [], [], 0.05)
            if r:
                chunk = os.read(fd, 65536).decode()
                if not chunk:
                    raise RuntimeError("Edax exited unexpectedly")
                buf += chunk
                if buf.rstrip().endswith(">"):
                    return buf
        raise TimeoutError(f"Edax did not answer within {self.timeout}s: {buf[-200:]!r}")

    def _cmd(self, line):
        self.proc.stdin.write(line + "\n")
        self.proc.stdin.flush()
        return self._read()

    def board_string(self, state):
        cells = []
        for sq in range(64):
            b = 1 << sq
            cells.append("*" if state.black & b else "O" if state.white & b else "-")
        return "".join(cells) + (" *" if state.player == 0 else " O")

    def act(self, state):
        moves = self.env.legal_moves(state)
        if len(moves) == 1:
            return moves[0]
        self._cmd("setboard " + self.board_string(state))
        out = self._cmd("go")
        for line in out.splitlines():
            if "Edax plays" in line:
                mv = line.split("Edax plays")[1].strip()[:2].lower()
                sq = (int(mv[1]) - 1) * 8 + "abcdefgh".index(mv[0])
                if sq not in moves:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Edax played illegal move {mv} in {self.board_string(state)}")
                return sq
        raise RuntimeError(f"no move in Edax output: {out[-200:]!r}")

    def close(self):
        if self.proc.poll() is None:
            try:
                self.proc.stdin.write("quit\n")
                self.proc.stdin.flush()
                self.proc.wait(timeout=5)
            except Exception:
                self.proc.kill()

    def __del__(self):
        try:
            self.close()
        except Exception:
            pass

cat > tests/test_edax.py <<'EOF'
import random

import pytest

from othello.agents.edax import EDAX_BIN
from othello.env import OthelloEnv

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not EDAX_BIN.exists(), reason="Edax not built (third_party/edax)")


def test_edax_plays_legal_moves_and_beats_random():
    from othello.agents import RandomAgent
    from othello.agents.edax import EdaxAgent
    from othello.eval.arena import play_game
    env = OthelloEnv(8)
    edax = EdaxAgent(env, level=2)
    rnd = RandomAgent(env, seed=0)
    wins = 0
    for g in range(4):
        black, white = (edax, rnd) if g % 2 == 0 else (rnd, edax)
        diff, moves = play_game(env, black, white, [])     # play_game checks legality via env.step
        wins += (diff > 0) == (g % 2 == 0) and diff != 0
    edax.close()
    assert wins >= 3


def test_edax_board_orientation_matches_engine():
    from othello.agents.edax import EdaxAgent
    env = OthelloEnv(8)
    edax = EdaxAgent(env, level=1)
    rng = random.Random(0)
    s = env.initial_state()
    for _ in range(12):                    # Edax's choice must be legal in our engine at every step
        m = edax.act(s)
        assert m in env.legal_moves(s)
        s = env.step(s, rng.choice(env.legal_moves(s)))
    edax.close()
EOF

new='''class AZAgent(Agent):
    """Playable AlphaZero agent: MCTS with `sims` simulations per move.

    Difficulty settings (as in the Othello-Player app, SPEC section 3.3):
      temperature: the move is sampled with probability proportional to N^(1/T)
                   over the root's visit counts N; T = 0 plays the most-visited move.
      noise:       weight epsilon of Dirichlet(dirichlet_alpha) noise mixed into the
                   root priors before searching; 0 disables it.
    """

    def __init__(self, env, net, sims=200, seed=None, name="alphazero", c_puct=1.5,
                 temperature=0.0, noise=0.0, dirichlet_alpha=0.5):
        super().__init__(env, seed)
        self.net, self.sims, self.name = net.eval(), sims, name
        self.temperature, self.noise = temperature, noise
        self.mcts = MCTS(env, Evaluator(env, net), c_puct=c_puct, dirichlet_alpha=dirichlet_alpha,
                         noise_frac=noise, rng=np.random.default_rng(seed))

    def act(self, state):
        moves = self.env.legal_moves(state)
        if len(moves) == 1:
            return moves[0]
        root = self.mcts.search([Node(state)], self.sims, add_noise=self.noise > 0)[0]
        return self.mcts.choose(root, self.temperature)


'''

def test_azagent_temperature_and_noise_knobs():
    from othello.rl.alphazero.selfplay import AZAgent
    env = OthelloEnv(6)

    assert picks <= set(env.legal_moves(s)) and len(picks) > 1     # T = 1 + noise: varied, always legal

    rng = random.Random(seed)

        stop = rng.randrange(0, 50)
        for _ in range(stop):
            if env.is_terminal(s):

            s = env.step(s, rng.choice(env.legal_moves(s)))
        if not env.is_terminal(s) and len(env.legal_moves(s)) > 1:
            out.append(s)
    return out

                       seed=4249, workers=8).summary()
        res[f"edax-l{lv}"] = r
        print(f"vs edax-l{lv}: score {r['score']:.3f} +- {r['score_ci95']:.3f}", flush=True)

        print(f"vs {name}: score {res[name]['score']:.3f}", flush=True)
    (out_dir(run) / "edax.json").write_text(json.dumps({"sims": sims, "results": res}, indent=2))

    for op in make_openings(env, 10, 6, 77):
        s = env.initial_state()
        for m in op:
            s = env.step(s, m)
        while not env.is_terminal(s) and len(times) < n_moves:
            t = time.time()
            m = agent.act(s)
            times.append(time.time() - t)
            s = env.step(s, rng.choice(env.legal_moves(s)) if rng.random() < 0.5 else m)
        if len(times) >= n_moves:
            break
    return {"mean_s": sum(times) / len(times), "max_s": max(times)}
