---
name: denormal-slowdown
description: Long CPU training runs slow ~10x when weights decay into denormal floats; OthelloRL nets now flush/clamp them
metadata:
  type: project
---

On 2026-10-10 the 8x8 AlphaZero seed 0 run had slowed ~7x after ~10k games (25k/100k games after 59 h). Cause: weight decay pushed weights into the denormal range (~1e-38); a forward pass on the 20k checkpoint took 516 ms vs 42 ms with `torch.set_flush_denormal(True)`. Fix (commit f560330): flush enabled on import in `othello/rl/alphazero/net.py`, `dqn.py`, `ppo.py`, plus weights with |w|<1e-30 zeroed after each AlphaZero training step. The run was restarted from scratch; the slow run is archived in `results/alphazero_8x8/seed0_aborted_denormal/`.

**Why:** Silent multi-day slowdowns waste the user's compute budget.
**How to apply:** For long runs, check throughput every ~5k games (compare seconds per 5k against the first interval). Diagnose with timing tests; profilers like py-spy need sudo here — the user said I may ask them to run profiler commands with sudo (e.g. `! sudo .venv/bin/py-spy dump --pid N`). Never `pkill -f` a pattern that also appears in my own shell command (it kills the shell); use exact PIDs.

We're still in Phase 5 (8×8), but seed 0's training had to be restarted. It hit a performance bug, which is now fixed.

What happened to seed 0 - Progress after about 59 hours: only 25k of 100k games. The first 10k games ran at the expected speed; after that the run slowed about 7-fold. - Cause: denormal floats. Weight decay had pushed thousands of weights down to near-zero "denormal" floating-point numbers, which this CPU processes very slowly. A network call on the 20k-game checkpoint took 516 ms instead of 42 ms. Nothing else was competing for the machine, and the CPU wasn't throttling. - Fix (committed): denormals are now flushed to zero in all network code (AlphaZero, DQN, PPO), and weights below 10⁻³⁰ are set to exactly zero after each training step. A regression test is included, and all 73 tests pass. Numerically this changes nothing meaningful, since the values involved are around 10⁻³⁸. - Restarted seed 0 from scratch at about 12:45 today. The slow run's results are kept in results/alphazero_8x8/seed0_aborted_denormal/. In terms of normal-speed progress, the restart loses only about 13 hours; continuing would have taken about 13 more days. - New expected finish: about 53 hours, so Monday 10/12, around 18:00. A watchdog will notify me at the 15k-game mark, about 8 hours from now, past the point where the old run slowed. That way I can confirm the fix holds instead of discovering a problem days later.

Notes - Profiling with sudo: if another slowdown needs investigating, I'll ask you to run the profiler with sudo, e.g. ! sudo .venv/bin/py-spy dump --pid <PID>. I saved this to memory. - A slip of mine: my first attempt to stop the old run used a pkill -f pattern that matched my own shell's command line and killed the shell, a repeat of an earlier mistake. No harm was done, and I've noted to use exact process IDs from now on.

Turn 67

what training is going on ? whjat are the 3 seeds for ?
Claude's response

What's training right now: an AlphaZero agent learning 8×8 Othello (the standard board) purely by self-play. This is Phase 5. It's the same recipe as Oroletto, which plays 6×6, with settings adapted for the bigger board: - Network: 6 residual blocks × 64 channels (Oroletto has 4 × 64), about 459k parameters. - Search: 150 MCTS simulations per move during self-play (Oroletto used 64). - Budget: 100k self-play games. It plays itself, trains on its own games, gets stronger, and repeats. - Checks along the way: every 5k games it's tested against minimax depth 4. Checkpoints are saved every 10k games.

When it finishes, it's evaluated against the Edax engine and the 8×8 bots, then exported to ONNX and packaged into the Othello-Player app, which is 8×8 only. The app's four levels (Easy to Master) will all be this one model.

What the 3 seeds are for: a seed is the random-number starting point of a run. It controls the random initial weights, which openings are played, the exploration noise, and so on. Three seeds mean the same recipe trained three times independently, with different luck. They serve two different purposes:

Seed Purpose
Seed 0 (running now) The model for the app. We only need one model to ship, so it goes first and gets packaged as soon as it's done.
Seeds 1–2 (after packaging) Scientific reliability. One run could be unusually lucky or unlucky. With three, the report can show mean ± spread and say whether results like "beats Edax level X" or "plateaus at Y games" hold for the recipe, not just one run.

Example from 6×6: Oroletto's three seeds scored 76–79% against minimax-d4. That tight spread is what let the report say the result is reliable.

You chose 3 seeds × 100k games earlier. Each seed takes about 53 hours, so seeds 1–2 add about 4.4 days after seed 0. If the app is what matters most, seeds 1–2 could be skipped or shortened later; the decision isn't needed until Monday.

770	\subsection{Why self-play? The frozen target of a fixed opponent}
771	\label{sec:frozen}
772	
773	The \emph{Point to Ponder} in \S\ref{sec:classical} asked whether DQN is held
774	back by its fixed training opponent. Before turning to self-play methods, we
775	test this directly.
776	
777	\paragraph{Design.} We train three Double DQNs that are identical to the
778	self-play DQN used later in this report (same network, replay buffer,
779	exploration schedule and budget). The only difference is their training
780	opponent: the random bot, the heuristic bot, or minimax at depth~3, one fixed
781	opponent each for the whole run. We compare them with two references trained
782	under the same conditions: the \emph{self-play} DQN, whose opponent is its own
783	live copy (\S\ref{sec:league}, $p=0$), and Phase~1's classical (vanilla) DQN,
784	which was also trained only against the heuristic bot. Every learner gets
785	\TrainGames{} games and 3 seeds.
786	
787	The learners are compared in three ways:
788	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
789	  \item \textbf{Trainer curves:} each fixed-opponent learner's saved checkpoints
790	        (50k, 100k, 150k and 200k games) play its own trainer and the other
791	        fixed bots;
792	  \item \textbf{Bot panel:} every final model plays all the rule-based bots;
793	  \item \textbf{Round robin:} the five learner groups play each other, over all
794	        9 seed pairs per group pair.
795	\end{itemize}
796	
797	\paragraph{Hypotheses.} We frame the question as a \emph{frozen target}. A
798	fixed opponent never improves, so once the learner beats it reliably, almost
799	every game is a win that carries little information, and learning stalls.
800	\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
801	  \item[(a) Frozen target:] each learner's score against its own trainer rises

805	  \item[(c) Self-play:] the self-play DQN matches or beats every fixed-opponent

807	\end{description}

summary=r'''%======================================================================
\section{Summary of Findings}
\label{sec:summary}

Table~\ref{tab:summary} collects the answer to each study's question. Read
together, the studies tell one story: \emph{what an agent learns is determined
by whom it plays and how well it can look ahead}.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item Fixed opponents freeze the learning target, and weak or mismatched
        opponents give games that teach little.
  \item An evenly matched opponent that keeps improving, which is exactly what
        self-play provides, keeps every game informative.
  \item Without search, every policy is capped by the horizon effect. Search is
        what lets AlphaZero break through, both when it plays and as the target
        its network learns from.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{The questions this report asked, and the answers (\bx{6}).}
\label{tab:summary}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}p{0.27\linewidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Question & Answer \\
\midrule
How strong are simple rule-based players? (\S\ref{sec:bots}) &
A clear ladder: random $<$ heuristic $<$ minimax. Corners and mobility carry
the heuristic's strength; disc count adds almost nothing. A few plies of
lookahead are worth more than any reweighting. \\
\addlinespace
Can traditional RL learn Othello from a fixed opponent? (\S\ref{sec:classical}) &
Only partly. Tabular methods never see most positions twice. Monte Carlo control
memorises lines against its trainer. Linear features cap out at the heuristic's
level. DQN is best, but loses heavily to minimax. \\
\addlinespace
Is a learner limited by its fixed opponent? (\S\ref{sec:frozen}) &
Yes, but not as a hard cap. The target freezes once it is beaten, and the
learner specialises in its opponent's style. Self-play beats every
fixed-opponent DQN head-to-head. \\
\addlinespace
Which self-play method is strongest? (\S\ref{sec:selfplay}) &
AlphaZero, by a wide margin. It beats minimax-d4 about 78\% of the time, and
even its network alone draws level with minimax-d4. DQN+ and PPO only match the
best fixed-opponent learner. The winner is released as \emph{Oroletto}. \\
\addlinespace
Does a league of weak opponents help DQN? (\S\ref{sec:league}) &
No. Strength falls as the league share grows: lopsided games teach little, even
about the league's own members. \\
\addlinespace
Do co-evolving populations beat self-play? (\S\ref{sec:coevo}) &
No. They are equal at equal experience per agent and weaker at equal total
compute. They are no more diverse and show no cycles: identical learners make
interchangeable opponents. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

'''
i=s.index('\\section{System Architecture}')
k=s.rfind('%======', 0, i)
s=s[:k]+summary+s[k:]
open(p,'w').write(s)

- **Why:** the app plays every level with **one model, the strongest one**, weakened only by its **move temperature** (decided 2026-10-12). The temperatures must give clearly separated levels.
- **Methodology:**
  - **One search budget for all levels:** the largest simulation count whose worst-case move time stays within 2 s per move on this machine (single thread). Start at 200.
  - **Temperature T on visit counts:** the move is sampled with probability ∝ N^(1/T); T = 0 plays the most-visited move. No root noise.
  - Play a ladder of candidate temperatures T ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} against each other (adjacent pairs, 400 games each), and each candidate against the 8x8 bots.

# Othello Player — Specification

A desktop application for playing Othello on your own machine. You can play against the computer at several difficulty levels, with the hardest levels played by **Oroletto**, the AlphaZero-style agent trained in the companion research repo [OthelloRL](../OthelloRL). Two people can also play each other on the same computer.

### 3.3 Play vs Computer — difficulty levels
**Four levels, one model.** Every level is played by the same AlphaZero-style network, Oroletto. Difficulty comes from three search settings:
- **MCTS simulations:** fewer simulations means shallower, weaker play.
- **Move temperature:** the move is sampled from visit counts ∝ N^(1/T). High T gives varied, error-prone play; T → 0 is greedy (most-visited move).
- **Root noise:** Dirichlet noise mixed into the root priors (weight ε) makes weaker levels explore moves the network does not favour.

| Level | Name | Simulations | Temperature | Root noise ε |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Easy | ~10 | 1.0 | 0.3 |
| 2 | Medium | ~50 | 0.5 | 0 |
| 3 | Hard | ~200 | 0.1 | 0 |
| 4 | Master | ~800 (as many as fit the 2 s budget) | 0 (greedy) | 0 |

The numbers are **placeholders**. They are tuned empirically once the 8×8 model exists: play the levels against each other and against reference bots (random, greedy, minimax from OthelloRL), then adjust until the gaps between levels are clear (e.g. each level beats the one below it ≥ 70%). The final values live in the model manifest or a settings file, not in code.

- The AI must respond within **≤ 2 s per move** on a typical laptop at every level; simulation counts are capped to that budget.
- The rule-based bots from OthelloRL (random, greedy, heuristic, minimax) are **not** player levels. They are kept as test baselines and as stand-ins during development before the model is ready.
- Temperature and noise apply only to the in-game move choice. Hints and the parity test use temperature 0 and no noise.

### 3.4 Two Players (local)
### 4.2 Oroletto model contract
- OthelloRL exports Oroletto to **ONNX**, with a new export script to be added there. The file is shipped in this repo under `models/` (~1.2 MB), together with a JSON manifest.
- **Input:** `float32[batch, 3, n, n]`, with planes (own discs, opponent discs, legal moves) from the side to move.
- **Outputs:** `policy_logits float32[batch, n*n+1]` (last index = pass); `value float32[batch]` in [−1, 1] for the side to move.
- **The manifest** (`models/oroletto-8x8.json`) records: board size, planes, `c_puct = 1.5`, default simulations per level, OthelloRL commit hash and run id (`results/alphazero/seed1`), and a SHA-256 of the ONNX file.
- **Search parity:** the app's MCTS matches OthelloRL's (PUCT, values negated each ply). The parity test runs with noise off and temperature 0 (greedy by visit count); noise and temperature are the app's difficulty knobs (§3.3), on top of the same search. A parity test checks that, for a fixed set of positions, the Rust/app search picks the same moves as OthelloRL's Python search with the same seed and simulation count (allowing ties).

---

3. ~~**Difficulty ladder**~~ — **decided: 4 levels, one AlphaZero model**, varied by simulations, temperature and root noise (§3.3). Exact values to be tuned once the 8×8 model exists.

s=s[:a]+'''### 3.3 Play vs Computer — difficulty levels
**Four levels, one model, one knob.** Every level is played by the same network, **the strongest 8×8 Oroletto model**, with the **same MCTS search budget**. Levels differ **only in the move temperature T**:
- After searching, the move is sampled from the root visit counts with probability ∝ N^(1/T).
- **T = 0** plays the most-visited move (full strength). **Higher T** spreads probability over the other moves the search visited, so play becomes more varied and makes more mistakes.
- There is **no root noise** and no change in the number of simulations between levels.

| Level | Name | Simulations | Temperature T |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Easy | shared (≈200) | high (placeholder 2.0) |
| 2 | Medium | shared | placeholder 1.0 |
| 3 | Hard | shared | placeholder 0.25 |
| 4 | Master | shared | 0 (most-visited move) |

The values are **placeholders** until OthelloRL calibrates them on the 8×8 model (OthelloRL PLAN Step 5.7):
- the shared simulation count is the largest that keeps the worst-case move within the 2 s budget;
- the four temperatures are chosen from candidates {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} so that each level beats the one below it at least 70% of the time.

The calibrated values are delivered in the model manifest (`models/oroletto-8x8.json`, fields `levels.sims` and `levels.ladder[].temperature`). They are read at runtime, not hard-coded.

- The AI must respond within **≤ 2 s per move** on a typical laptop at every level. Every level uses the same search, so they all cost the same.
- The rule-based bots from OthelloRL (random, greedy, heuristic, minimax) are **not** player levels. They are kept as test baselines and as stand-ins during development before the model is ready.
- Temperature applies only to the in-game move choice. Hints and the parity test use temperature 0.

What the temperature calibration is for. You decided the app plays every level with one model (the strongest) and the same search budget, made weaker only by the move temperature T. The calibration picks the four T values, Easy → Master, so that: 1. Each level is clearly stronger than the one below: it should win at least 70% of games against it, so a player notices the difference. 2. Together they cover a useful range, from beatable by a beginner up to full strength. 3. Every level replies within 2 s per move. Every level uses the same search, so they all cost the same: here 0.42 s on average and 0.52 s at worst, at 200 simulations.

How: the move is chosen from the search's visit counts with probability ∝ N^(1/T). T = 0 always plays the most-visited move; higher T spreads the choice over weaker moves. I tried T ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, each against the next value (400 games per pair), and each against our 8×8 bots.

Results (seed 0, 200 simulations):

Pair Stronger side's score
T=0 vs T=0.25 49.5%, no real difference
T=0.25 vs T=0.5 58%
T=0.5 vs T=1 78%
T=1 vs T=2 84%
T=2 vs T=4 68%
T vs random vs heuristic vs minimax-d4
0 100% 99.5% 99%
1 99% 98.5% 86.5%
2 98% 91.5% 37%
4 95% 62.5% 13%

What this suggests: T below 0.5 barely weakens the model. The real steps happen at T = 1, 2 and 4. A first ladder would be Master T=0, Hard T=1, Medium T=2, Easy T=4, with two problems: - Medium vs Easy is 68%, just short of the 70% target. - Easy (T=4) still beats the heuristic bot 62% of the time, which is probably too strong for a real beginner. Easy likely needs a higher T, around 8.

Master vs Hard wasn't played directly; the chain of results suggests roughly 80%. The verify stage plays the chosen four levels against each other directly, and I'll include T = 8 for Easy.

Shipping: the model is exported (ONNX matches PyTorch to within 2.5 × 10⁻⁶). I'm putting it into Othello-Player now, with this provisional ladder in the manifest, marked levels_calibrated: false. The app can start working with it immediately, and I'll update just the manifest once the verify run settles the temperatures.

What the temperature calibration is for All four levels play the same model with the same search. The only difference is how strictly each picks the search's best move: T = 0 always plays it, higher T sometimes picks weaker moves. The calibration chooses four T values so that: - each level wins at least 70% of games against the level below, so players feel a clear step; - the levels span beginner to full strength; - every move takes under 2 seconds. code=r'''# ------------------------------------------------------------------ scaling to 8x8 (Phase 5)
def scale8():
    import numpy as np
    run = RES / "alphazero_8x8" / "seed0"

    if not (run / "final.json").exists() or not (ev / "edax.json").exists():
        print("scale8: results missing")
        return
    tune = json.loads((RES / "baselines_8x8" / "heuristic_tuning.json").read_text())
    tune6 = load("baselines/heuristic_tuning.json")
    depth = json.loads((RES / "baselines_8x8" / "minimax_depth.json").read_text())
    gate8 = json.loads((RES / "baselines_8x8" / "gate.json").read_text())["sizes"]["8"]["matches"]
    meta = json.loads((run / "meta.json").read_text())
    cfg = json.loads((run / "config.json").read_text())
    fin = json.loads((run / "final.json").read_text())
    edax = json.loads((ev / "edax.json").read_text())
    lad = json.loads((ev / "ladder.json").read_text()) if (ev / "ladder.json").exists() else None

    # ---- macros
    W = tune["best"]
    macros = [rf"\newcommand{{\EightWeights}}{{corner {W['corner']:g}, mobility {W['mobility']:g}, disc {W['disc']:g}, X-square {W['xsquare']:g}}}",
              rf"\newcommand{{\EightSameWeights}}{{{'identical to' if W == tune6['best'] else 'different from'}}}",
              rf"\newcommand{{\EightGames}}{{{meta['games']:,}}}".replace(",", "{,}"),
              rf"\newcommand{{\EightHours}}{{{meta['train_seconds'] / 3600:.1f}}}",
              rf"\newcommand{{\EightParams}}{{{meta['params']:,}}}".replace(",", "{,}"),
              rf"\newcommand{{\EightBlocks}}{{{cfg['blocks']}}}", rf"\newcommand{{\EightChannels}}{{{cfg['channels']}}}",
              rf"\newcommand{{\EightSims}}{{{cfg['sims']}}}", rf"\newcommand{{\EightEvalSims}}{{{edax['sims']}}}"]
    if lad:
        macros += [rf"\newcommand{{\EightLevelSims}}{{{lad['sims']}}}",
                   rf"\newcommand{{\EightMoveMean}}{{{lad['move_time']['mean_s']:.2f}}}",
                   rf"\newcommand{{\EightMoveMax}}{{{lad['move_time']['max_s']:.2f}}}"]
    write("s8_meta.tex", "\n".join(macros) + "\n")

    # ---- bots: depth sweep + gate
    rows = [rf"{r['depth']} & {score_ci(r)} & {r['nodes_per_move']:.0f} & {1000 * r['sec_per_game_both_sides']:.0f} \\" for r in depth]
    write("s8_depth.tex", "\n".join(rows) + "\n")
    rows = [rf"{m['a']} vs {m['b']} & {m['games']} & {score_ci(m)} \\" for m in gate8]
    write("s8_gate.tex", "\n".join(rows) + "\n")

    # ---- final evaluation (with search / network only) + Edax
    rows = []
    for b in ("random", "heuristic", "minimax-d4"):
        rows.append(rf"{b} & {pct(fin[b]['score'])} & {pct(fin['policy_only/' + b]['score'])} & {fin[b]['games']} \\")
    write("s8_final.tex", "\n".join(rows) + "\n")
    rows = [rf"Edax level {k.split('-l')[1]} & {score_ci(v)} & {pct(v['win_rate'])} & {v['mean_margin']:+.1f} & {v['games']} \\"
            for k, v in edax["results"].items() if k.startswith("edax")]
    write("s8_edax.tex", "\n".join(rows) + "\n")

    FIG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.edgecolor": INK2, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
                         "xtick.color": INK2, "ytick.color": INK2})
    # ---- learning curves vs minimax-d4
    cv = _curve(run)

%======================================================================
\section{Scaling to \bx{8}}
\label{sec:scale8}

\glance{\textbf{Question:} does the self-play recipe that produced Oroletto on
\bx{6} carry over to the standard \bx{8} board? \textbf{Answer:} yes. With a
slightly larger network and more search, one 8$\times$8 AlphaZero run
(\EightGames{} self-play games) beats every rule-based bot almost always, and
plays at the level of the Edax engine between its search levels 3 and 5. This
model is now the engine behind every difficulty level of the
\emph{Othello-Player} app.}

\paragraph{Motivation.} Everything so far was studied on \bx{6}, where games are
short and training is cheap. \bx{8} is the board people actually play, and the
one the companion app uses. Moving to it tests whether our conclusions are
artefacts of the small board. It also gives access to an external yardstick:
\emph{Edax}, a world-class open-source \bx{8} engine.

\subsection{Re-baselining the rule-based bots}
The bots' weights had been tuned on \bx{6}, so we repeated the weight search and
the minimax depth sweep on \bx{8} (same protocol as \S\ref{sec:bots}). The best
\bx{8} weights (\EightWeights) are \EightSameWeights{} the \bx{6} ones. This
\emph{refutes} our earlier hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:bots_compare}) that the
heuristic bot falls further behind minimax on larger boards because of
mis-tuned weights. The larger gap must come from the longer games, which give
lookahead more chances to pay off.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.52\linewidth}\centering
\caption{\bx{8} minimax depth sweep against the heuristic bot.}
\label{tab:s8_depth}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rlrr@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & Score (\%) & Nodes/move & ms/game \\
\midrule
\tabinput{report/tables/s8_depth.tex}
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.45\linewidth}\centering
\caption{\bx{8} reference ladder (score of the first-named bot).}
\label{tab:s8_gate}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrl@{}}
\toprule
Match-up & Games & Score (\%) \\
\midrule
\tabinput{report/tables/s8_gate.tex}
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{minipage}
\end{table}

\noindent The ladder random $<$ heuristic $<$ minimax holds on \bx{8}, but
minimax-d4 now beats the heuristic bot almost every game
(Table~\ref{tab:s8_gate}). Our own bots therefore can no longer tell strong
agents apart at the top. That is why Edax is used as an additional yardstick
below.

\subsection{Training setup}
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline,itemsep=2pt]
  \item[Algorithm:] AlphaZero, as in \S\ref{sec:selfplay}: self-play against its
        live copy, with MCTS targets, eight-fold symmetry augmentation and a
        replay window.
  \item[Network:] \EightBlocks{} residual blocks $\times$ \EightChannels{}
        channels (\EightParams{} parameters), slightly deeper than the \bx{6}
        Oroletto (4 $\times$ 64) for the larger board.
  \item[Search:] \EightSims{} simulations per self-play move (64 on \bx{6}),
        because \bx{8} positions have more legal moves.
  \item[Adapted for the board size:] sampling by visit count for the first 20
        plies (10 on \bx{6}), a replay window of 300{,}000 positions, and 200
        training steps per iteration (keeping about four samples per new
        position). Everything else is as on \bx{6}.
  \item[Budget:] \EightGames{} self-play games, taking \EightHours{} hours of
        wall-clock time on 8 CPU cores. Three seeds are planned. This section
        reports seed~0; seeds 1--2 are still to be trained.
  \item[Evaluation:] every 5{,}000 games against minimax-d4. At the end:
        against random, heuristic and minimax-d4, both with search and as the
        network alone, and against Edax at four search levels.
\end{description}

a853a89 report: scaling to 8x8 section

I added the 8×8 results to the report as a new section 8, "Scaling to 8×8" (now pages 36–40 of report.pdf), and committed it (a853a89). It compiles cleanly with no undefined references, and I checked each page visually.

What the section covers: - Why scale up: 8×8 is the board people play and the one the app uses, and it lets us measure against the Edax engine. - Re-tuning the rule-based bots: the best 8×8 weights are identical to the 6×6 ones. That rules out our earlier idea that the heuristic bot falls behind on bigger boards because its weights were tuned for 6×6. Minimax depth 4 now beats the heuristic bot 98.9% of the time, so our own bots can no longer separate strong agents. That's why Edax is needed. - Training setup: 6 blocks × 64 channels, 150 simulations per move, 100,096 games in 52.4 hours. A short note explains the tiny-number (denormal) slowdown and why the run was restarted. - Results: - The learning curve with search beats minimax depth 4 at the first check (5,000 games) and finishes at 96.6%. - Without search, the network alone finishes at 64.4% against it. - Against Edax the score drops from 98% at level 1 to 14% at level 8, which puts the model between Edax levels 3 and 5. - App difficulty levels: explains the temperature-only design. The temperature table and figure show: - temperatures below about 0.5 barely weaken the model; - even at T=4 it still beats the heuristic bot 62.5% of the time; - a move takes 0.42 s on average and 0.52 s at worst. - Shipping: the ONNX model, manifest and parity test data sent to the app. - Limitations: the results come from one training seed, and Edax played without its opening book.

I also added a row for 8×8 to the Summary of Findings table, rewrote the 8×8 item in Next Steps as the remaining work (seeds 1–2, finalising levels), and updated step 5.9 in PLAN.md.

Still open: the check that plays the four chosen levels (Easy T=8, Medium T=2, Hard T=1, Master T=0) against each other hasn't produced results yet. Until it does, the report shows a "verification running" box. When it finishes, the results table will appear in the report automatically once I regenerate the report tables. I'll then mark the levels as calibrated, or adjust the temperatures if any level beats the one below it less than 70% of the time.

safe. PPO uses the same opponent pool as DQN+, and only the learner's own moves
are used for updates, so the data stay on-policy.

\paragraph{AlphaZero.} Following \cite{silver2018}, a single residual network
$f_\theta(s) = (\mathbf{p}, v)$ outputs a move distribution $\mathbf{p}$ and a value
$v\in[-1,1]$. It has 4 residual blocks of 64 channels (about 0.3\,M parameters),
and its input planes are own discs, opponent discs and legal moves. Moves are
chosen by \emph{Monte Carlo tree search} (MCTS) guided by the network. Each of
the 64 simulations per move descends the tree by the PUCT rule
\[
  a^\ast = \arg\max_a \Big[\, Q(s,a) + c_{\text{puct}}\, P(s,a)\,
  \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1+N(s,a)} \Big],
\]
where $Q$ is the mean value of the simulations through $(s,a)$, $P$ the network's
prior, $N$ visit counts and $c_{\text{puct}}=1.5$. The leaf is evaluated by the
network rather than by a random rollout. In self-play, Dirichlet noise is mixed
into the root priors, and the first 10 plies are sampled in proportion to visit
counts to diversify the games; after that the most-visited move is played. Each
position stores its visit distribution $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ and the final result
$z$. The network is trained on a sliding window of the latest 150{,}000 positions
to minimise
\[
  \mathcal{L} = (z - v)^2 \;-\; \boldsymbol{\pi}^{\top}\log \mathbf{p} \;+\; c\,\lVert\theta\rVert^2 ,
\]
and each batch is transformed by a random one of the 8 board symmetries. The key
idea is that \emph{search acts as a policy-improvement operator}. MCTS with the
current network plays better than the network alone, and the network is then
trained to imitate the search. The next search starts from a better prior, and
so on.

\subsection{Common setup for training and evaluation}
\label{sec:selfplay_setup}

Only partly. Section 5.2 (the "AlphaZero" paragraph, report.tex:953–978) covers the mechanics but not the reasoning you're asking about.

What it already says: - the network outputs move probabilities p and a value v; - the search formula used to pick which move to explore (PUCT), with Q as the mean value of the simulations through a move; - leaf positions are scored by the network instead of random playouts; - the first 10 plies are sampled by visit count, after which the most-visited move is played; - the loss trains v toward the final result z and p toward the visit distribution π; - one line saying "search acts as a policy-improvement operator".

What it doesn't explain: 1. Why the move is the one with the most visits, not the highest Q. Visit counts follow Q: the search keeps sending simulations to a move only while its average stays high, and the exploration bonus shrinks as 1/(1+N). A move with few visits has a Q averaged from one or two network evaluations, so it's noisy. Picking the highest Q would favour moves that just got lucky, because the largest of several noisy estimates is biased upward. A high visit count means the move's value held up under repeated checking. If its average had dropped, the search would have moved its simulations elsewhere. So "most visited" is the robust decision. 2. Why averaging makes the values robust. Minimax backs up the max or min of its leaf scores, so one badly misjudged leaf can decide the move. Q is the mean over many network-evaluated leaves, which smooths out the network's individual errors. That's why a good-but-imperfect network plus search is strong. 3. Why training on the visit distribution π works. The visit distribution is a better policy than the network's own p, because it has been improved by lookahead. It's also a full distribution over moves rather than a single chosen move, which gives a richer training target. Imitating it pulls the network toward what search found; the next search starts from a better prior, and the loop repeats. 4. The value target. v is trained on the actual game result z (a Monte Carlo target). Unlike the DQN family, it doesn't bootstrap from its own estimates, which ties in with the bootstrapping problems discussed in §4. 5. Temperature. The 8×8 app section (§8.4) uses temperature (moves picked with probability ∝ N^(1/T)), but §5.2 never connects it to "pick the most-visited move".

"""PUCT Monte Carlo tree search, batched across many independent games.

Each simulation descends every tree once, collects the leaves that need a
network evaluation, evaluates them in a single forward pass, then expands and
backs up. Values are always from the perspective of the player to move at the
node; since Othello alternates the side to move on every action (passes
included), a value flips sign at each step up the tree.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import math

import numpy as np
import torch

from othello.rl.alphazero.net import FastEncoder


class Node:
    __slots__ = ("state", "moves", "P", "N", "W", "children", "expanded", "terminal", "value", "sumN")

    def __init__(self, state):
        self.state = state
        self.moves = None
        self.P = self.N = self.W = None
        self.children = None
        self.expanded = False
        self.terminal = False
        self.value = 0.0
        self.sumN = 0


def terminal_value(env, state):
    """Exact result for the side to move at a terminal state."""
    d = env.score(state) * (1 if state.player == 0 else -1)
    return 1.0 if d > 0 else -1.0 if d < 0 else 0.0


class Evaluator:
    """Batched network evaluation: priors over legal moves and a value per state."""

    def __init__(self, env, net):
        self.env, self.net = env, net
        self.enc = FastEncoder(env)
        self.calls = 0

    @torch.no_grad()
    def __call__(self, states):
        self.calls += 1
        x = torch.from_numpy(np.stack([self.enc.encode(s) for s in states]))
        logits, v = self.net(x)
        logits = logits.numpy()
        out = []
        for i, s in enumerate(states):
            moves = self.env.legal_moves(s)
            lg = logits[i, moves]
            p = np.exp(lg - lg.max())
            out.append((moves, (p / p.sum()).tolist()))
        return out, v.numpy().tolist()


class MCTS:
    def __init__(self, env, evaluator, c_puct=1.5, dirichlet_alpha=0.5, noise_frac=0.25, rng=None):
        self.env, self.ev = env, evaluator
        self.c_puct, self.alpha, self.eps = c_puct, dirichlet_alpha, noise_frac
        self.rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()

    def _expand(self, node, moves, priors):
        node.moves = moves
        node.P = priors
        node.N = [0] * len(moves)
        node.W = [0.0] * len(moves)
        node.children = [None] * len(moves)
        node.expanded = True

    def _select(self, node):
        sq = self.c_puct * math.sqrt(node.sumN + 1)
        best, best_i = -1e9, 0
        N, W, P = node.N, node.W, node.P
        for i in range(len(P)):
            n = N[i]
            u = (W[i] / n if n else 0.0) + sq * P[i] / (1 + n)
            if u > best:
                best, best_i = u, i
        return best_i

    def search(self, roots, sims, add_noise):
        """Run `sims` simulations from each root (Node). Returns the roots."""
        env = self.env
        fresh = [r for r in roots if not r.expanded and not env.is_terminal(r.state)]
        if fresh:
            outs, _ = self.ev([r.state for r in fresh])
            for r, (moves, pri) in zip(fresh, outs):
                self._expand(r, moves, pri)
        if add_noise:
            for r in roots:
                if r.expanded and len(r.moves) > 1:
                    noise = self.rng.dirichlet([self.alpha] * len(r.moves))
                    r.P = [(1 - self.eps) * p + self.eps * z for p, z in zip(r.P, noise)]
        for _ in range(sims):
            pending, paths = [], []
            for root in roots:
                if not root.expanded:
                    continue
                node, path = root, []
                while node.expanded:
                    i = self._select(node)
                    path.append((node, i))
                    child = node.children[i]
                    if child is None:
                        child = Node(env.step(node.state, node.moves[i]))
                        if env.is_terminal(child.state):
                            chi

"""Worked example of one AlphaZero search for the report (Sec. "How AlphaZero works").

  .venv/bin/python scripts/make_az_example.py

Runs Oroletto's search (no root noise, 64 simulations as in 6x6 self-play) on sampled
positions and keeps one where the move with the highest mean value Q is *not* the
most-visited move. Writes results/az_example.json.
"""
import json
import random
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from othello.env import OthelloEnv  # noqa: E402
from othello.rl.alphazero.mcts import MCTS, Evaluator, Node  # noqa: E402
from othello.rl.alphazero.selfplay import build_net  # noqa: E402

SIMS = 64


def main():
    ptr = json.loads((ROOT / "models/oroletto.json").read_text())
    run = ROOT / ptr["path"]
    cfg = json.loads((run / "config.json").read_text())
    env = OthelloEnv(cfg["board_size"])
    net = build_net(env.n, cfg)
    net.load_state_dict(torch.load(run / "model.pt", map_location="cpu"))
    net.eval()
    ev = Evaluator(env, net)
    rng = random.Random(3)
    for _ in range(2000):
        s = env.initial_state()
        for _ in range(rng.randrange(6, 16)):
            if env.is_terminal(s):
                break
            s = env.step(s, rng.choice(env.legal_moves(s)))
        if env.is_terminal(s) or not 4 <= len(env.legal_moves(s)) <= 7:
            continue
        root = MCTS(env, ev, c_puct=cfg["c_puct"], rng=np.random.default_rng(0)).search([Node(s)], SIMS, False)[0]
        q = [w / n if n else None for w, n in zip(root.W, root.N)]
        best_n = max(range(len(root.N)), key=lambda i: root.N[i])
        best_q = max((i for i in range(len(q)) if q[i] is not None), key=lambda i: q[i])
        if best_q != best_n and root.N[best_q] <= 3 and q[best_q] > q[best_n] + 0.05:
            rows = [{"move": env.action_name(m), "prior": p, "visits": n, "q": qq}
                    for m, p, n, qq in zip(root.moves, root.P, root.N, q)]
            rows.sort(key=lambda r: -r["visits"])
            out = {"sims": SIMS, "c_puct": cfg["c_puct"], "model": ptr["path"], "board": env.render(s),
                   "to_move": "black" if s.player == 0 else "white", "black": s.black, "white": s.white,
                   "rows": rows}
            (ROOT / "results/az_example.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=1))
            print(env.render(s))
            for r in rows:
                print(r)
            return
    print("no example found")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

  capture/.style={-{Stealth[length=2.2mm]}, red!75!black, line width=1.6pt, opacity=0.85, shorten >=1.5mm, shorten <=3.2mm},

  coord/.style={font=\large\sffamily, text=black!75},
  halo/.style={white, line width=3.4pt, opacity=0.75, shorten >=1.5mm, shorten <=3.2mm},
}"""


def sq_xy(n, sq):
    r, c = divmod(sq, n)
    return c + 0.5, n - r - 0.5          # row 1 at the top


def name(n, sq):
    r, c = divmod(sq, n)
    return f"{COLS[c]}{r + 1}"


def capture_lines(env, state, move):
    """[(flipped squares in order, anchor square)] for each direction the move captures in."""
    n = env.n
    own, opp = state.own(), state.opp()
    r0, c0 = divmod(move, n)
    lines = []
    for dr, dc in DIRS:
        r, c, run = r0 + dr, c0 + dc, []
        while 0 <= r < n and 0 <= c < n and opp >> (r * n + c) & 1:
            run.append(r * n + c)
            r, c = r + dr, c + dc
        if run and 0 <= r < n and 0 <= c < n and own >> (r * n + c) & 1:
            lines.append((run, r * n + c))
    return lines


def tikz(env, state, ghosts=(), new=None, flipped=(), arrows=(), illegal=(), scale=0.62, label_mover=False):
    n = env.n
    L = [r"\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=%s, every node/.style={transform shape}]" % scale]
    L.append(rf"\fill[board] (0,0) rectangle ({n},{n});")
    for i in range(1, n):
        L.append(rf"\draw[grid] ({i},0) -- ({i},{n}); \draw[grid] (0,{i}) -- ({n},{i});")
    L.append(rf"\draw[feltdark, line width=1.2pt] (0,0) rectangle ({n},{n});")
    for c in range(n):

    for r in range(n):
        L.append(rf"\node[coord] at (-0.4,{n - r - 0.5}) {{{r + 1}}};")
    for sq in range(n * n):
        x, y = sq_xy(n, sq)
        if state.black >> sq & 1 or state.white >> sq & 1:
            L.append(rf"\node[shadow] at ({x + 0.06},{y - 0.07}) {{}};")
            L.append(rf"\node[{'bdisc' if state.black >> sq & 1 else 'wdisc'}] at ({x},{y}) {{}};")
    ghost_style = "ghostb" if state.player == BLACK else "ghostw"
    for sq in ghosts:
        x, y = sq_xy(n, sq)
        L.append(rf"\node[{ghost_style}] at ({x},{y}) {{}};")
    for sq in flipped:
        x, y = sq_xy(n, sq)
        L.append(rf"\node[flipmark] at ({x},{y}) {{}};")
    if new is not None:
        x, y = sq_xy(n, new)
        L.append(rf"\node[newmark] at ({x},{y}) {{}};")
    for a, b in arrows:
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = sq_xy(n, a), sq_xy(n, b)
        L.append(rf"\draw[halo] ({x0},{y0}) -- ({x1},{y1});")
        L.append(rf"\draw[capture] ({x0},{y0}) -- ({x1},{y1});")
    for sq in illegal:

        L.append(rf"\draw[illegal] ({x - 0.28},{y - 0.28}) -- ({x + 0.28},{y + 0.28}) "
                 rf"({x - 0.28},{y + 0.28}) -- ({x + 0.28},{y - 0.28});")
    L.append(r"\end{tikzpicture}")
    return "\n".join(L)

cat > /tmp/claude-1001/-home-palak-raisinghani-my-courses-OthelloRL/bdad683d-7fba-464a-be96-7414ac7e0812/scratchpad/az.tex <<'EOF'
\paragraph{AlphaZero.} Following \cite{silver2018}, a residual network proposes
moves and evaluates positions, and a tree search guided by the network chooses
the move actually played. The network is trained to reproduce what the search
found. Because AlphaZero is the strongest method in this report and the engine
of the app, \S\ref{sec:az} explains how it works and why.

\subsection{How AlphaZero works}
\label{sec:az}

\paragraph{The network.} A single residual network
$f_\theta(s) = (\mathbf{p}, v)$ reads the board from the side to move (planes:
own discs, opponent discs, legal moves). It outputs a \emph{prior}
$\mathbf{p}$, a probability for every legal move, and a \emph{value}
$v\in[-1,1]$, the expected result for the side to move ($+1$ win, $-1$ loss).
On \bx{6} it has 4 residual blocks of 64 channels (about 0.3\,M parameters).
The network is a fast \emph{intuition}: one forward pass, no lookahead.

\paragraph{The search.} Before each move, AlphaZero runs a fixed number of
\emph{simulations} (64 in \bx{6} self-play) of Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS).
Every edge $(s,a)$ in the tree stores a visit count $N(s,a)$, the sum $W(s,a)$
of the values backed up through it and its prior $P(s,a)$. One simulation has
three steps:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Select.} From the root, repeatedly follow the move maximising
  \[
    a^\ast = \arg\max_a \Big[\, \underbrace{Q(s,a)}_{\text{evidence}} +
    \underbrace{c_{\text{puct}}\, P(s,a)\, \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1+N(s,a)}}_{\text{exploration bonus}} \Big],
    \qquad Q(s,a) = \frac{W(s,a)}{N(s,a)},
  \]
  until reaching a position not yet in the tree. $N(s)$ is the number of
  visits to $s$ and $c_{\text{puct}}=1.5$. An unvisited move has $Q=0$.
  \item \textbf{Expand and evaluate.} The network evaluates the new position
  once. Its prior initialises the new edges, and its value $v$ is the score of
  the simulation. No random playout is played, unlike classical MCTS.
  \item \textbf{Back up.} $v$ is added to $W$ and $N$ is increased by one on
  every edge of the path, flipping the sign at each ply because the side to move
  alternates.
\end{enumerate}
$Q(s,a)$ is therefore the \emph{average} value of all the simulations that went
through $a$. The exploration bonus is large for moves the network likes but the
search has rarely tried, and it shrinks as $1/(1+N)$ once a move has been
checked. Early on, simulations follow the prior. As evidence accumulates, they
follow $Q$.

\paragraph{Choosing the move: most visits, not the highest average.} After the
search, AlphaZero plays the \emph{most-visited} root move, not the one with the
highest $Q$. The two usually agree, but the visit count is the more robust
signal. A move's $Q$ is an average of network evaluations, and with few visits
it is noisy. Taking the largest of several noisy averages favours the move whose
estimate happens to be too high, typically one with very few visits: the
maximum of noisy estimates is biased upward. A visit count cannot be inflated
this way. The search keeps sending simulations to a move only while its average
\emph{stays} high under repeated checking. A move whose early estimate was lucky
loses its simulations as soon as more evidence pulls its average down. So a high
visit count means ``this move held up'', and the most-visited move is a vote
weighted by both evidence and confidence.

\paragraph{Worked example.} Table~\ref{tab:az_example} shows Oroletto's search
on a real position (Fig.~\ref{fig:az_example}), run at the self-play budget of
64 simulations and then repeated with far larger budgets.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \emph{A lucky average.} At 64 simulations d6 has the highest $Q$, from a
        single visit. Picking the highest average would play it. With more
        search its average falls well below the two main candidates, and it

832b76f report: how AlphaZero works

I added a new subsection 5.3, "How AlphaZero works" (pages 22–24), and committed it (832b76f). The report compiles with no errors or undefined references, and I checked the new pages visually. The old AlphaZero paragraph in "The methods" is now a short lead-in that points to it.

What it covers: - The network: a fast "intuition" that gives a probability for each move and a value for the position, with one forward pass and no lookahead. - The search: the three steps of each simulation (select, expand and evaluate, back up), showing that Q is the average value of all simulations through a move. The exploration bonus shrinks as 1/(1+N), so the search follows the network's prior at first and the evidence later. - Why the most-visited move is played, not the highest Q: the largest of several noisy averages is biased upward, and usually belongs to a move with very few visits. A visit count can't be inflated that way, because the search only keeps visiting a move while its average holds up. - Why averaging is robust: minimax backs up the best child at every node, so one misjudged leaf can decide the move. Averaging partly cancels the network's errors and still approaches the minimax value as visits concentrate on the best reply. This is why 64 simulations are enough to beat minimax depth 4 (76–79% across the three seeds, which I checked). - Training: the policy is trained toward the visit distribution, so the network learns to predict where the search will put its visits. That explains both "search improves the policy" and why the network alone does well. The value is trained toward the real game result, without bootstrapping from its own estimates as DQN does. - Temperature and noise: temperature controls how the move is picked from the visit counts. The section covers its use in self-play and links it to the app's difficulty levels.

Worked example: a real position searched by Oroletto at 64, 800 and 3,200 simulations, with a board diagram and a table of prior, visits and Q for each move: - d6: it has the highest Q at 64 simulations, from just one visit. Picking the highest average would play it, but with more search its value drops to about +0.6. - a4 vs c5: the network's prior strongly favours a4, and it's still the most visited at 64 simulations even though c5 averages higher. By 3,200 simulations c5 has twice as many visits, so the evidence overrules the network.

The example is generated by a new script, scripts/make_az_example.py. It searches sampled positions for one where the highest-Q move isn't the most-visited one, then writes the board diagram and the table, so every number in the example comes from the real model.

\noindent Every step clears the 70\% target, including the lower end of its
95\% CI, so the ladder is accepted and shipped as calibrated. The levels also
line up with the rule-based bots, which gives players a familiar reference:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Easy} is roughly as strong as the heuristic bot, and almost
        always loses to minimax-d4.
  \item \textbf{Medium} clearly beats the heuristic bot but loses more often
        than not to minimax-d4.
  \item \textbf{Hard} beats minimax-d4 most of the time.
  \item \textbf{Master} is the unweakened model.
\end{itemize}
The steps are not evenly spaced: Easy to Medium is the smallest gap. Easy still
beats a random player almost always, because even at $T=8$ it samples only
among moves its search visited, and the search rarely visits blunders. A true
beginner level would therefore need a different weakening (for example fewer
simulations or a random move now and then). We kept temperature as the only
knob, as decided, and the four levels already span from heuristic-bot strength
to the full model.

No experiments are running right now. The background job that was training the 8×8 seeds 1 and 2 was stopped on 13 Oct. Its stop notice came through as a system message with no explanation, and nothing in its log shows a crash or error.

Where it stopped: - Seed 1 was killed after about 20,000 of its 100,000 games, roughly 11 hours in. - Seed 2 never started. - Was seed 1 healthy? Yes. It ran at the same speed as seed 0 (about 2.7 h per 5,000 games), so the earlier slowdown hadn't come back. Its scores were tracking seed 0's: 90.7% against minimax-d4 at 20k games, versus 89–94% for seed 0 at that point.

Everything else is done: - seed 0 trained, evaluated (including Edax) and shipped to the app; - the four difficulty levels verified and shipped as calibrated; - the report updated with the 8×8 results, the AlphaZero explainer and the verified levels.

Still to do: seeds 1 and 2, then a head-to-head against seed 0 to decide whether the shipped model gets replaced.

The training script can't resume a stopped run. The checkpoint on disk only holds the network weights, not the replay buffer or optimiser state. So there are two ways to continue:

  1. Restart seed 1 from scratch, then seed 2 (my recommendation). This keeps all three seeds trained the same way, so they're directly comparable. It costs the 11 hours already spent, and both seeds take about 4.4 days in total.
  2. Add a resume option and continue from the 20k-game checkpoint. This saves about 11 hours. The replay buffer would start empty and refill, so seed 1's training would differ slightly from seeds 0 and 2. I'd mark that in the report.

# Compatibility-graph pipeline (replaces SPEC §7.2 on-demand composer)

Decided by the product owner after M3. Outfits are **precomputed**, not composed per request.

## Stages
1. **Pair generation (code).** Only slot-valid pairs (`SLOT_PAIRS` in `slots.ts`): dress+shoes, top+bottom, outfit+earrings, ...
2. **Rule scoring (code).** `pairScore()` = colour harmony, formality, season, style/occasion overlap, neckline-to-jewellery, pattern rule, metal tone. Score ≥ `GOOD` → settled good; ≤ `BAD` (or a hard fail) → settled bad; between → **uncertain**.
3. **Vision judge (LLM, batched).** Only uncertain pairs. Batches of N pairs with both thumbnails; returns `{score, reason}` per pair. Stored with `source='vision'`.
4. **Beam search (code).** Assemble full outfits around each hero piece (dress / onepiece / top+bottom / outerwear). Beam keeps top-K partial outfits by mean pair score + whole-set penalties (too many statement pieces, mixed metals, pattern clash) because individually good pairs can clash as a set.
5. **Curator (LLM).** Picks the best 3–5 looks per hero from the beam finalists; writes title + reasoning.
6. **Critic (LLM with tools).** Tools: `view_item(id)`, `check_pair(a,b)`, `validate_outfit(items)`. 1–2 revision rounds; may replace items, never invent ids.
7. **Store.** `pair_scores`, `looks`, `wardrobe_graph_stats` (orphans = items with no good pair; gaps = slots whose best pairs are weak).

## Incremental updates
Each pair row stores a `fingerprint` (hash of both items' scoring-relevant tags). A new or edited item changes its fingerprint, so only its own pairs are re-scored; looks containing it are marked stale and regenerated. Anchor requests become lookups against `looks` (+ a code swap/fallback when none exist).

## Guardrails kept from the spec
- LLMs only see/return ids from supplied sets; all output is Zod-parsed and re-validated by `validate.ts`.
- Every call goes through `ai/client.ts` (caps, logging). Precompute jobs count toward the global spend cap.
- Hard gates from §11.2 still apply, now measured on stored looks.

## Cost controls (open decisions, defaults chosen)
- Vision judge only on the uncertain band; max `MAX_VISION_PAIRS_PER_RUN` per job (default 150) — the rest stay rule-scored until the next run.
- Hero pieces processed in recency order; critic runs once per hero.
# Decisions

- M0: Scaffolded manually (not create-next-app) into the existing repo dir; Tailwind v4 (CSS-first, no tailwind.config); shadcn/ui configured via `components.json` — components are added on demand with `npx shadcn add`.
- Spec file lives at `SPECFashion.md`; `CLAUDE.md` refers to it.
- AI keys: v1 uses a single server-side `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (owner's key) for all users. A per-user key (BYOK) may come later, so `src/lib/ai/client.ts` (M3) must resolve the key through one function, `getAnthropicKey(userId)`, which today returns the env key. All AI calls go through that client, so nothing else needs to change. Per-user keys would be stored encrypted server-side, never exposed to the browser. Spend caps and `llm_calls` logging stay keyed by `user_id`, so they keep working either way.
- M2: Uploaded-but-untagged items are stored with `slot = category = 'untagged'` (columns are NOT NULL in the spec schema); the tagger (M3) overwrites them. The closet shows an "Untagged" tab.
- M2: Background removal is opt-in (checkbox, default off) because it downloads a large WASM/ONNX model on first use; any failure or 45s timeout falls back to the plain photo.
- M2: Uploads go through server-issued signed upload URLs (`/api/items/upload-urls`) scoped to the caller's own folder; `POST /api/items` re-downloads the original and validates it with `sharp` (JPEG, long side ≤ 1032px, ≤ 10 MB).
- M2: Unauthenticated `/api/*` requests get a 401 JSON response instead of a redirect.
- M3: Photos the tagger rejects are NOT deleted. They stay as `untagged` with `items.rejection_reason` set (migration 4), appear in the Untagged tab with an "Edit" badge,

The scoring rules give jeans nearly the same score with every partner, and those pairs never reach the vision model, which is the only part that looks at the images. I worked this out from the code (src/lib/styling/config.ts, pairScore.ts); I haven't checked your stored jeans pairs.

Why the scores come out the same: 1. Colour: if one item in a pair is neutral, the pair gets a flat 0.9. Blue jeans almost always count as neutral, either tagged "navy" or low in colour saturation. Colour is 40% of the score and also scales the whole result, so it decides most of the outcome. 2. Other factors: formality (casual vs casual), season and occasion match for nearly every top, so they add almost the same amount to every pair. 3. No image check: the pairs land above the 0.75 "good" line, so they're filed as settled and never sent to the vision judge. Only the uncertain band gets looked at. 4. Missing tags: the tags can't express what makes jeans work with one top and not another: fit (skinny, straight, wide-leg, baggy), wash (light, mid, dark, black), top length and fit, proportion, and style family (minimal, street, indo-western).

What I suggest, in three layers

1. Make the app selective now (no new data). - Add tags for fit, length, wash or shade, and style family, plus proportion rules such as "wide-leg + fitted or cropped top" or "skinny + relaxed top". - Treat denim as its own colour family, with a score that rewards light/dark contrast, instead of a flat "neutral 0.9". - Have the vision judge rank all of an item's candidate partners in one call (best to worst), instead of scoring pairs one at a time. Language models give compressed absolute scores, around 0.7–0.8 for anything reasonable, but they're much more discriminating when they compare options side by side. This also fixes the problem that "good" pairs are never checked. - Rescale scores per item (relative to its other candidates), so selectMatches sees real gaps.

2. Learn style from curated outfit data (a stable base). - Sources: public datasets of outfits put together by people, such as Polyvore Outfits (about 68k outfits) and Alibaba's iFashion/POG (about 1M outfits). - Model: fine-tune an image model built for fashion, such as FashionCLIP or Marqo-FashionSigLIP, to predict whether two items go together. Export it to ONNX, the same approach as the Othello model, and run it in Node via transformers.js. That keeps SPEC §2.2's "no separate Python service" rule; only the offline training would be in Python. - Cost of use: each item gets embedded once, when it's tagged. After that, each pair's score is a cheap calculation, so every pair can be scored by a learned model from the images, not just the uncertain ones. - Limitation: these datasets are a few years old, so this layer learns lasting style principles, not current trends.

3. Keep up with current trends. - Weekly trend sheet: a weekly job asks Gemini, with Google Search grounding, to summarise current trends into a fixed, validated structure: trending fits and silhouettes, colours, pairings that are in or out. It's saved with a version number. This uses the provider you already have, and its cost is a few calls a week. - Re-scoring: the trend version goes into the judge prompt and into the pair fingerprint (as the prompt version already does), so pairs are re-scored automatically when trends change. - Optional extra signal: the Pinterest Trends API (official, needs a business account) for rising search terms. Avoid scraping Instagram, retailers' "shop the look" pages or Vogue Runway: their terms of service forbid it. - Personal layer: your own likes and wears (SPEC M7) tune all of this to your taste.

How to tell whether it worked: pick about 10 anchor items, such as the jeans. For each, you rank its partners by hand. Then measure how spread out the app's scores are and how closely its ranking agrees with yours. That's a short addition to evals/, and every change above can be checked against it.

Recommendation: do layer 1 first. It's a few days of work and directly fixes "jeans score the same with everything". Then the trend sheet (layer 3), since it's cheap and fits the current setup. The learned model (layer 2) is the largest piece and is worth planning separately.

Turn 81

CAN WE MAKE A rl MODEL THAT OBSERVES THE OPPONENTS PLAYS AND FINDS OUT WEEKNESSES ?
Claude's response

Yes, and this project already has the pieces for it. I checked on seed 1 first: it's still training normally and isn't affected by any of this.

What it would look like

1. Opponent model + search (my recommendation) - Watch: collect the opponent's moves from past games and train a small network to predict which move it plays in a given position. It starts from Oroletto's policy network, so it needs few games to adapt. - Exploit: today, Oroletto's search assumes the opponent plays its best reply. In the exploiting version, the search instead expects the replies this opponent actually tends to play. It then looks for lines where this opponent tends to go wrong, such as giving away a corner or misplaying the endgame. - Safety: if the model of the opponent is wrong, the exploiter can itself be punished. So it may only choose a move whose value, judged the normal way, is within a small margin ε of the best move. Exploiting can then gain a lot but cost at most ε. We measure the gain against weak opponents and check that nothing is lost against strong ones.

2. Exploiter training (AlphaStar-style) - A fresh agent is trained by RL only against one frozen target until it finds that target's weaknesses. - It's powerful, but each target needs a full training run, and it only works offline. This was Phase 6, which you cancelled.

3. Weakness report (comes free with option 1) - Compare each of the opponent's moves with a strong engine (Edax, which is effectively perfect near the end of the game). - Group the costly mistakes by game phase and by concept: corners, X-squares, mobility, parity. - Output: for example, "loses about 6 discs per game in the endgame, often plays X-squares early". In the app this could become a coach mode that tells human players their weaknesses.

Where it would actually pay off

The opponents need to have weaknesses we can still exploit: - On 8×8: Oroletto already beats minimax-d4 97% of the time, so there's little left to gain. Edax level 5 (42%) and level 8 (14%) leave plenty of room. - Edax without its opening book is deterministic. It always plays the same move in the same position, so an agent that watches it can find a winning line once and repeat it. That's a striking result: beating level 8 by exploitation, which plain strength can't do. - On 6×6: Oroletto beats minimax-d4 only 78% of the time, so there's room there too, and experiments are cheaper. - Built-in test opponents: the bots and the app's temperature levels each have a known style (greedy one-move, horizon effects, random choices among good moves), so we can check whether the weakness report finds the right weakness.

Main measures: - Exploitation gain: the exploiter's score minus normal Oroletto's score against the same opponent. - Adaptation speed: how many observed games it needs to adapt. - Safety: its score against a strong opponent it misjudges, which should not drop.

Compute: seeds 1–2 are using the CPUs until about 18–19 Oct. Building and testing on 6×6 can run alongside, but slows the seeds slightly. The large 8×8 runs should wait.

This would be a new phase in PLAN.md, and as usual I'd settle the design with you before running anything.

Two questions that shape the design: 1. What's the main goal? More wins for the research (exploiting bots and Edax), or a feature for the app (coaching humans on their weaknesses, or a level that adapts to the player)? 2. When should it adapt? Within a single game, from a few moves, which needs a starting guess about the opponent type. Or across games, from a history of games, which is much easier and gives stronger results.

I checked the Phase 7 plan in PLAN.md against the current code. One thing changes the design.

The current networks can't run on another board size at all. Their output layers are sized for a single board (the policy head flattens a 2×n×n map into a fixed layer). So step 7.1 as written ("evaluate the 8×8 network on 6×6 and 10×10") would only show that it doesn't run. A real zero-shot test needs the new size-agnostic network trained on one size, then tested on the others.

Proposed design

Network: the same 6 blocks × 64 channels as on 8×8, with output heads that work at any size: - policy head: one score per square from a 1×1 convolution, plus a pass score computed from pooled features; - value head: the board is averaged down to one vector (global pooling) before it.

The same weights then run on 6×6, 8×8 and 10×10. Each training batch uses a single board size, so no padding or masking is needed.

Runs, each given the same compute rather than the same number of games (a 10×10 game costs about 2.5 times an 8×8 one):

Run Trains on Purpose
S (specialist) 8×8 only zero-shot baseline: test on 6×6 and 10×10 without ever seeing them
M (mixed) 6, 8 and 10 together, from the start does one network learn all sizes?
C (curriculum) 6, then add 8, then add 10 does small-to-large beat mixing?

Evaluation: a train × test matrix, with the three runs as rows and the three board sizes as columns. That's the headline result. - Opponent: minimax-d4 on every size. The heuristic bot is too weak to separate strong agents. - Specialist comparison: head-to-head against the size specialists we already have, 6×6 Oroletto and 8×8 seed 0. This answers "does one network match a specialist?" - 10×10: no specialist exists for it, so it's measured against minimax only.

Compute and timing: - Per run: about 60 hours, roughly one 8×8 seed. - Total: S + M + C is about 7.5 days of CPU after seeds 1–2 finish on 19 Oct, which fits the plan's 2.5 weeks. - Before then: the code (network, multi-size self-play) and short test runs can be done now, at a small cost to seed 2's speed.

Claude's response

You asked whether we could build an RL model that watches an opponent's games and finds its weaknesses. I proposed a design for that.

The idea

Today Oroletto plays the same way against everyone: it assumes the opponent always plays its best move. An opponent-modelling version would learn how this particular opponent plays and use that against it.

  1. Watch: collect the opponent's moves and train a small network to predict which move it plays in a given position. It starts from Oroletto's own policy network, so it adapts from relatively few games.
  2. Exploit: in Oroletto's search, the opponent's turns use the moves this opponent actually tends to play, rather than assuming its best reply. The search then finds lines where this opponent tends to go wrong, such as giving up a corner or misplaying the endgame.
  3. Stay safe: if the model of the opponent is wrong, an exploiting agent can be punished. So it may only choose a move whose normal evaluation is within a small margin of the best move: a small worst-case cost for a potentially large gain.
  4. Weakness report (a by-product): compare the opponent's moves with a near-perfect engine (Edax) and group its costly mistakes by game phase and type, such as corners, X-squares or mobility. For example: "loses about 6 discs per game in the endgame and plays X-squares too early."

Where it would pay off

  • Edax level 8: Oroletto scores only about 14% against it. Without its opening book Edax always plays the same move in the same position, so once an exploiter finds a winning line it can win every game by repeating it. Raw strength can't do that.
  • Edax level 5 (42%) and minimax-d4 on 6×6 (78%) also leave room to gain.
  • Known test opponents: the rule-based bots and the app's temperature levels each have a known style, so we can check whether the weakness report identifies the right weakness.
  • Not useful: 8×8 minimax-d4, which Oroletto already beats 97% of the time.

Measures: how much more it wins than normal Oroletto against the same opponent, how many observed games it needs to adapt, and whether it holds its score against strong opponents.

For the app: it could become a coach mode that tells players their weaknesses, or a level that adapts to the player.

Two decisions shape it

  1. Goal: more wins for the research (exploiting bots and Edax), or an app feature (coaching or adaptive difficulty)?
  2. When it adapts: across games, learning from a history of games (simpler, and gives stronger results), or within a single game, from a few moves (harder; it needs a starting guess about what kind of opponent this is)?

My suggestion: start with the research version, adapting across games, on 6×6 first because it's cheap, then try Edax on 8×8. The 6×6 work can start alongside the seed training at a small cost to its speed. As with the other phases, I'd write the steps into PLAN.md and agree them with you before running anything.

"""`othello` — play Othello in the terminal against bots or trained models."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import random
import sys
import textwrap
from pathlib import Path

from othello.agents.heuristic import HeuristicAgent, HeuristicWeights
from othello.agents.minimax import MinimaxAgent
from othello.agents.random_agent import RandomAgent
from othello.env import BLACK, WHITE, OthelloEnv

# Tuned on 6x6 (results/baselines/heuristic_tuning.json).
TUNED = HeuristicWeights(disc=1, mobility=5, corner=50, xsquare=-25)

LEVELS = {
    1: ("beginner", "plays uniformly random legal moves", lambda env, s: RandomAgent(env, seed=s)),
    2: ("easy", "grabs as many discs as it can (greedy)",
        lambda env, s: HeuristicAgent(env, HeuristicWeights(disc=1, mobility=0, corner=0, xsquare=0), seed=s)),
    3: ("medium", "greedy, values corners and mobility",
        lambda env, s: HeuristicAgent(env, TUNED, seed=s)),
    4: ("hard", "alpha-beta search, 3 moves ahead", lambda env, s: MinimaxAgent(env, depth=3, weights=TUNED, seed=s)),
    5: ("expert", "alpha-beta search, 5 moves ahead", lambda env, s: MinimaxAgent(env, depth=5, weights=TUNED, seed=s)),
}
LEVEL_NAMES = {name: k for k, (name, _, _) in LEVELS.items()}
COLS = "abcdefghijklmnop"

# The project's final trained model. models/oroletto.json points at its run
# directory once it exists: {"path": "...", "board_size": N, "about": "..."}.
FINAL_MODEL_NAME = "Oroletto"
FINAL_MODEL_POINTER = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "models" / "oroletto.json"
# Interim suggestion until Oroletto is trained (strongest classical-RL model so far).
INTERIM_MODEL = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "results/classical/dqn/seed0"


def load_oroletto(env):
    import json
    from othello.models import load_model
    if not FINAL_MODEL_POINTER.exists():
        raise ValueError(
            f"{FINAL_MODEL_NAME} has not been trained yet. It will be the project's final self-play model.\n"
            f"  For now, try the strongest model so far:  othello --model {INTERIM_MODEL}\n"
            f"  or the strongest bot:                    othello --play expert")
    info = json.loads(FINAL_MODEL_POINTER.read_text())
    path = Path(info["path"])
    if not path.is_absolute():
        path = FINAL_MODEL_POINTER.parents[1] / path
    if info.get("board_size") and info["board_size"] != env.n:
        raise ValueError(f"{FINAL_MODEL_NAME} plays {info['board_size']}x{info['board_size']}; "
                         f"use --size {info['board_size']}")
    agent = load_model(path, env, sims=info.get("play_sims"))
    agent.name = FINAL_MODEL_NAME
    return agent

61	\begin{abstract}
62	Othello has simple rules, but its strategy is deep and often counter-intuitive. Moves that bring high immediate rewards can prove to be harmful later, and moves that seem to be of no great immediate value can prove extremely beneficial later on in the game. Othello is thus a strong benchmark to prove capabilty in learning delayed rewards.
63	This project tests several different Rule Based and RL models on their ability to learn how to play Othello. Finally we develop a solid model for the game and offer an attractive interface to play the game against our RL-build Model that we call \textit{Oroletto}.
64	
65	\end{abstract}

70	
71	\section{Why Reinforcement Learning for Games}
72	\label{sec:whyrl}
73	
74	\subsection{Games as reinforcement-learning problems}
75	\hspace{2em} Reinforcement learning studies agents that learn to act by trial and error, in
76	order to maximise a cumulative reward \cite{sutton2018}. They learn better policies while interacting with the environment. To do so they balance exploration and exploitation. This project looks at the classic board game of Othello and trains a RL model for the same. Historically, programmers developed rule-based bots which operated on handwritten rules.\\
77	For complicated games, like chess, this was hard and a tree search based approach was adopted. These bots were capable of choosing optimal actions at each step but were very computationally expensive. \\
78	With the advent of RL, games and especially board games found a new player. Board games offer two
79	things that real-world RL problems rarely do:
80	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
81	  \item \textbf{A perfect, free simulator.} Rules are exact and games can be
82	        replayed millions of times, so data is limited only by compute.
83	  \item \textbf{Self-play.} An agent can play against copies of itself. It then
84	        always faces an opponent of its own strength, which produces an
85	        automatic curriculum without human data.
86	\end{itemize}
87	Games are also hard in a way that makes them useful benchmarks. The reward is
88	\emph{sparse} and \emph{delayed}: a single number after dozens of moves. The
89	learner must therefore solve the \emph{credit-assignment problem}, which is
90	working out which earlier moves caused the result. State spaces are also far too
91	large to tabulate, so the agent has to \emph{generalise} from positions it has
92	seen to positions it has not.
93

479	three rule-based bots. The question is not only how well each method plays, but

482	\subsection{The Traditional RL Methods}
483	\label{sec:classical_methods}
484	
485	\paragraph{Tabular Q-learning \cite{watkins1992}.} Keeps a table entry $Q(s,a)$
486	for every state--action pair it has visited and updates it toward a bootstrapped
487	one-step target:
488	\[
489	  Q(s_t,a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t) + \alpha\big[r_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a') - Q(s_t,a_t)\big].
490	\]
491	The $\max$ makes it \emph{off-policy}: it learns the value of the greedy policy
492	while it behaves $\varepsilon$-greedily. To give the table its best chance, each
493	position is stored in a canonical form under the 8 symmetries of the board, so
494	symmetric positions share one entry. Unvisited entries read as 0.
495	
496	\paragraph{SARSA \cite{rummery1994}.} Identical to Q-learning except that the
497	target uses the action $a_{t+1}$ the agent \emph{actually} took next, i.e.
498	$r_{t+1} + \gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})$. It is therefore \emph{on-policy}: it values
499	the exploring policy itself, including its exploratory mistakes.
500	
501	\paragraph{First-visit Monte Carlo control \cite{sutton2018}.} Does not
502	bootstrap. After the game ends, every visited pair is moved toward the observed
503	return $G_t$ (here the final result) by a sample average,
504	$Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a) + \tfrac{1}{N(s,a)}\,[G_t - Q(s,a)]$. Its targets are
505	unbiased but have high \emph{variance}: each one is a single noisy game outcome
506	that depends on every later move by both players. (Positions never repeat within
507	an Othello game, so first-visit and every-visit MC coincide.)
508	
509	\paragraph{Linear function-approximation Q-learning.} Replaces the table with a
510	weighted sum of features, $Q(s,a)=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(s\!\oplus\!a)$,
511	where $s\!\oplus\!a$ is the \emph{afterstate}: the position right after the
512	learner's move. The features are disc difference, mobility difference, corner
513	difference, X-square difference, stable-edge-disc difference and a bias, each
514	scaled to roughly unit range. The weights are learned by semi-gradient
515	Q-learning, $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha\,\delta_t\,\boldsymbol{\phi}$.
516	Unlike a table, it \emph{generalises}: every position with similar features gets a
517	similar value, even if it has never been seen. But it can only represent
518	evaluations that are linear in those features.
519	
520	\paragraph{Vanilla DQN \cite{mnih2015}.} Replaces the table with a neural network
521	$Q_\theta$: an MLP with two hidden layers of 256 units over three input planes
522	(own discs, opponent discs, legal moves). It outputs one value per square plus
523	pass. Two components stabilise training:
524	an \emph{experience-replay} buffer (200k transitions, sampled uniformly), which
525	breaks the correlation between consecutive positions, and a \emph{target
526	network} $Q_{\theta^-}$, synced every 2{,}000 updates, which keeps the bootstrap
527	target from chasing itself. The loss is
528	$\mathrm{Huber}\big(Q_\theta(s,a) - [r + \gamma\max_{a'\,\text{legal}} Q_{\theta^-}(s',a')]\big)$.
529	Illegal actions are masked both when acting and in the max. Unlike the linear
530	model, the network can learn its own features from raw discs.
531	
532	\paragraph{Disc-count ablation (linear FA).} To test the disc-count trap
533	(\S\ref{sec:concepts}) on a learner, the linear method is trained three more
534	ways: without the disc feature, with \emph{only} the disc feature (plus bias),
535	and with the full feature set but rewarded by the final \emph{disc margin}
536	instead of win/loss.
537

541	All five methods (and the ablation variants) are trained and evaluated under
542	exactly the same conditions. Only the learning algorithm differs.

2011	\section{Summary of Findings}
2012	\label{sec:summary}
2013	
2014	Table~\ref{tab:summary} collects the answer to each study's question. Read
2015	together, the studies tell one story: \emph{what an agent learns is determined
2016	by whom it plays and how well it can look ahead}.
2017	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
2018	  \item Fixed opponents freeze the learning target, and weak or mismatched
2019	        opponents give games that teach little.
2020	  \item An evenly matched opponent that keeps improving, which is exactly what
2021	        self-play provides, keeps every game informative.
2022	  \item Without search, every policy is capped by the horizon effect. Search is
2023	        what lets AlphaZero break through, both when it plays and as the target
2024	        its network learns from.
2025	\end{itemize}
2026	
2027	\begin{table}[H]
2028	\centering
2029	\caption{The questions this report asked, and the answers.}
2030	\label{tab:summary}
2031	\small
2032	\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}p{0.27\linewidth}X@{}}
2033	\toprule
2034	Question & Answer \\
2035	\midrule
2036	How strong are simple rule-based players? (\S\ref{sec:bots}) &
2037	A clear ladder: random $<$ heuristic $<$ minimax. Corners and mobility carry
2038	the heuristic's strength; disc count adds almost nothing. A few plies of
2039	lookahead are worth more than any reweighting. \\
2040	\addlinespace
2041	Can traditional RL learn Othello from a fixed opponent? (\S\ref{sec:classical}) &
2042	Only partly. Tabular methods never see most positions twice. Monte Carlo control
2043	memorises lines against its trainer. Linear features cap out at the heuristic's
2044	level. DQN is best, but loses heavily to minimax. \\
2045	\addlinespace
2046	Is a learner limited by its fixed opponent? (\S\ref{sec:frozen}) &
2047	Yes, but not as a hard cap. The target freezes once it is beaten, and the
2048	learner specialises in its opponent's style. Self-play beats every
2049	fixed-opponent DQN head-to-head. \\
2050	\addlinespace
2051	Which self-play method is strongest? (\S\ref{sec:selfplay}) &
2052	AlphaZero, by a wide margin. It beats minimax-d4 about 78\% of the time, and
2053	even its network alone draws level with minimax-d4. DQN+ and PPO only match the
2054	best fixed-opponent learner. The winner is released as \emph{Oroletto}. \\
2055	\addlinespace
2056	Does a league of weak opponents help DQN? (\S\ref{sec:league}) &
2057	No. Strength falls as the league share grows: lopsided games teach little, even
2058	about the league's own members. \\
2059	\addlinespace
2060	Do co-evolving populations beat self-play? (\S\ref{sec:coevo}) &
2061	No. They are equal at equal experience per agent and weaker at equal total
2062	compute. They are no more diverse and show no cycles: identical learners make
2063	interchangeable opponents. \\
2064	\addlinespace
2065	Does the recipe scale to \bx{8}? (\S\ref{sec:scale8}) &
2066	Yes. One AlphaZero run beats every rule-based bot and plays between Edax levels
2067	3 and 5. It now drives all four difficulty levels of the Othello-Player app,
2068	which are weakened only by the move temperature. \\
2069	\bottomrule
2070	\end{tabularx}
2071	\end{table}
